items.title: Perú ratifica a Julio Velarde por cinco años más en el banco central
body: Read the story in English En uno de los países con mayor inestabilidad política del mundo, un banquero central ha sobrevivido gobierno tras gobierno como ancla de estabilidad económica, sin que ninguno se haya atrevido a correr el riesgo de perderlo.

Diez presidentes han pasado por Perú desde que Julio Velarde asumió al frente del banco central en 2006. Desde entonces, su influencia se ha extendido mucho más allá del ámbito técnico de la política monetaria. El economista de 74 años recibe ovaciones de estudiantes universitarios y líderes empresariales, es celebrado por figuras de las redes sociales e incluso es imitado por comediantes.

Incluso ahora, con Keiko Fujimori, favorable a los mercados, en el poder y con mucho menos riesgo de que la jubilación de Velarde desate el tipo de pánico entre inversionistas que siguió a la elección de Pedro Castillo en 2021, le pidieron que se quedara. Aceptó y este miércoles fue ratificado por el Senado.

Tras ganar la presidencia en su cuarto intento y por un margen extremadamente estrecho, Fujimori actuó con rapidez para enviar una señal de continuidad y confianza. Una de sus primeras reuniones como presidenta electa fue con Velarde, a quien pidió permanecer otros cinco años en el cargo. Reemplazarlo habría añadido una fuente innecesaria de incertidumbre.
Seguir en el puesto, a su vez, prolonga la influencia de Velarde y lo deja en posición de ayudar a definir su eventual sucesión durante el que probablemente será su último mandato.

“Si hubiera habido más estabilidad, su permanencia en el cargo no hubiera sido tan necesaria”, dijo la economista Liliana Rojas-Suárez, directora de la Iniciativa para América Latina del Center for Global Development. “Es un poco el temor de los políticos de perder esa ancla”.
Velarde, que nunca se casó y no tiene hijos, ha convertido al banco central en algo muy parecido a la misión de su vida.

Bajo su liderazgo, Perú ha mantenido la inflación bajo control con una de las tasas de interés de referencia más bajas entre las economías emergentes. El sol cotiza aproximadamente al mismo nivel frente al dólar que hace un cuarto de siglo, mientras que las reservas internacionales han aumentado hasta representar cerca de 30% del producto interno bruto.

Lo que distingue a Velarde, según Rojas-Suárez, es su rechazo a aplicar una fórmula única. En lugar de depender principalmente de las tasas de interés, como hacen muchos otros bancos centrales, adaptó la política monetaria a un desafío particular de Perú: ser una economía parcialmente dolarizada.

Eso implicó permitir que el sol flotara, al tiempo que acumulaba un amplio colchón de reservas internacionales e intervenía en el mercado cambiario cuando era necesario. Esas reservas sirvieron de amortiguador financiero durante episodios de turbulencia como la crisis financiera global de 2008 y la pandemia. Cuando aparecieron presiones inflacionarias tras esta última, Perú estuvo entre los primeros países en reaccionar y elevó las tasas de interés incluso antes que la Reserva Federal.

“Si hay algo que unifica a los peruanos es el miedo a la inflación”, dijo Rojas-Suárez, al recordar la hiperinflación que sufrió el país a finales de la década de 1980 y comienzos de la de 1990. “Julio se ha vuelto el representante de esto”.

Después de dejar el poder en 1990 con una inflación de 3.000%, Alan García regresó a la presidencia en 2006 con la necesidad de reconstruir su credibilidad económica. Recurrió a Velarde y lo nombró por primera vez al frente del banco central.
“En ese momento, Velarde ya tenía prestigio”, dijo Jorge del Castillo, quien fue primer ministro de García, y agregó que el nombramiento también tenía un componente político de inclusión.

A comienzos de ese año, Velarde había encabezado el programa económico del conservador Partido Popular Cristiano, cuya candidata presidencial, Lourdes Flores Nano, quedó en tercer lugar con un importante respaldo del sector empresarial. Formado en Alemania y EE.UU., Velarde había estado vinculado al partido desde su juventud, en la década de 1980, dijo Flores Nano.
“Siempre llevaba la voz cantante en materia macroeconómica”, dijo. “Siempre muy técnico y muy brillante”.

En la década de 1990, Velarde asesoró al primer titular de Economía del expresidente Alberto Fujimori, padre de Keiko, cuyas reformas orientadas al mercado ayudaron a sacar a la economía peruana del colapso y a abrir el país a los mercados internacionales. Durante esos años, Velarde también enseñó en una universidad local y formó parte del directorio del banco central. Regresó al mismo a comienzos de la década de 2000.
Quienes lo conocen describen a un hombre tan cómodo hablando de ópera y literatura como de política monetaria.

La trayectoria de Velarde le ha dado una combinación poco común de experiencia técnica e instinto político. De carácter mesurado, ha evitado en gran medida las controversias. Una de las pocas excepciones ocurrió en 2008, cuando fue criticado tras sugerir que los habitantes de los barrios más pobres de Lima cultivaran verduras en sus azoteas para mitigar el alza de los precios de los alimentos.

Sus explicaciones técnicas pueden ser difíciles de seguir para quienes no son economistas, en parte porque tiende a atropellar las palabras y a dejar frases inconclusas. Sin embargo, su serenidad y credibilidad suelen compensarlo.
“El nivel de confianza alcanzado por este hombre es tan alto que usted puede no entenderle, pero supone que está bien lo que está diciendo”, dijo Del Castillo.
Traducción editada por Malu Poveda.
Nota original: Ten Presidents, One Central Banker: Velarde Prevents Peru Chaos

items.title: Ukraine War: Putin Must Be Convinced Ending Conflict Is His Best Bet
body: Last week’s visit to Ukraine by US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner appeared to achieve little: After they left Kyiv, Russian missiles again struck the Ukrainian capital, killing civilians and damaging homes, a school and a clinic. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s blunt forecast that the war looks set to continue into the winter was less a rejection of diplomacy than frank acknowledgement of its limits.

The real problem is that Kremlin officials still envisage a Ukraine that’s smaller, militarily weaker and denied the alliances that could deter a new invasion. Russian President Vladimir Putin hasn’t abandoned his bet that continued fighting will weaken his opponent, yield more territory and exhaust Western backers. Before any peace proposals can gain traction, the White House first needs to disabuse Putin of this faith that time is on his side.

Facts on the battlefield clearly won’t be enough. So far this year, Russia has failed to achieve a decisive breakthrough despite thousands of Russian casualties a week. Instead, Putin has intensified attacks on civilians and infrastructure: July brought the highest level of civilian casualties since the early months of the full-scale invasion. Russia has also stepped up sabotage, cyberattacks and other operations against European infrastructure.

Ukraine is raising Russia’s costs in return. Deep strikes have disrupted refineries, logistics and grain exports. Zelenskyy recently warned commercial airlines and insurers that “Russian airspace is becoming completely unsafe.”

The problem is that Putin can also see Ukraine’s weaknesses, starting with a critical shortage of ballistic missile defenses. With civilian targets — and in particular the energy grid — vulnerable to massed missile and drone salvos, the Kremlin can convince itself that one more winter of brutal attacks will finally break the will of Ukrainians. Meanwhile, a rumored partial mobilization this fall could produce tens of thousands of new troops to feed the meat grinder along the front lines. Putin has little incentive to compromise until he sees the results of those efforts.

The task for Ukraine’s backers, including the US, is to ensure they fail. That must start with air defenses, especially US-made Patriot interceptors. US inventories are reported to be dangerously low after heavy expenditure in the Iran conflict. Ukraine says deliveries of air defense missiles have fallen to roughly one-third of 2025 levels this year, even as Russia is accelerating its own ballistic missile production.

European countries with existing Patriot stocks should release more of them. The US should, too. Scarcity is real, but that is also an argument for allocating marginal weapons — for which Europe is paying — where they will have the greatest strategic effect. Even a modest US contribution would cast doubt on Russia’s plans for a winter air offensive.

Economic pressure also needs to be intensified. New Russia sanctions legislation, passed by Congress this week, will help strengthen leverage at the bargaining table; the White House should make wise use of it. Both the US and Europe should also target the banks, refineries, traders and service providers doing the most to enable Russian sanctions evasion.

None of this is a prescription for endless war. As Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski has argued, failing to challenge Putin carries greater risks for Europe and North Atlantic Treaty Organization allies than acting. Deterring Russia from further aggression reduces the risk of a wider, costlier conflict that could eventually draw in the US.
The Russian leader will bargain in earnest only when he sees fighting on as a losing move. If the US truly wants to promote peace, it should be doing everything it can to hasten that day.

items.title: DoorDash, Uber Expand Costco Delivery Partnership in the US
body: DoorDash Inc. and Uber Technologies Inc. are expanding their delivery partnership with Costco Wholesale Corp., ratcheting up competition with Instacart as the big-box retailer expands its digital reach.

DoorDash users will be able to order same-day service from every US Costco warehouse starting Thursday, the delivery-app company said in a statement. An active Costco membership is required and can be linked within the DoorDash app.

Costco has been a major holdout for DoorDash in the US, where users of the app have been known to frequently type in “Costco” as a search term, according to the delivery company. DoorDash already works with the retailer in other markets, including Australia, New Zealand, Sweden, Iceland and Puerto Rico.

The highly requested addition comes a day after Uber also announced an expansion of its existing Costco delivery partnership to 47 US states, up from 17. The growing availability of Costco on third-party delivery apps increases the competition for rival Instacart, which was one of Costco’s first third-party partners. Instacart continues to work with Costco   in other areas, including fulfillment and building Costco’s e-commerce website.

Across the retail sector, e-commerce is accounting for an increasing chunk of consumer spending, and major chains are offering on-demand deliveries for a wider range of goods. Walmart Inc., for example, ships restaurant food, while Kroger Co. can drop off prescriptions.

At the same time, online delivery remains an area that’s notoriously expensive due to transportation and labor costs, and companies are looking for ways to make their digital businesses more profitable.

Costco, the largest warehouse club chain in the US, has been expanding its online footprint primarily through a string of partnerships. While it’s playing catch-up with competitors that are further ahead with their digital offerings, Costco’s e-commerce business is growing faster than core merchandising sales. Traffic to both its website and mobile app have been on the rise.
Read More:   Costco Reports Higher-Than-Expected Profit Amid Rising Sales

The company has generated strong sales growth in recent years, attracting price-conscious households with its popular Kirkland store brand and bulk-size selections. Like most retailers, it’s seeking to deliver orders faster and is introducing more personalized product recommendations to deepen customer loyalty. Costco has said younger people are signing up for memberships online partly due to these efforts, though they typically renew at a lower rate.

items.title: Democrats' Chance to Flip the Senate Is Growing - But Not Certain
body: Figuring out why Democrats are poised to score a massive upset in the battle for control of the US Senate doesn’t require the computational power of AI: Gas costs more than $4 per gallon on average; diesel is running $6-plus; ground chuck is roughly $7 a pound — and a Republican occupies the White House.

These economic storm clouds, combined with most voters blaming President Donald Trump for the bad weather, have transformed Democrats from early longshots to flip the GOP’s 53-47 majority to fashionable underdogs seven weeks out from Election Day. DDHQ, a nonpartisan campaign handicapper with a stellar track record, is now projecting a Democratic takeover, as are Kalshi and Polymarket. Conditions for Republicans have deteriorated so much that Kansas, which hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate in almost 100 years, is now in play.

Perennially red states Alaska, Iowa, Ohio and Texas are also hosting unusually competitive Senate contests for the Trump era. Then there’s purple North Carolina, where Democrats are favored, as well as blue Maine, where Republican Senator Susan Collins is mired in yet another tossup campaign. And don’t even bother with Georgia. Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff is headed to victory in the Southern battleground after Republicans long since cut bait.

With the final primary contest having concluded in Delaware this week, I dialed up pollster John Anzalone to get a better sense of how Democratic political professionals view the Senate terrain. He specializes in guiding candidates running for office in red states, and his resume includes advising former President Joe Biden’s winning 2020 presidential campaign and collaborating with Republican (and Trump) pollster Tony Fabrizio on a series of bipartisan Senate race surveys this election cycle. So, what stands out to Anzalone in the data?

The generic ballot gauging voters’ party preference for control of Congress has jumped from a 4-percentage-point Democratic advantage on Jan. 1 to 8 points today. That edge resembles voter attitudes in past Democratic wave elections. Simultaneously, the GOP’s favorability rating has plunged and is now on par with Democrats, whose brand with voters had been in the political cellar for quite some time. Perhaps most importantly, Democrats are outpacing Republicans on two key “diagnostics” that tend to foreshadow elections: They’re romping among independents and winning “double-haters” — voters fed up with both political parties.
“The diagnostics are very good,” Anzalone told me. “We win when they lose, and they’re losing spectacularly. Trump and the Republicans keep giving us gift after gift after gift.”

Disenchantment with both parties could also motivate split-ticket voting, possibly boosting certain Democrats in Georgia, Iowa, Texas and other states with overlapping gubernatorial and Senate contests. “I think that drives voters, in this environment, to maybe start thinking: ‘It’s not about party anymore; it’s about the candidate,’” Anzalone explained.

As much trouble as Republicans are in, their Senate majority is protected by a ruby red firewall that seemed all but impenetrable just a little over six months ago. To bust through on Nov. 3, Democrats will need to catch every break they can get, while limiting self-inflicted wounds to near zero.

Democrats’ only road to the majority lies in flipping four seats in hostile Republican territory. And the party has to do it while managing not to fritter away a Senate seat in swing-state Michigan, where Democrat Abdul El-Sayed is underperforming; while defending a seat in New Hampshire from John Sununu, a Republican made formidable by his famous family ties; and while stopping Collins from pulling yet another political Houdini act. That’s not to mention the party’s aggregate financial disadvantage.
So Democratic partisans should be cautiously optimistic, with an extra emphasis on “cautiously,” about the party’s chances of capturing the Senate.

To be sure, veteran Republican operatives I talk to regularly concede that Trump’s brittle position with voters has poisoned the political well for the GOP as the midterm elections approach. Private surveys produced by some of the best Republican pollsters in the business are painting a similarly bleak picture, despite the president and some grassroots conservatives’ views that the party’s precarious standing is the product of bias, fake news or faulty surveys.

But it’s only mid-September and Anzalone isn’t satisfied, having learned over the years what a durable lead in the polls looks like. As he detailed in our conversation, a candidate’s lead, and the margin of that lead, can be less important than vote share. Anzalone said he’ll breathe easier if Democrats still look strong in mid-October, and if the data shows their vote shares just below or at the 50% threshold (if not above it.) According to that metric, Democratic Senate nominees like Iowa’s Josh Turek, Maine’s Troy Jackson, Michigan’s El-Sayed and New Hampshire’s Nick Pappas have work to do.
“We don’t want to get ahead ourselves,” Anzalone said. “I’m not comfortable with a lead if they’re at 46% or 47%. Get up there at 49% and 50%. That’s what I look for.”

In some ways, Election Day has all but arrived. Absentee ballots begin making their way to voters in dozens of states this month, and Democrats already appear on the cusp of an improbable One Shining Moment in November. But look through an unfiltered lens, and the extent of the party’s challenges to take control of the Senate clarifies.

items.title: Canada's Tech Startups Head to the US, and Carney Wants Them Back
body: When Miles Schwartz co-founded payment company Zūm Rails Inc. in Montreal in 2019, he knocked on almost every Canadian venture capitalist’s door looking for funds. They all turned him down.
So by 2024, Zūm Rails was working on a US expansion, and Schwartz moved to Miami. The company raised C$10.5 million ($7.5 million) from US-based growth equity firm Arthur Ventures LLC that year.
“We tried raising with Canadian VCs,” said Schwartz, 35. “American VCs were hungrier, faster — between them reaching out to us, getting a term sheet was like literally one week.”

Zūm Rails is one of many Canadian startups that have moved to the US to expand over recent years. Workplace tool Slack was conceived in Vancouver but moved to San Francisco before it was acquired by Salesforce.com Inc. for $27.7 billion in 2020.

A survey earlier this year by tech community organization TechTO found that of 48 Canadian Y Combinator founders who responded, 91% initially incorporated in Canada and 75% later established a US entity.
But now the problem is getting fresh attention from Canada’s government and business leaders, and they’re searching for ways to keep startups at home.

It’s part of a broader effort by Prime Minister Mark Carney to build an economy less reliant on the US, as it reels from President Donald Trump’s tariffs and threats. The latest part of his strategy was the first-of-a-kind Canada Investment Summit this week, which gathered the world’s top money managers in Toronto.

That summit resulted in a slew of patriotic announcements to rejuvenate Canadian business. Toronto-headquartered Radical Ventures unveiled a new late-stage growth fund with more than $1 billion of capital after an initial close, with much of it committed by Canadian pension plans and banks, Bloomberg News reported earlier.
Carney said that new fund will “help Canadian AI companies scale up and stay Canadian.”

Canada has produced successful technology companies thanks to its highly educated workforce, government incentives, and a still-growing VC scene. But with the exception of firms like Shopify Inc., the country has struggled to create global tech firms, and has nothing on the scale of Apple Inc. or Alphabet Inc.

Aidan Gomez, co-founder and CEO of Canada’s top artificial intelligence firm Cohere Inc., said in an interview that there’s been a lack of Canadian options for growth funding, and bigger Canadian companies “haven’t really supported and bought from the local ecosystem.”
“These two things really pull companies south,” he said.

With a population roughly one-eighth the US’s, Canadian firms have fewer domestic customers. But what’s more, the US also has a greater propensity to keep investing in “high-stage risk” companies, said John Ruffolo, founder of Maverix Private Equity.

In 2022, about a third of seed rounds in Canada had purely Canadian investors, but that fell to just 9% in later rounds, according to a report from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development.

“There’s been a turning of the back on the entrepreneur over the past 10 or 15 years,” Robert Janson, chief investment officer of Toronto-based Westcourt Capital Corp. said in an interview. The entire business ecosystem — from funding to banking and finding talent to tax — has pushed entrepreneurs to the US, he said.

University graduates “somehow have a perception that if they want to have more success in building a technology company, they are better off in doing so in the United States,” Ruffolo said. “This, to me, is the real alarm bell.”
There is, however, a large pool of capital to be tapped: retirement savings. With more than C$2.8 trillion of assets, Canada’s top pension plans are among the world’s largest institutional investors.

Ruffolo, who founded the venture arm of the Ontario Municipal Employees Retirement System, said there’s been an “implicit bias that the returns and companies are superior outside of Canada” at those firms, he said.

Facing pressure to invest more domestically, the heads of the so-called Maple Eight biggest pension managers have said they’re open to doing so. The idea is not new. Caisse de Depot et Placement du Quebec, for example, has a dual mandate of generating returns and supporting Quebec’s economy.

The pension funds’ involvement in the new Radical Ventures vehicle is sign of a sea change. The new fund — backed by Canada Pension Plan Investment Board, PSP Investments and Ontario’s healthcare employees plan, known as Hoopp — is aimed at creating trillion-dollar companies.

Many founders have pointed out that Canada’s proximity to the US creates a tough competition on tax. The northern nation’s general corporate tax rate is 15%, lower than the 21% rate south of the border. But depending on location, other taxes layer on top of that. And Canada’s personal regime has been regularly criticized for stifling productivity, with some analysts suggesting the highest income bracket kicks in too early.

Tax reform could stem the brain drain, said Andrea Johnson, national corporate group leader at law firm Dentons. “Founders and young entrepreneurs leave Canada for capital availability but also because the US tax environment better calibrates risk and reward,” she said.

On Tuesday, Carney announced a step in trying to change that. Canada is expanding the scope of a major investment tax write-off, adding fiber-optic cables, computer equipment, software and more to the list of assets eligible for accelerated deductions in Canada.

It’s one of the most significant tax changes in decades. The government said the relief will reduce Canada’s marginal effective tax rate on new business investment to 6.4% from 13% — the lowest among Group of Seven countries, and half the rate in the US.
Christian Weedbrook, founder of Toronto-based Xanadu Quantum Technologies Ltd., called the news “fantastic.”

“When I put the lens on being an investor, I see these announcements and think, ‘Well, this is a good country to invest in because of these types of tax announcements,’” he told Canada Investment Summit attendees.
As for Zūm Rails, it continues to grow on both sides of the border.

“Canada shouldn’t measure success by how many companies stay inside its borders,” said Schwartz, the company’s co-founder. “It should measure success by how many Canadian companies become global leaders.”

items.title: Russian Hybrid Warfare Stirs Alarm in Europe
body: Welcome to Balance of Power, bringing you the latest in global politics. If you haven’t yet, sign up here.
To European governments, the past two months have been a watershed for Russia’s malign activities on their territory.
An explosives-laden UAV found at Leipzig-Halle airport near a Ukrainian cargo jet. An armed maritime drone discovered off a Romanian gas project under construction in the Black Sea.
Multiple unexplained suspected arson attacks on weapons makers. Fighter jets scrambled to down drones over NATO airspace.

All these so-called hybrid attacks take place in a gray zone between war and peace, making them easily deniable — and harder for governments at the sharp end to develop a deterrent. To date, a common European or NATO response has been conspicuously absent.

Leipzig may have been a turning point, with the German government publicly calling out Moscow for the incident on Sept. 1. Others go unattributed, however, both to avert escalation and to avoid revealing intelligence methods.

Government officials see Russia undertaking a more aggressive campaign with a higher risk of fatalities as it targets European support for Ukraine in a bid to raise the cost of aiding Kyiv. President Donald Trump’s ambivalence toward NATO only emboldens the Kremlin.
Yet even as tensions ratchet up, there is little sign that Russia is achieving its aims.

Germany’s public response to the Leipzig attack was to reach for soft targets, closing a consulate in Bonn and a Russian cultural center in Berlin. More quietly, it made additional weaponry available to Ukraine and remains Kyiv’s largest foreign backer.

Russia has long been accused of carrying out covert activities on European soil, from disinformation campaigns to targeted assassinations. It regards itself as retaliating against Europe for aiding Ukrainian attacks on Russia.
But what’s being witnessed now is of a different scale, with incidents not just increasing in number but in the scope of their recklessness.
The fear heard across Europe is that it’s only a matter of time until a hybrid attack results in civilian casualties.

Trump floated hitting goods imported from the European Union with fresh tariffs or even cutting off some trade if he determines a push to make Canada an associate of the bloc is harmful to the US. Prime Minister Mark Carney’s effort meanwhile to formalize a deeper relationship with Europe is broadly supported by Canadians, who have grown increasingly disillusioned with Washington and the hostility from Trump.

Saudi Arabia is seeking to return about half the capacity of its cross-country oil pipeline within days after the link was halted last week following drone attacks, a source says. The timelines for the East-West pipeline’s resumption and the volume of oil it can carry for export are being closely watched by traders after Saudi Arabia used it to circumnavigate the severely disrupted Strait of Hormuz.

Sweden’s center-left opposition bloc is projected to narrowly win Sunday’s general election after days of limbo, effectively closing off — for now — the prospect of the far right entering government. With 99% of votes counted, former Prime Minister Magdalena Andersson was on track for 176 seats in parliament to 173 for the incumbent premier, Ulf Kristersson, and his allies.

In one of the world’s most politically turbulent countries, a central banker has endured as an anchor of economic stability. Ten presidents have come and gone in Peru since Julio Velarde took over the central bank in 2006 and along the way, his influence has spread far beyond the world of monetary policy. The 74-year-old economist was confirmed yesterday for another five-year term at the behest of President Keiko Fujimori.

British monarch King Charles III plans to ask some of the most important figures in artificial intelligence for reassurances they can keep their inventions under control just as OpenAI shared several undisclosed incidents of its models misbehaving. Meanwhile, Huawei is accelerating the debut of its next-generation chip by several months to replace Nvidia in China and compete in the global AI stakes.

French far-right leader Marine Le Pen kept open the possibility of a no-confidence vote in the government over the 2027 budget, while at the same time pledging not to take action that would damage the country’s strained finances.

One of Argentina’s most outspoken opposition governors is bringing back a local currency for his province, doubling down on an interventionist economic model just as President Javier Milei tries to convince investors that the country has embraced free markets for good.

Australia’s government is moving to reduce immigration, planning a clampdown on people who have overstayed their visas and restrict most student-visa holders from bringing family members into the country.
Taiwan’s coast guard is planning its first visit to the Philippines in decades, strengthening ties as China boosts naval activity in the region.
In this week’s Trumponomics, Stephanie Flanders is joined by Bloomberg Opinion columnist John Authers and Jamie Rush of Bloomberg Economics to discuss what’s reshaping the price of money.
Sign up for the Washington Edition newsletter for news from the US capital and watch Balance of Power at 1 and 5 p.m. ET weekdays on Bloomberg Television.

Europe is set for one of its smallest potato harvests yet after a succession of heat waves and lingering drought battered the water-hungry staple, the latest blow to the region’s farming industry. The squeeze could soon show up on supermarket shelves in the form of smaller baked potatoes, shorter fries and ultimately higher prices. Searing temperatures that cut yields were compounded by a decline in plantings, following a potato glut last year.

The small Greek city of Kozani in a former lignite coal-mining area is at the heart of plans to build one of Europe’s largest data centers. The €5.8 billion ($6.7 billion) investment to create a technology and clean energy hub is the sort of project that’s spawned protest movements from Sacramento to Scotland. But in Kozani, it’s seen as a potential lifeline for one of Greece’s poorest regions.

items.title: Uganda's Central Bank Hikes Reserve Ratio to Defend Shilling
body: The Bank of Uganda raised the cash reserve requirement for commercial banks as the shilling continues to slide.
Banks will be required to increase their cash reserves to 13.5% from 11% from Sept. 24, the central bank said in a Sept. 15 circular.
The measure will help drain liquidity and stabilize the shilling, Absa Group Ltd.’s Ridle Markus and Phumelele Mbiyo said in a note Thursday.
The shilling has weakened almost 6% in the past month to 3,930 per dollar, making it the worst performing currency in Africa of those tracked by Bloomberg.
Read More: Uganda Shilling Dips to Lowest Since 2024 as FX Demand Soars

“Heightened tensions in the Middle East and global concerns around oil supply have dampened investor appetite for emerging debt markets such as Ugandan debt,” Markus and Mbiyo said. “Such offshore holdings have either been trimmed or covered with FX purchases.”

Also, many of the bonds matured this year increasing liquidity in the market, Gerald Paul Kasaato, the deputy managing director for Uganda’s National Social Security Fund told reporters earlier this week.
Absa also attributed the weakness in the shilling to demand for foreign currency from local companies including in the telecommunications and manufacturing sectors.

items.title: Traders Applaud Warsh's Fight Against Inflation
body: Given a choice between keeping Donald Trump happy or soothing stock and bond investors, Kevin Warsh chose the latter.

The Fed chairman and his colleagues agreed unanimously yesterday to raise interest rates for the first time in more than three years and, after some waffling, investors decided that was a good thing. Stocks are headed higher this morning and the yield on the 10-year US Treasury note is back below 5%.

After all Trump’s jawboning about how rates should be at 1% or less, not 3.75% to 4% as they are now, Warsh still decided that the greater risk was letting above-trend inflation persist. (Trump was still at it after the decision, though he blamed the rest of the Fed board, not his hand-picked chairman.)

For bond traders, that goes a long way to bolstering Warsh’s bona fides as a warrior against higher prices, the enemy of all fixed-income investments. Stock traders are taking comfort in the fact that, by raising short-term rates now and signaling more hikes if needed, the central bank will rein in inflation.
“The market is taking this as a much more credible Fed chair,” Jeffrey Rosenberg, a senior portfolio manager at BlackRock, said on Bloomberg Television. —Phil Serafino
Where will US interest rates peak in a Fed hiking cycle? Let us know in the latest Markets Pulse survey.
So it’s all clear for further gains in the bond market, now that the Fed has committed itself to fighting inflation, right? Well, maybe not.
Although energy prices have been the scourge of bond markets this year, investors are worrying that the next spike in prices will come from food.
They see a risk that a “Super” El Niño, tight fertilizer supplies, attacks on shipping and fallout from Europe’s record hot summer will push the cost of everyday staples higher.

“I think the next supply shock will be on food,” said Marie-Anne Allier, a bond manager at Carmignac in Paris. “I don’t think that’s priced in the market at the moment, especially as we expect it to be slow but persistent.” —George Nixon and Andras Gergely

items.title: Key South African Legislation Stuck in Parliamentary Limbo
body: The process of passing legislation in South Africa has slowed to a crawl, with a number of key bills awaiting approval by parliament years after they were first proposed.

Some 24 laws have been presented to the National Assembly since it reconvened in February and only three — all related to government spending — have been passed, along with eight others that were introduced in previous years, the legislature’s records show.

A presentation made by parliament’s legal advisers to a lawmakers’ panel last month showed it takes an average of 34 months to to pass laws that affect the national and provincial administrations, up from six months in 2004.

A key law that proposes the introduction of support thresholds that political parties will have to meet to qualify for seats on municipal councils is among those caught up in the logjam. The country is due to hold local government elections on Nov. 4, and its approval could smooth the process of forming coalitions in towns where no party wins an outright majority.

Other pieces of legislation that have been held up include the Electronic Communications Amendment Bill, which will overhaul the regulatory framework for the telecommunications industry, a bill that proposes the creation of a single state-owned petro-chemical company, and at least two bills aimed at curbing money laundering and corruption.

Legislators were taking additional time to hold hearings and consider public submissions on key bills and faced logistical constraints, including a shortage of committee rooms following a fire in 2022 that burnt down the National Assembly, the legal advisers said.

They also attributed the delays to changing political dynamics after the 2024 national elections, which saw the African National Congress lose its parliamentary majority for the first time since it took power three decades earlier and enter into a coalition with nine rivals to retain power.

items.title: BOE's QT Plans May Eclipse Rates as Key Decision for Bond Market
body: Bond investors are more focused on the Bank of England’s plan for its quantitative-tightening program for the next year than its interest-rate decision at Thursday’s policy meeting.

Markets are interested in whether the BOE will scale back — or even halt — active bond sales from its balance sheet, while they widely expect rates to stay on hold. Analysts are split on the QT outcome, with any reduction in active sales potentially a tailwind for gilts.

“QT is the bigger market event. The announcement may matter more than rates,” said Mizuho strategist Evelyne Gomez-Liechti. Her base case is for a shift away from active sales to only passive QT, where the BOE lets bonds naturally roll off its books at maturity, which she said would support gilts.
Read more: BOE Set to Hold While Warning on Inflation: Decision Guide

The BOE’s QT program involves unwinding the gilt purchases made under its pandemic-era quantitative easing. These bond sales have come under scrutiny for potentially adding pressure to a market selloff that has taken the UK’s long-term borrowing costs to the highest levels since 1998. The spike in yields has also eroded the government’s fiscal headroom ahead of a budget due next month.

“I do think the lender of last resort will at some point need to step in to support UK government bonds,” said Remi Olu-Pitan, Schroders’ head of multi-asset growth and income. “I think that if we do have a situation where bond yields in the UK continue to rise, action will need to be taken.”

A BOE survey of market participants saw it slowing the pace of its balance-sheet runoff to £50 billion ($67 billion) a year in the 12 months from October. That would imply active gilt sales of about £20 billion. Yet a Telegraph report earlier this week suggested the central bank could halt sales of long-dated debt altogether, sparking fresh debate on the matter.

Morgan Stanley strategists Fabio Bassanin and Luca Salford said that “heavy gilt issuance and declining BOE holdings” has had a more pronounced impact on longer-dated gilts, where demand from pension funds has waned in recent years. They estimate that QT has added 70 basis points onto 30-year yields.
The program has come under fire given sales of long maturity gilts are now being done at a loss, costing the government billions.

Still, any halt in gilt sales might only have a marginal impact as UK debt remains vulnerable to external shocks, such as the conflict in the Middle East driving up oil prices and fanning inflation fears.
Read more: UK’s Post-Truss Efforts to Prop Up Gilts Are Being Overwhelmed

The BOE has already shrunk its portfolio to £489 billion from nearly double that since February 2022. Its stated intention is to sell the whole stock and has three principles guiding the process: that interest rates remain the MPC’s main tool, that sales do not disrupt the functioning of markets, and that they are done in a gradual and predictable manner.
The premium of 30-year gilts over comparable swaps — one gauge of concerns about the supply of bonds — has been broadly steady this year even as yields surged.

Some market participants caution that the BOE may make no drastic change outside of consensus at all, given concerns that altering its sales strategy to accommodate the government’s fiscal needs could raise questions about the central bank’s independence.
Jamie Searle, strategist at Citigroup Inc., said that while a change of approach is possible, he suspects “the status quo to avoid blurring monetary policy control of QT.”

items.title: AI Raises Biological Threats Faster Than Governments Can Respond
body: Anthropic PBC researcher Jacob Coxon quit last week and posted on social media that it was because “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.” Evan Hubinger, who leads the artificial intelligence company’s alignment science team, put the odds above 10% in the next 10 years. Anthropic Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei called for a slowdown in the AI frontier to help mitigate the risks, an idea echoed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and xAI CEO Elon Musk.

You might be imagining doom from killer robots with thick Austrian accents. But the greatest risk comes from cells, not steel. An Institute for Security and Technology survey of 111 national security practitioners found that 70% believe AI meaningfully increases – or soon will -bioweapon risk. Imagine an AI-aided researcher inserting an immune-signaling gene into a poxvirus that suppresses the immune response so thoroughly it kills every unvaccinated animal it infects and most who are immunized.

That’s a nightmare. But it’s not science fiction. It happened more than 25 years ago without any help from AI. Mousepox with the gene for interleukin-4 did exactly that to mice, and it was described in a paper published in the Journal of Virology in February 2001. The Australian researchers who built it weren’t even trying to kill mice; they were just trying to limit mouse reproduction.

The natural world provides aspiring terrorists with plenty of pathogens. Making them worse is something that we can already do, albeit with some difficulty. AI might make the process easier, but it’s never been the primary roadblock. The hard part was taking a virus’s genome (natural or engineered) and turning it into something dangerous. That still needs a lab and trained scientists. And the skills one would need aren’t easily learned from textbooks. They’re what’s called “tacit knowledge,” which has long been thought to require experience and apprenticeship.

In 1917, France asked America to build copies of its 75mm field gun. Even with complete plans, the United States was unable to produce a single copy in the 18 months before the war ended. That’s because the drawings never described the screw threads on the gun carriage, and when Americans measured an actual gun they found six types, none of them used in this instance. As military historian H.A. De Weerd wrote, “the only secret about the French recoil system was the difficulty of its construction.” That’s tacit knowledge.

Over time, tacit knowledge often becomes less important. A factory today could make those guns from emailed files. Although tacit knowledge remains an important safeguard, that process is just beginning in biology. I’ve been concerned about its effects on biological risk since long before AI was a thing. In 2009 I wrote a paper with MIT’s Kenneth Oye and Boston University’s Scott Mohr arguing that synthetic biology was an attempt to minimize the importance of tacit knowledge in bioengineering, and that it could increase biological threats.

AI may have far more impact on the importance of tacit knowledge than synthetic biology ever did. The biologist Roger Brent and RAND’s Greg McKelvey, Jr. argue that we should retire the assumption that tacit knowledge is even required. They showed that foundation models available in 2024 provided “accurate instructions and guidance for recovering a live poliovirus from a construct built from commercially obtained synthetic DNA.” Venture capital firms are also investing in “automated labs” which could, at least in theory, eliminate much of the human skill element in experimental biology and rapidly increase the rate at which experiments can be conducted. That’s great news for defenders, and for anyone who wants medical science to progress more quickly. But without guardrails, it could also be great news for attackers.

One key safeguard is to mandate that any sequence of DNA which is synthesized must be screened for possible use in a pathogen. Today most synthesized DNA is bought from companies, but desktop DNA synthesizers are on the market. Many, but not all, DNA synthesis companies already screen, but a Microsoft Corp.-led team showed that AI protein design tools can already produce sequences the screening software misses, though whether those sequences would still work is unproven.

The federal government currently requests, but does not mandate, screening, and a revised framework has been in limbo for the 16 months since an executive order called for it. It should mandate screening, and DNA screening companies and the frontier AI labs should pool their resources to create bounties to reward anyone who beats AI-based DNA screening. And as automated labs proliferate, they should only work with verified researchers from accredited research institutions and be subject to the same screening requirements.

These are no-lose policies. They’d be a good idea even without AI, and they’re a better one with it. Implementing them would be much easier with federal help. Unfortunately, instead of chipping in, the White House has opposed AI regulation, with President Donald Trump saying that “AI taking over the World, destroying Humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX” and that “The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!”

Just in case that High-IQ President needs some expert advice, it might have been helpful to have it institutionalized within the government instead of dissolving the National Counterproliferation and Biosecurity Center and Homeland Security’s counter-WMD office. The administration even suspended updated screening frameworks that would have closed the loophole letting novel agents through.

Until the government decides to step in, leaders in the private sector will need to fill the gap. Anthropic has already reported blocking five attempts to use Claude for research that could support biological weapons development, and says it can no longer assume its newest models fall below the threshold for meaningful help in building them. Even a minor attack using a biological agent that AI helped develop will surely result in industry-stifling regulation. We should make sure we don’t end up like those Australian mice.

items.title: RBI Drains 500 Billion Rupees of Banking Cash Through Debt Sales
body: India’s central bank sold 500 billion rupees ($5.2 billion) of bonds under its open market operation program as it stepped up efforts to drain surplus cash in the banking system.

The Reserve Bank of India sold bonds as planned in the 2029-2032 tenors, the authority said in a statement. The cutoff prices were in a band of 102.25 rupees to 105.63 rupees, broadly in line with estimates in a survey.
Yields climbed after the auction results, with that on the five-year bond last trading six basis points higher at 6.83%.
The sales were the first tranche of the 1-trillion rupee ($10.5 billion) mop-up announced by the central bank on Sept. 11 using the tool. The other two are scheduled for Sept. 21 and Sept 28.

Excess cash in India’s banking system hit a record 11 trillion rupees earlier this month as a deluge of dollars from a diaspora deposit program led to a surge in cash with lenders. Yields have jumped since the RBI announced the bond sales last week as fears of excess supply weighed on the market.
Read More: Traders Brace for Prolonged India Bond Slump as RBI Mops Up Cash

items.title: Tata Sons to List, Asks Chairman to Stay On to Steady Group
body: Tata Sons Pvt. is said to have approved going public and asked Chairman Natarajan Chandrasekaran to stay on for five more years, as one of India’s biggest business houses tries to keep leadership steady through the transition.

The board proposed heeding the Reserve Bank of India’s directive on pursuing a listing, according to people familiar with the matter. The directors also asked Chandra, as he’s widely known, to stay on to steer the sprawling group, the people said, asking not to be identified discussing internal company matters.
Shares of Tata Group stocks surged. Tata Chemicals Ltd. shares jump as much as 13%, while Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles Ltd. gained 4.7%.

Chandra last month said he plans to leave when his term ends in February 2027. His decision followed months of friction with Tata Trusts Chairman Noel Tata over the listing issue and capital allocation across the sprawling conglomerate.
Representatives for Tata Sons, the holding company of Tata Group, did not immediately respond to an email seeking comments.

The leadership question comes at a sensitive moment. Tata Sons was confronted with a mandatory public float push, which entails tighter regulatory oversight. For Tata Trusts, which own 66% of Tata Sons, a listing risks diluting their control and weakening the board’s ability to fend off hostile takeovers.

The RBI rejected Tata Sons’ earlier plea for an exemption from initial public offer. The RBI had also filed a caveat in the Bombay High Court to ensure its position is heard before any order is passed should Tata Sons seek legal relief.

Meanwhile, minority shareholder Shapoorji Pallonji Group had been advocating for a listing for months, saying it is essential to unlock value for investors. SP Group holds an 18.4% stake worth billions of rupees and a listing would help it monetize its stake and reduce costly debt.
Read More: Tata Sons IPO Order Backs Reclusive Tycoon’s Long-Running Ask

items.title: Clearlake Todd Boehly: Are Chelsea Also-Rans Really Worth £5 Billion?
body: There are far less stressful ways to make a modest profit than dabbling in an English Premier League football club. But financier Todd Boehly must feel some relief to be leaving Chelsea FC without financial injury four years into a tough turnaround. He has handed US buyout firm Clearlake Capital full control — but control only counts for so much when you have limited freedom of movement.

A consortium led by Boehly and Clearlake bought the club debt-free for £2.5 billion ($2.9 billion) from sanctioned oligarch Roman Abramovich in 2022 and later injected £450 million into the business. Clearlake had a majority holding and on Wednesday its co-founders Behdad Eghbali and José E Feliciano agreed a deal to buy 25% held in separate stakes by Boehly and his business ally Mark Walter.

The transaction values Chelsea at £5 billion, according to Bloomberg News. That is more than the combination of the original purchase price, the capital injection and debt-funded investments made in the club. Assume its net borrowings are still roughly in line with the £1.3 billion in the 2024-2025 accounts and the 100% equity value indicated by this sale would be somewhere around £3.7 billion. That’s a comfortable gain on the total £3 billion outlay.

For a deal between co-investors with strained relations, you can see the logic. This is not a market-based valuation, as football consultant  Paul Quinn has pointed out. The junior partners have reasons to want an early exit, given reported strategic differences and Walter’s moves to simplify his empire following regulatory scrutiny. Clearlake previously shared governance with Boehly despite his smaller economic investment. The private equity firm is paying up to get boardroom dominance.

Can the £5 billion figure be rationalized? Soccer club valuations, typically based on revenue multiples, were boosted by the World Cup. Moreover, European football revenue is projected to hit €46 billion ($53 billion) this season, 50% more than in 2021-2022, according to Deloitte’s Annual Review of Football. Billionaire Jeff Bezos’s deal for a minority stake in Liverpool FC was struck at a $6 billion value, Bloomberg News reported, underscoring the trophy status of big-name English clubs. The original Chelsea deal was inked at five times 2021-2022 revenue and this sale is likely to be well above that.

The Chelsea holding company is also a more substantial business since acquiring a majority stake in smaller French side Racing Club de Strasbourg Alsace. Accounts for the 2025-2026 financial year are yet to surface. But to get close to the mooted valuation you have to assume revenue will increase meaningfully from the £540 million made in the previous season and then apply a generous multiple. The wildcard is gains on player trading, where Chelsea has been a prolific dealmaker.

Clearlake has a massive job to finish. The strategy thus far has been to fill the squad with younger players who have more of their career ahead of them. With acquisition costs smoothed out over long contracts, there’s some financial logic to this approach. But results on the pitch have been mixed at best, even with the addition of genuine superstars such as Cole Palmer.

The failure of the men’s team to qualify for the European Champion’s League is a sore point this season. In a sense, the situation is comparable to many leveraged buyouts a few years in, when heavy investment has been made and the payback is lagging, while the sector overall has enjoyed a broader upward revaluation.

And there are only so many levers Clearlake can pull on. Broadcasting income depends on sporting success. Player spending is necessary, but doesn’t guarantee a winning side — as Chelsea shows. The pressure to plow revenue gains back into clubs is relentless for all of them. The Premier League’s aggregate pretax losses were nearly £1 billion last season, per Deloitte. As Boehly told Bloomberg TV last year, the great thing about this league is that it’s so competitive, and that’s the frustrating thing too.

Lucrative team-shirt sponsorship is tied in part to sporting success, and it depends too on attracting digital eyeballs. A key part of the Chelsea investment story is building and monetizing an international fanbase.

There are two other important levers for boosting profit. One would be to rebuild or relocate the Stamford Bridge stadium and sell more tickets, pies and scarves. Whether that is cost-effective or logistically possible remains open to question. Developing or redeveloping large sites in monied West London is a huge challenge. The other lever is cutting costs and wages. Chelsea has had some success in getting rid of high-earning players, but the big stars like Palmer still need juicy contracts.
Clearlake will hope that paying up to end the club’s messy governance will improve decision making. It has its work cut out to give Boehly seller’s remorse.

items.title: Peru's Velarde, Central Banker to 10 Presidents, Confirmed for New Term
body: Lea en español
In one of the world’s most politically turbulent countries, a central banker has endured as an anchor of economic stability through government after government, none willing to risk his departure.

Ten presidents have come and gone in Peru since Julio Velarde took over the central bank in 2006. Along the way, his influence has spread far beyond the technical world of monetary policy. The 74-year-old economist draws standing ovations from college students, business leaders, social media stars and is impersonated by comedians.

Even now, with market-friendly Keiko Fujimori in office and Velarde’s retirement far less likely to spark the kind of investor panic that followed Pedro Castillo’s election in 2021, he was asked to stay. He accepted and, on Wednesday, was confirmed by the Senate.

After winning the presidency on her fourth attempt by the slimmest of margins, Fujimori moved quickly to send a signal of continuity and confidence. One of her first meetings as president-elect was with Velarde, whom she asked to remain for another five-year term. Replacing him would have created an unnecessary source of uncertainty.
Staying, meanwhile, extends Velarde’s influence and positions him to help shape his eventual succession in what’s likely to be his final term.

“If there had been more stability, his staying in office for so long wouldn’t have been as necessary,” said economist Liliana Rojas-Suárez, director of the Latin American Initiative at the Center for Global Development. “There’s this fear from politicians of losing that anchor.”
Never married and with no children, Velarde has made the central bank something close to a life’s mission.

Under his leadership, Peru has kept inflation in check with one of the lowest benchmark interest rates among emerging-market economies. The sol is trading at roughly the same level against the dollar as it did a quarter-century ago, while international reserves have grown to nearly 30% of gross domestic product.

What sets Velarde apart, Rojas-Suárez said, is his refusal to follow a one-size-fits-all playbook. Rather than rely primarily on interest rates, as many other central banks do, he adapted policy to Peru’s particular challenge as a semi-dollarized economy.

That meant allowing the sol to float while building a large stockpile of international reserves and intervening in currency markets when needed. Those reserves became a financial buffer during shocks, including the 2008 global financial crisis and the pandemic. When inflationary pressures emerged after the latter, Peru was among the first countries to respond, raising interest rates even before the Federal Reserve.

“If there’s one thing that unites Peruvians, it’s the fear of inflation,” Rojas-Suárez said, recalling the country’s hyperinflation of the late 1980s and early 1990s. “Julio has become the representative of this.”

After leaving office in 1990 with inflation hitting 3,000%, Alan García returned to the presidency in 2006 needing to rebuild his economic credibility. He turned to Velarde, appointing him to lead the central bank for the first time.
“By then, Velarde already had prestige,” said García’s then-prime minister, Jorge del Castillo, adding that the appointment also carried a political gesture of inclusion.

Earlier that year, Velarde had led the economic platform of the conservative Christian People’s Party, whose presidential candidate Lourdes Flores Nano came in third with significant business sector support. Educated in Germany and the US, Velarde had been linked to the party since his youth in the 1980s, Flores Nano said.
“He was always the leading voice on macroeconomics,” she said. “Exceptionally technical, exceptionally brilliant.”

In the 1990s, Velarde advised the first economy minister under former President Alberto Fujimori, Keiko’s father, whose market-oriented reforms helped pull Peru’s economy back from collapse and opened the country to international markets. During the same decade, Velarde taught at a local university and served on the central bank’s board. He returned to the board in the early 2000s.
Read More: Fujimori Legacy Shows Limits of Trump’s Anti-China Push in Peru
People who know him describe a man as comfortable discussing opera and literature as monetary policy.

Velarde’s background has given him a rare combination of technical expertise and political instinct. Measured by nature, he has largely avoided controversy. One of the few exceptions came in 2008, when he drew criticism after suggesting that residents of Lima’s poorest neighborhoods grow vegetables on their rooftops to help offset rising food prices.

His technical explanations can be difficult for non-economists to follow, not least because he tends to run words together and leave sentences unfinished. Yet his calm demeanor and credibility tend to make up for it.
“The level of trust this man has earned is so high, that you may not understand what he’s saying, but you assume he’s right,” Del Castillo said.
