items.title: Fender Takes On the Electric Guitar Industry Over Stratocaster Copyright
body: Step into Carl Verheyen’s home in Topanga, California, and you’ll see his lifelong commitment to the guitar everywhere you look. “There’s about 30 or 40 guitars under there,” he says, opening a closet door under a staircase. The unused fifth bathroom? “Twenty-two in the shower.” Nearby, shelves hold his 18 solo albums, CDs from a career that’s included sessions with Dolly Parton, Miley Cyrus and the Bee Gees, and magazines with published articles about him. “My ego shelf,” he says with a smile.

Verheyen has a test for every electric guitar he considers buying: Hold it by the headstock at the end of the neck, pluck an open B string, then feel and listen to how the wood vibrates. The guitar speaks or it doesn’t. His collection includes three vintage Fender Stratocasters — one from 1958 and two from the early 1960s. Those vintage Strats have become one of the most recognizable guitar shapes in music: a slim, contoured body with a narrow waist and two sweeping horns reaching up around the neck.

Then there’s his signature model: a Strat-style guitar built by LsL Instruments, a husband-and-wife shop in Santa Clarita, California. It’s the result of a failed courtship with Fender. In 2009, Fender flew Verheyen to its headquarters, then in Scottsdale, Arizona, hoping to build a model based on his 1961 seafoam-green Stratocaster, one of the guitars Verheyen played in arenas with Supertramp. Over a martini lunch, the team proposed a $6,000 limited-edition replica — what Verheyen dismissed as a “lawyer guitar.” He wanted something players could afford. He wanted to work side by side with a builder. Fender put him in touch with its factory in Corona, California. The Corona people referred him back to Scottsdale, saying he needed to deal with corporate first. “It was so lame, I just gave up,” he says.

Then Lance Lerman of LsL called. He listened to what Verheyen wanted and built it — scratches, nicks and Verheyen-specified adjustments included — a near replica of the 1961 Strat that Fender also wanted to re-create. Now, watching Fender and its lawyers threatening LsL and scores of other builders, Verheyen says he’s unlikely to play his Fenders much in public. In the studio, sure, but onstage? “I’m just not sure I want to be seen playing Fender publicly,” he says.

For Fender, the Stratocaster’s greatest triumph has become its greatest vulnerability. The instrument made famous by the likes of Eric Clapton, David Gilmour, Jimi Hendrix and Bonnie Raitt has become so universal that its shape can seem less a design than a fact. The guitar emoji on your smartphone? That’s a Stratocaster. Now, 72 years after Leo Fender introduced the Strat, the company that bears his name is engaged in a messy legal war to claim rights to the world’s most iconic guitar shape.

Fender saw an opening in the German court system and pounced. The company won a ruling last December against a Chinese seller of S-style guitars on AliExpress. It was an easy victory: The defendant never showed, so the court took Fender’s account of the facts as true, ruling in its favor. Fender took that win and ran with it, going after makers and sellers of Strat-like guitars sold in Europe.

The cease and desist letters landed hard. Fender’s law firm, Bird & Bird, sent batches starting in March, hitting 60 companies — small shops including LsL, which started a GoFundMe for its legal fees, and bigger names such as  Yamaha Corp.,  PRS Guitars,  Schecter Guitar Research, Ernie Ball Music Man and Germany’s Thomann GmbH, which calls itself the world’s largest instrument retailer and makes budget S-style guitars under its Harley Benton house brand. Fender told recipients of its letters to recall and destroy the guitars, then send Fender proof the job was done. The backlash was swift, mainly from popular YouTubers and pro players accusing Fender of letting quality slip and instead trying to crush competition and stifle innovation. One prominent session guitarist called it “brand suicide.” In a meeting with dealers that leaked on YouTube, Fender Chief Executive Officer Edward “Bud” Cole tried to clarify Fender’s intentions: The company wasn’t suing anyone, wasn’t asking anyone to destroy inventory and had approached only “a handful” of companies, he said. That did little to quiet the outrage.

The revolt also came from people with something to lose. “We sweat and bleed on these instruments. They’re lifelong friends,” says Mary Spender, a British singer-songwriter and YouTuber with almost 800,000 subscribers. Her concern is that Fender, a brand she loves and has worked with for years, could damage her own. “I know I’m losing work, but I’m not going to be reviewing any of their new models. I need to see them fix this.”

Fixing it, in whatever shape that takes, falls to Cole, a longtime  Fender Musical Instruments Corp. executive who took over as CEO in February with the campaign already in motion. He concedes that Fender should have carried this out differently. “There’s been a lot of introspection about this,” he says, sitting in a Fender conference room in Corona lined with enough Stratocasters to make any player drool. It’s his first interview about the legal campaign. “It’s clear to me that this got ahead of us — the legal process got ahead of us — and that we could have done this better.”
What he doesn’t concede is the claim itself. And, by his account, it’s working.

When Leo Fender introduced the Stratocaster in 1954, players mostly ignored it. Too many contours, too many knobs, too strange for the country pickers loyal to the Fender Telecaster. The Strat had its moments in the 1950s (Buddy Holly holds it on an album cover), but it was the British Invasion — blues-steeped kids sending American music back across the Atlantic — that began turning it into an icon. Clapton was among the converts. Then came the moments that turned it into myth: Bob Dylan going electric with a sunburst Strat at the Newport Folk Festival in 1965; Hendrix playing his white Strat at Woodstock four years later. By the end of the decade, the Stratocaster had stopped being a Fender guitar. It had become the guitar.

Music has of course changed many times over the decades, but the basic designs of the most popular electric guitars have not. At core, the electric guitar is a simple machine: A coiled magnetic pickup sits under steel strings and their vibrations disturb the magnetic field, generating a faint signal that runs to an amplifier and moves a speaker.

The three main guitars of the ’50s started from very different places. The Telecaster (played by Keith Richards and Bruce Springsteen) is the plainest; it’s two single-coil pickups, a near-slab body, a bright tone. The Gibson Les Paul (picture Slash or Jimmy Page) runs two humbucker pickups — paired coils that cancel hum for a thicker, heftier sound. The Stratocaster splits the difference and then some. The traditional version has three single coils and a five-way switch, a glassy sound for the pickup closest to the neck and a brighter tone for the one at the bridge. The Strat’s magic lives in the in-between settings, where two pickups blur into a hollow chime. That’s where you get the pulsing line in Mark Knopfler’s “Sultans of Swing,” the scratchy funk of Nile Rodgers on Chic’s “Le Freak.” And though the Tele and Les Paul anchor their strings to a fixed bridge, the Strat floats its bridge on springs (the whammy bar), letting the player bend every string at once, from a shimmer to a dive.

The Strat’s rise happened with little help from its maker. The same year Dylan went electric, Leo Fender sold the company to CBS for $13 million. Production expanded, the guitars changed, and quality became notoriously uneven. The world’s guitar heroes were making the Strat the instrument to own, but the pre-CBS Strats they played were versions Fender no longer made.

That gap created an industry. By the mid-1970s, Wayne Charvel was making replacement Fender parts in Southern California, while David Schecter opened a shop in nearby Van Nuys devoted entirely to parts. Around 1977, Eddie Van Halen built his striped “Frankenstrat” around a $50 factory-second body bought at Charvel’s shop. It was the hottest guitar around, assembled from parts.

Soon the parts makers became guitar builders. Charvel and Schecter grew into full-fledged manufacturers; Tom Anderson, who ran Schecter’s wood shop, eventually opened his own company. All built variations on the familiar Stratocaster shape without asking permission.

Yet Fender did police its trademarks. In 1989 it went after Anderson — not over his Strat-shaped bodies, but over a headstock he thought was sufficiently different from Fender’s. Anderson told the Fender rep he already had guitars in production and couldn’t simply toss them. No problem, Fender told him — sell them over the next year, and change the design going forward. The headstock was Fender’s, but the body carried no trademark. “We never gave it a second thought,” Anderson says. “These were the shapes of guitars that people wanted, and they were so generic, it never occurred to us that we couldn’t build them.”

The distinction had precedent. Through the CBS years, Fender went after the closest copycats: Japanese brands with names, logos and headstocks a shade too close to its own. In 1985, CBS sold Fender, by then barely alive, to its managers, and in 2002, the company bought Charvel and Jackson, both born in the aftermarket it had once let flourish.

Then Fender tried, for the first time, to claim rights to the Stratocaster body itself. In 2003 it applied to trademark the shapes of the Stratocaster, Telecaster and Precision Bass in the US. The move was initially opposed by 16 builders and one retailer, Anderson and Schecter among them. Six years later, the US Trademark Trial and Appeal Board rejected Fender’s claims, finding that the shapes had become generic. The Strat was so ubiquitous, the board pointed out, that a version of it appeared in a dictionary to illustrate the very idea of an electric guitar.
The attorney who beat Fender was Ronald Bienstock. Today he represents LsL and a dozen other builders and distributors.

This decade has been an especially bumpy one for Fender. The pandemic turned from near disaster to windfall. Locked-down Americans bought guitars in record numbers, and Fender, the market leader, ramped up production. Orders topped $1 billion, more than it could fill, and revenue peaked at about $945 million. Then the boom ended. In 2022 retailers canceled orders of roughly $100 million. Revenue fell to about $840 million by 2024 and stayed relatively flat last year, according to Fender and Music Trades, the magazine the industry relies on for data.

The pressure hasn’t let up. In March 2025, S&P Global Ratings cut Fender’s credit rating deeper into junk, warning that tariffs and weaker consumer spending would squeeze the business and drive its already-high leverage higher. They did: By the end of the year, adjusted earnings had fallen 17% on a 3.5% revenue decline, and leverage had climbed from 5.9 to 7.4 times earnings. S&P revised its outlook to stable earlier this year. Fender had already cut deep, from about 3,900 employees at its 2021 peak to about 3,000 last year, by its own count. In February 2026, a month before the first lawyer letters went out, Fender said 60 more jobs would go in California.

To Fender’s fans-turned-critics, the legal campaign has an obvious author: Fender’s private equity owner, squeezing a struggling company for cash — a handy scapegoat, but untrue. Servco Pacific Inc., the century-old Honolulu-based conglomerate that controls Fender, built its business on auto dealerships. But its ties to Fender go way back. It’s been an investor since 1985, when it helped back the management buyout from CBS. In 2020 it bought out Fender’s private equity co-owner, TPG Growth, taking majority control; Servco’s executive chairman, Mark Fukunaga, also chairs Fender’s board. Servco is a family company with a long horizon, Cole says, not a fund built for a quick flip. “These people are amazing stewards and care deeply about the Fender brand,” he says. “I don’t see that changing for years to come.”

Servco has other interests in the Fender case. In June 2025, Servco and another investor bought Chicago-based Reverb, the world’s largest marketplace for music gear. About 219,000 electric guitars are listed on Reverb at any given moment, just under 18% of them S-style, and roughly half of those used. Music Trades says the vast used market impedes new-instrument sales, although Cole dismisses the idea. “We feel like the industry is healthy for new guitars,” he says, “and we haven’t really seen any effect from that in our business.” The CEOs of both Reverb and Fender stress that Fender gets no preferential treatment.

Which brings us to the key question: Why start this campaign at all? An effort that from the get-go was certain to rankle musicians and the guitar community the world over? Was it not about sales? Cole won’t quite say: “We believe that investing in innovation and creativity makes our business and everybody’s business better and richer.”

Fender has long sought a way to claim legal ownership of the Strat shape. Its lawyers had been tracking European case law — an accumulation of rulings extending copyright, the protection that shields works of art, to everyday industrial objects. A case involving clothing had established that utilitarian designs need not clear some special bar of artistic merit. Another, over a folding bicycle, held that a shape partly dictated by function could still be protected if its designer made sufficiently creative choices. If clothing and bicycles could be copyrighted works of applied art, why not a guitar? The legal theory was different from the US case: the Stratocaster shape not as a brand identifier, but as a work of art Leo Fender had authored.

Fender looked for a place to make its stand. The chamber it chose, in Dusseldorf, had ruled that a modular office shelving system was a protected work of art — a position an appeals court had overturned, and one that was pending before the European Court of Justice. In April 2025, Fender arranged to buy a Chinese-made Strat copy and have it shipped to Germany inside the Dusseldorf jurisdiction. Then, in early December 2025, the European court answered the legal questions raised by the shelving case and sharpened the standard for when an industrial design qualifies for copyright. It was an important setup for Fender.

Just weeks later, the Dusseldorf court ruled for Fender in the default judgment against the no-show Chinese seller, finding that Leo Fender’s aesthetic choices gave the body the character of an authored work of art. The court was required to accept Fender’s account, and its description reads like it: “soft curves that evoke associations with a female torso consisting of hips, waist and arms,” with the body appearing to tilt slightly to the right “like a dancer leaning to one side.”

But winning a default judgment isn’t the same as a victory in a contested case, says Arno Grohmann, an intellectual-property lawyer in Stuttgart who isn’t involved in the dispute. “Fender could just present the facts they want,” Grohmann says. “They have to take the facts as presented by the plaintiff, and this is the basis for the judgment.”
The strategy worked. With the judgment in hand, Fender broadened the fight, and the letters started landing in inboxes.

Lance and Lisa Lerman founded LsL in 2008. The company has a dozen employees and makes about 450 guitars a year — boutique by any measure. To Lisa, the email that arrived on May 11 reads less like a standard legal letter and more like an ultimatum. “I’ve never seen one that was so blatantly aggressive,” she says. What unsettled her most was the broad reach of Fender’s proposal. “What you were agreeing to was that you wouldn’t make them ever, anywhere,” she says.

LsL didn’t sign. Instead the Lermans hired Bienstock and started a GoFundMe for legal fees; it raised $53,765 before the Lermans paused it in early August, deciding they had enough for now. “We’re now famous for being pathetic,” Lisa says, referring to LsL as a tiny shop crowdfunding its defense against one of the most storied names in American music.

The president of Schecter was annoyed but not intimidated. Michael Ciravolo had fought Fender in 2009. “We’ve never used the word Stratocaster or Telecaster — we’re not dumb — and we do separate ourselves,” he says. “I wish Fender, and the industry, would work to fight actual counterfeit guitars, like the bootlegs sold on Alibaba, rather than going after small builders. This is bad juju for the industry.”

Fender’s campaign sparked a backlash it couldn’t contain. The story that took hold was simple and emotionally potent: a giant corporation using a foreign court to crush the small shops that have kept Fender-inspired designs alive. Fender had no competing story ready. Into the vacuum rushed the people who talk to guitarists all day — angry YouTubers with millions of followers.

One letter feels personal. It’s the one sent to PRS Guitars aimed at the Silver Sky, the guitar developed by Paul Reed Smith with John Mayer, a former Fender artist. The Silver Sky was designed to capture the sounds of Mayer’s vintage Fender Strats. Cole won’t discuss the impact of the Silver Sky (the first version was introduced in 2018, followed by a budget SE version in 2022), but the data points must hurt. Some version of the Silver Sky has spent years on Reverb’s bestseller lists, alongside the Fender Stratocaster, the Telecaster and the Les Paul.

The Silver Sky isn’t a Strat replica. The PRS headstock is nothing like Fender’s — it has three tuners on top, three on the bottom, against Fender’s six in a row — and nobody buying one could mistake it for a Strat. What it shares is the body shape. Whether the body alone is enough is the question the whole dispute turns on. Smith and Mayer declined to comment.

For all the noise, the underlying question is narrow and unsettled: Does Fender’s claim actually hold up? The judgment names that it protects the uneven radii of the body’s two S-lines, the left horn elongated so the two horns aren’t a matched pair, the flattened front left side and narrower left rear, the pickguard echoing the body’s curves, and the output jack set parallel to the lower right end of the pickguard.

The Chinese seller later tried to undo the Dusseldorf judgment on procedural grounds, arguing that it hadn’t been properly served. The court dismissed the challenge as inadmissible on June 25, according to a Fender court filing, leaving the judgment intact. But nobody has yet contested the merits.

Thomann intends to do just that. Fender sent it a cease and desist letter over Thomann’s S-style guitars in its Harley Benton line. Thomann executives were caught off guard. As a giant retailer, Thomann has been selling Fender guitars for decades, moving about 10,000 Fender Stratocasters annually.

On March 6, Cole traveled to Treppendorf, in northern Bavaria, where Thomann has been based since 1954. He toured the sprawling campus and had lunch with CEO Hans Thomann, whose father founded the company, and Dominic Wagner, the chief marketing officer.

Wagner described the conversation as open and constructive. Nobody mentioned lawyers. The following Monday, March 9, Fender issued a press release from Dusseldorf announcing the landmark ruling protecting the Stratocaster body design. The same day, a letter reached Treppendorf, citing the judgment and saying Fender would no longer tolerate the sale of non-Fender Strat-style bodies in Europe.

“Many of us are Fender players,” Wagner says. “We were therefore surprised and disappointed by Fender’s recent actions.” Given the meeting three days earlier, he says, Thomann would have welcomed the chance to discuss the matter before receiving a formal legal demand.
Cole, who acknowledged the trip, says, “I won’t comment on any meetings that we had with Thomann.”

Three months later, Thomann asked the court in Nuremberg to declare that Thomann’s Harley Benton S-style guitars weren’t infringing. Fender responded with its own infringement suit back in Dusseldorf. Because of German legal procedure, Thomann now finds itself the defendant in Fender’s chosen venue. (Fender is also in litigation with German bass maker Warwick GmbH over S-style guitars it distributes for a Chinese manufacturer.)

Fender’s first challenge is authorship. To claim copyright, Fender must show that the Strat was created by Leo Fender and reflects his personality through what European courts call his free and creative choices. The company’s own account complicates that story. Its website notes that guitarist Rex Gallion is often credited with the insight that a solid-body guitar didn’t need squared-off edges — “Why not get away from a body that is always digging into your ribs?” he asked Leo — and that a new arrival, Freddie Tavares, sketched out the body shape in the spring of 1953, adapting Leo’s own two-horned shape from the Precision Bass. The Strat, the site concludes, was “in one sense Leo’s baby through and through,” but “in another sense the collaborative work of a remarkable group of designers and musicians.”

That collaboration could also affect Fender’s second problem: proving it owns whatever was created. Under German law, Thomann attorney Rainer Heimler explains, joint authors “can transfer the copyright or grant a right of use only collectively.” If others qualify as authors, he argues, Leo Fender “could not transfer the alleged copyright to his former company without the involvement of the other authors,” complicating every transfer that followed.

Fender says no transfer was needed. Its filing argues that Tavares was employed by Fender Electric Instrument Co. when the Stratocaster was created and that Leo Fender was its managing director and part owner, so the rights sat with the company from the start. The rest, Fender says, is a paper trail. Each time Fender changed hands — to CBS, then to investors in 1985, then to its current ownership — the intellectual property went with it. Fender has put purchase agreements before the Dusseldorf court. There’s been no ruling on whether they establish the chain Fender claims.

To establish the Stratocaster’s stature, Fender piles up evidence of its ubiquity: Its shape is the Apple, Google, Samsung and WhatsApp guitar emoji. (Judges are invited to check their own smartphones.) The body, Fender’s lawyers write, “corresponds to a kind of ‘generic form’ — if there were only one electric guitar in the world, it would be this one.” Fender offers that as tribute. It also echoes the finding that led to the company’s US defeat in 2009: The shape had stopped functioning as a brand identifier and had become the way you draw an electric guitar. That finding governed US trademark law, not European copyright, a distinction Fender’s lawyers press, and a real one.

There may also be a cost to all the years Fender let others use the shape. Grohmann points to a German doctrine called Verwirkung, or forfeiture. Under the civil code’s good-faith principle, he says, a rights holder who knows about an infringement, and tolerates it long enough, can lose the ability to act later. He goes further: A court might find that Fender’s decades of tolerance amounted to tacit consent, permission that reaches forward rather than merely excusing the past. Arguably, guitar builders’ longstanding argument that Fender let everybody make copies is right there in German civil law.

Since the letters went out, guitar forums and YouTube have turned Cole into a villain, someone who doesn’t care about musicians, “some corporate raider type with an MBA,” in the words of one Reddit commenter. Never mind that Cole doesn’t have an MBA or that the legal strategy predates his promotion. By his own telling, his first love was music — writing songs, singing, playing guitar. For a period, that was his full-time gig, playing in bands in Arizona, where he went to college.

After a series of personal setbacks while living in Augusta, Georgia, which culminated with his girlfriend dumping him at a Waffle House, Cole headed back west, eventually making his way to San Francisco. He landed a business-development role with spirits company Pernod Ricard. The job took him to Asia on frequent business trips and eventually relocated him to Tokyo. It was there, in 2014, that he got a call from Fender, asking him to develop its business in Asia. He initially worked out of the basement of his house. Cole built the company’s first owned commercial operation in Japan and extended it across Australia, China and South Korea, turning what had been a set of distributor relationships into Fender’s own Asia-Pacific business.

Cole’s case for the legal campaign starts with how the guitar industry itself has changed. Today, companies can replicate existing products and distribute them around the world at extraordinary speed and scale. “They’re simply copying designs, and that does not help our industry,” he says. “We all start out with the same piece of wood. There are unlimited ways to design a guitar with that piece of wood.”

What Cole won’t do is say precisely what a Stratocaster is. Instead, he describes it as most others do: recognizable, unique. Asked what makes a Strat body a Strat body — the question before a German court — he goes back to Leo Fender, to beauty, to function, to the piece of wood. Defining it turns out to be slippery, closer to Justice Potter Stewart on obscenity (“I know it when I see it”) than to a precise, measurable set of specifications.

Cole knew about the Dusseldorf judgment when it came down in December, two months before he became CEO and almost three before the first letters went out. Asked about his own role, he returns to the timing. “Once that legal process got going, it got going,” he says. It’s the second time he describes the campaign as something that moved under its own power; earlier, he said the legal process “got ahead of us.”

The question of who greenlit the campaign is harder. Asked whether Servco approved it, he first talks about creativity and innovation. Asked again, he talks about investment. Told he isn’t answering the question, he says, “We led that. That was Fender, the company.”

Then comes the distinction Fender failed to make when the letters went out — or since. Cole says the company isn’t taking aim at the shops that generated much of the backlash. “We are very, very focused solely on large manufacturers now,” he says. “We are not focused at all now on boutique builders.” What about tiny LsL? “We are not focused on small builders.”
So why did LsL even get the letter?

“The idea was to begin conversations with people,” he says. “That has always been our objective.” The letters, he says, were meant to explain that Fender saw a likeness to the Stratocaster and open a discussion about how companies might “begin to design something that is not a direct copy.”
“In hindsight,” he says, “there was probably a better way to do that.”

What Cole keeps coming back to, unprompted, is not the law but the reaction. “What came across very clearly to me was how personal players feel about guitar playing, their instruments, their gear, the designs, their creativity,” he says. He says he’s heard from all of them, including a 10-year-old whose father and grandfather played Stratocasters and wanted Fender to defend the design.
“It’s bigger than all of us,” Cole says. “This brand is important to a lot of people, and it’s very special to everyone in their own way.”

So far, the campaign has produced something messier than victory and messier than defeat. Some guitar makers have engaged with Fender to figure out a solution. “We’ve reached out to several builders,” Cole says, and they’ve agreed to “stop making the Stratocaster and take it in a different direction and redo the design.” Fender says it’s working with 32 builders, 18 of whom have signed agreements. The company won’t name any of them, citing confidentiality agreements. Fender keeps a list of designs it considers sufficiently different, which it shares only with companies it’s negotiating with. It declined to share the list.
LsL has heard nothing. Nor has Bienstock or any of his other clients.

At Fender dealer Wild West Guitars in Pasadena, California, sales manager Leroy Braxton says the backlash shows up on the floor. The store spends as much as $800,000 a year stocking Fender Custom Shop and master-built instruments, but since the campaign went public, some customers have been steering toward other brands. The morning he spoke to Bloomberg Businessweek, a longtime Fender player unhappy about the company’s tactics walked out with a PRS Silver Sky. The sentiment Braxton says he hears most: “No one likes a bully.”

The numbers suggest something less dramatic. Orders for the Silver Sky on Reverb ticked up from late May into mid-June as the story spread, then settled back; demand for the Fender American Professional II Stratocaster, Reverb’s bestselling electric guitar of 2025, stayed unchanged. Nor was there a measurable rise in used Fenders listed for sale. The upshot: a flash of protest, not an exodus.

The quieter effect is in the workshops. LsL stopped shipping to Europe its standard Saticoy, the guitar Fender called out as infringing. It turned instead to the Saticoy 24, a sharp, pointy model aimed at progressive players, of which it had sold fewer than 10. Over several months it reworked the guitar, building a back surface that felt like a traditional S-style body and completely changing the front contours into a hybrid of vintage and modern.

The changes were “a direct result in our strategy to build something that is safe to ship,” says Johny Miller, LsL’s director of business development. The way Miller read it, Fender’s cease and desist letter threatened $14,000 for every S-style guitar sent to the European Union. The actual terms were harder to parse than that. What the letter said was this: Agree to what we’re asking, and then, if you break that agreement, face a penalty for every S-style guitar you make or sell anywhere, not just Europe — €10,000 ($11,500) in the letter’s German original, €15,000 in its English translation — and also wire legal fees directly to Fender’s law firm. “We needed a replacement,” Miller says.

LsL never spoke to Fender about its redesign. It guessed where the line might be and worked from there. Fender says what it’s asking for is for builders to stop copying and start creating. What emerged at LsL is a reimagined guitar. What remains is a question Fender still hasn’t answered: What, exactly, makes a Stratocaster a Stratocaster?

items.title: The Fed Never Hikes Just Once? Alan Greenspan Disagreed
body: Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh on Wednesday presided over the first US interest rate increase since 2023, and rate hikes are generally a package deal, as the aphorism goes. Versions of that folk wisdom circulated ahead of the decision, delivered by the likes of former president of the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis Jim Bullard and one-time Fed Vice Chair Richard Clarida. Their conviction is reflected in market pricing, with swaps traders anticipating around three more increases by late 2027.

The heuristic has a reasonable basis in financial market mechanics: Under most circumstances, a single quarter-point rate adjustment rarely does much to sway the broader bond market, financial conditions or the economy. But there is a clear exception to the rule — Alan Greenspan’s mid-cycle one-and-done rate move in March 1997. It’s an excellent analog to the present moment, and shows that some economies cry out for subtle, even trivial-seeming tinkering.

In a survey of policymakers released with the decision, the median participant thought the Fed would probably lift rates once more by the end of 2026. The poll covered 18 Federal Reserve bank presidents and Federal Reserve Board members, but not the chair. The vast majority of respondents, though, also acknowledged heightened uncertainty around their inflation forecasts. When asked during the post-decision press conference for his view on what’s next, Warsh was tight-lipped: “I’m not going to prejudge any future decisions we make,” he said. So are multiple rate hikes really baked in?

Let’s begin with the basics. In the modern history of the FedI count from 1994, when the Fed started publicly and contemporaneously announcing policy rate decisions., nearly all hiking cycles have started with rates ultra low once an economic recovery from recession was in place, so policymakers had a lot of ground to cover. The sole exceptions were 1997 and todayThere is potentially one other exception: December 2015, when the Fed hiked once and then waited another year to get on with further rate increases. It's a judgement call, but I lump that together with the 2016-2018 hikes as part of a broader series., with rates having moved to 3.75%-4%.

Like Greenspan, who was known as the “Maestro,” rookie Chair Warsh finds himself in fine-tuning mode. Squint past the noise of volatile oil prices and other temporary factors, and underlying inflation may be as low as 2.3%-2.7% — above the 2% objective, but hardly an inferno. Warsh’s problem is that it’s been above target for five and a half years and is no longer cooling, and it probably needs a nudge to resume its 2022-2024 disinflationary trend.

Greenspan’s calibration challenge was similarly nuanced: Economic growth was strong and unemployment had fallen sharply. Policymakers wondered if the economy was at risk of overheating, triggering inflation down the road. Though it was still under control at the time of the hike, the Fed’s internal models forecast that the core consumer price index would rise modestly by about 3.2% in 1998 due to labor market tightness.

Another similarity: Warsh finds himself adjusting to a potential technological jolt from artificial intelligence that could drive up productivity and growth, and change assumptions about how interest rates work. Greenspan was contending with the start of the internet revolution.

When the ground shifts under them, policymakers can’t be sure what constitutes a “restrictive,” “neutral” or “accommodative” stance of policy rates. They’re feeling around in the dark, as evidenced by the latest rise in their estimates of the neutral rate — the theoretical equilibrium level that neither restrains nor stimulates the economy — to 3.2%, the highest in a decade. The internal Fed survey also signaled that policymakers may take their time bringing rates back down from the peak to that perceived neutral level. In reality, productivity-led growth is somewhat unpredictable for rates, potentially limiting inflation but also raising demand for borrowing.

In 1997 too, the rate-setting committee openly debated the implications of a surreptitiously rising neutral rate: “If monetary policy failed to recognize the changes in the equilibrium situation and did not adjust nominal interest rates higher, then effectively, to use the language we normally employ, we would have eased monetary policy even if we maintained the same level of nominal interest rates,” Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond President J. Alfred Broaddus told Greenspan at the time, according to a transcript of the meeting — a sentence that could just as well have been written in September 2026.

Finally, the Fed’s actions Wednesday buttress its credibility. Appointed by President Donald Trump, the biggest monetary policy interventionist to hold the presidency in recent history, Warsh began his tenure with questions already swirling about his independence, deservedly or not. Trump has publicly demanded cuts in recent weeks, as the rate hike became a consensus expectation in markets. A failure to act would have looked as if Warsh was cowed by the president ahead of midterm elections in November.

Greenspan’s Fed understood the importance of credibility too, since the committee hadn’t flexed its hiking muscles since the tightening of 1994 to 1995. “My reading of the economy supports the conclusion that we are at risk of losing the hard-won credibility of our commitment to hold inflation,” Thomas C. Melzer, the president of the Fed Bank of St. Louis, told the committee at the meeting.

Greenspan has received significant praise, including from Warsh himself, for his prescient prediction that inflation would remain contained, and his refusal to stamp out a strong economy. Yet he also got somewhat lucky, helped by a global collapse in energy prices, a strong dollar that made imports cheap and a hard-won institutional reputation burnished by Greenspan’s predecessor Paul Volcker. Also worth noting: Greenspan and his colleagues didn’t explicitly intend for 1997 to be one-and-done from the outset. But he developed a thesis about productivity keeping a lid on inflation over subsequent meetings, and by 1998, a Russian default and the collapse of hedge fund Long-Term Capital Management put the Fed back in cutting mode.

So what’s the point of a tiny adjustment? Having taken action to protect Fed credibility, Warsh has bought himself cheap optionality. If the economy ends up needing more, he can still deliver it down the road. But he’s probably not too far from his final destination. And with some Greenspanian luck, he might already be there.

items.title: Lula, Bolsonaro Tied as Bank Scandal Weighs on Both Campaigns
body: President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro are locked in a tie ahead of Brazil’s October election, according to a new poll that suggests the fallout of a major bank scandal is hitting both campaigns.

Lula and Bolsonaro would each receive roughly 47% of the vote in a runoff, according to an AtlasIntel poll for Bloomberg News published Thursday. The results are little changed from the previous survey released last week.

Polls have consistently shown the two candidates in a dead heat in runoff scenarios. Brazilians will vote in a first-round election on Oct. 4, with Lula and Bolsonaro — the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro — virtually certain to advance to a runoff three weeks later.
Lula is ahead in the first round by 2 points, 44% to 42%, according to the survey, down from 6 points in the prior poll.

Lula, who held a comfortable lead two months ago, has seen his advantage disappear as a weakening economy and corruption allegations against one of his sons have weighed on his reelection bid. The leftist leader is now struggling to dodge the fallout of an unprecedented crisis inside the nation’s powerful Supreme Court.

In early September, the publication of private messages appeared to deepen links between Justice Alexandre de Moraes and former Banco Master SA owner Daniel Vorcaro, the man at the center of a massive bank fraud probe that has eroded faith in Brazil’s governing elite. The release of the messages has triggered an internal feud that has clouded the presidential race.

Roughly half of respondents say they expect the court crisis to hurt Lula more than Bolsonaro. Although he didn’t appoint Moraes, the president is widely seen as an ally of the judge who oversaw the trial that convicted Jair Bolsonaro of plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election.
Flávio Bolsonaro has seized on the court’s troubles, calling for Moraes’ impeachment and attempting to turn the race into a referendum on the court’s vast powers.

But the poll indicates that hasn’t fully helped him distract from a federal police investigation into his own links to Vorcaro, after the senator acknowledged seeking funding for a film about his father from the banker.

Brazilians remain evenly split on which candidate is more closely tied to the Banco Master case, with 41% saying allies of Bolsonaro are the most involved against 40% who say the same about associates of Lula.

The court scandal spilled further into public view Tuesday, when justices postponed a decision on whether to open an investigation into Moraes following a tense session in which they traded accusations of political bias.
Lula has called for full transparency around the case in a bid to contain the damage, and has backed reforms to the judiciary.

He praised Moraes for doing an “extraordinary job” defending democracy by convicting Jair Bolsonaro during a Wednesday podcast interview, accusing Flávio of targeting the judge because he’s nervous about his ties to Vorcaro.
AtlasIntel interviewed 5,018 people from Sept. 11-16. The survey has a margin of error of plus or minus 1 percentage point.

items.title: UBS Capital Bill Stays in Swiss Parliament in Boost to Bank
body: The upper house of Switzerland’s parliament began its debate over UBS Group AG’s capital requirements, with lawmakers focusing on how much equity is needed to prevent a repeat of Credit Suisse’s 2023 collapse.
The chamber proceeded with the debate on Thursday after a lawmaker who’d proposed handing the decision back to the government withdrew his motion.

That decision means that the draft law which could entail as much as a $20 billion increase in capital requirements for Switzerland’s biggest bank will continue its path through both houses as planned. Keeping the debate in parliament increases the chances that the final law will differ from what the government wants.
Read More: Swiss Lawmakers Propose Handing UBS Decision to Government

The key thrust of the Federal Council’s reforms is that UBS should back the full value of its foreign subsidiaries with the highest-quality capital, CET1, at home. UBS has called those proposals “extreme” and argued that they would make it uncompetitive.
UBS shares reversed early losses to gain as much as 1.3% on Thursday after the decision. Shares traded at 42.11 Swiss francs at 11:10 a.m.

UBS has gained some support for its position in parliament, and lawmakers in the upper house’s influential Economic Affairs and Taxation Committee have sought to broker a compromise. A new effort late last month emerged that would allow UBS to use a type of hybrid debt known as AT1 bonds to meet half of the new capital requirements. This would substantially reduce the need for UBS to find fresh equity capital as a result of the new rules.
That effort is however less likely to find support among left-of-center lawmakers.

AT1 bonds “can’t absorb losses” during the stabilization phase of a bank, said Social Democrat lawmaker Eva Herzog, one of the critics of the committee compromise. “That’s smoke and mirrors. Only CET1 can absorb losses.”
The proposal filed by upper house member Andrea Caroni on Wednesday had argued that the executive would be better placed to determine new rules.

“The will of parliament to decide, now it has the proposal on the table, is unchanged,” Caroni said when he withdrew his motion. “If in the end it produces a result that we don’t like, we have the possibility to vote it down.”
Read more: UBS Faces Protracted Capital Battle as Minister Hits Back
In the debate on Thursday, the upper house will begin the process of deciding on amendments to the government bill.

Lawmakers will go through the bill article by article and decide whether they back the government’s or the proposals surfaced in the committee, or one of the other options on the table. A vote is expected later on Thursday.

The result of that debate would then be passed to the lower house, likely later this year, for further debate. A final ruling on UBS’s capital requirements isn’t likely until next year at the earliest.

The debate over UBS’s regulation has weighed on the bank’s share price over the past two years and caused uncertainty over investor payouts. The bank has even considered moving its headquarters out of the country in response to what it sees as over-regulation.
Lawmakers are seeking to balance preventing a future financial crisis from overwhelming the resources of the state, with preserving the competitiveness of Switzerland’s financial center.
“We don’t want UBS to leave the country, and also not that it’s taken over by foreigners,” said centrist lawmaker Pirmin Bischof.

items.title: Major Bathla Creditor Explores Debt Sale as Crisis Persists
body: Centuria Bass Credit, a major Bathla Group backer, is exploring options to sell some debt tied to the insolvent Sydney builder, the latest sign that some creditors could be looking to trim their exposure.

Centuria Bass, a unit of Centuria Capital Group, held talks with potential investors but no deal is imminent, according to people familiar with the matter, who asked not to be identified discussing private matters. Some investors are seeking at least 20% to 30% discount of the assets, one of the people said.

Centuria Bass declined to comment on potential discounts. It will “assess opportunities to maximize outcomes for investors” as it continues to actively manage its Bathla-related exposure, a spokesperson said on Thursday.

Centuria Bass last month disclosed it had A$278 million ($198 million) in Bathla debt secured against six residential projects in Victoria and New South Wales. The firm “temporarily paused,” redemptions from two of its funds following heightened scrutiny of its Bathla holdings, according to a Centuria Bass spokesperson.

Bathla Group owes around A$3.4 billion to creditors, largely private credit funds, and in August appointed voluntary administrator Teneo Australia after struggling to service its debts. Teneo has secured emergency financing of around A$4 million and is now looking to arrange a broader funding package.

The crisis follows rising interest rates and inflation in Australia, which have increased borrowing and construction costs, while real estate prices and sales have fallen, adding pressure on indebted developers like Bathla.

The tumult has cast a spotlight on Australia’s A$200 billion private credit market, where around half of assets are tied up in real estate development, according to the Australian Securities and Investments Commission. ASIC has called for greater disclosure for private credit fund managers to reduce the opacity of the market.
Centuria Capital Group is a major Australian real estate fund manager, managing A$22.2 billion in assets, according to its website.

items.title: ECB's Makhlouf Says Each Meeting Is 'Live' Including October
body: European Central Bank Governing Council member Gabriel Makhlouf declined to rule out an interest-rate hike in October if circumstances require it.

The Irish central-bank chief told Bloomberg Television on Thursday that while there’s currently no worrying sign of inflation spreading into wages, officials will take each decision on borrowing costs as it comes.

“At a time of uncertainty, every meeting is a live meeting for the European Central Bank,” Makhlouf said when asked if that was the case for the next one on Oct. 29. “You can’t rule out anything that might happen in future meetings, nor can you rule them in.”

The Irish governor spoke in the wake of the US Federal Reserve’s rate hike on Wednesday, and at a time when markets are undecided on whether the ECB itself will follow up with a consecutive move so soon after its increase last week.
Makhlouf declined to offer a view on bets by investors who are pricing at least three more quarter-point hikes over the next 12 months.

“Markets understand that we’re committed to delivering on our 2% inflation target, and at the moment the numbers aren’t as strong as we want them to be,” he said. “I’m not in the business of saying whether markets are right or wrong.”

In the wake of this month’s decision, policymakers viewed another step possible as soon as October, according to people familiar with the matter. With the next quarterly forecasts due in December, economists tend to view that meeting as the more likely moment to act.

Makhlouf, speaking before a gathering of European finance ministers and central bankers in Dublin, expressed a tone of vigilance given the international backdrop. With oil and natural gas prices continuing to soar, euro-area inflation is poised to quicken past its current level of 3.2%, even further from the ECB’s 2% target.

“At the moment, we’re certainly not seeing signs of concerning second-round effects but it’s pretty clear that the shock, the energy shock that started with the war in Iran isn’t going away,” he said. “The risks to inflation remain on the upside.”
The ECB’s most recent hike brought its deposit rate to 2.5%. Asked whether a further move would shift the stance of borrowing costs into restrictive territory, Makhlouf wouldn’t speculate.

“Where we are now remains within the neutral band,” he said. “There’s theory of neutral rates, but then there’s also the judgments that we have to exercise in making our monetary policy decision. So I’m not really going to go into, ‘is there a defining moment on whether we’re restrictive or not?’”

items.title: Turkish Regulator to Liquidate Funds Run by Tera and Others
body: Turkey’s market regulator said it will liquidate some funds run by asset managers including Tera Portfoy and Pusula Portfoy as officials move to stem the turmoil that’s shaken the country’s investment industry.

The announcement comes after three asset managers failed to meet redemption requests on some of their funds, triggering a steep selloff in the Turkish equity market this week. Stocks steadied on Thursday after Turkey’s Financial Stability Committee pledged measures to ease a liquidity crunch.

The developments have put a spotlight on the risks created by Turkey’s fast-growing fund industry, where some managers built large positions in relatively illiquid shares. Regulators tightened rules on such holdings in late August, forcing funds to unwind excess positions while investors have continued to ask for their money back.

That tipped off a crisis in Turkish markets and forced regulators into action to ease the stress. As well, the local market regulator filed criminal complaints against dozens of people and imposed trading bans over alleged share-price manipulation.

The Capital Markets Board cited alleged manipulation involving shares of Katilimevim, Gundogdu Gida and Destek Finans Faktoring AS. The regulator filed criminal complaints and two-year trading bans against some fund managers at Pusula Portfoy and Tera Portfoy, according to a statement late Wednesday.

The recent volatility stemmed from credit and liquidity problems at some funds managed by a limited number of portfolio companies, the committee said. The benchmark Borsa Istanbul 100 Index rose 1.3% on Thursday after slumping almost 10% in the past three days and triggering a market-wide circuit breaker.

The problems are concentrated in a specific segment of the fund market and are “temporary and manageable,” according to a statement following a meeting chaired by Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Simsek on Thursday.

Measures agreed at the meeting will focus primarily on resolving the liquidity crunch and preventing the problems from spreading, the committee said, adding that relevant authorities would implement necessary steps swiftly.
Read more: Turkish Stocks Slump After Fund Default Heightens Investor Fears

Separately, the central bank said it would increase funding through one-week repo auctions when needed, depending on liquidity conditions. It also said it would revise banks’ borrowing limits and reduce collateral haircuts in central-bank markets.

Tera Portfoy Yonetimi said late Wednesday that two of its funds with $7.5 billion of assets had failed to meet redemption payments from investors, following a similar disclosure by Pusula Portfoy earlier in the week.
A third fund manager, Atlas Portfoy, disclosed Thursday that there are delays in redemption payments for its Atlas Portfoy Money Market Fund.
Read more: Behind the 40,000% Stock Surge That’s Mystifying Traders in Turkey

The stricter regulations capped hedge-fund ownership of companies’ free-float shares and restricted investments in affiliated entities. Funds were given until year-end to reduce positions that exceed the new limits.

Tera Portfoy had about 730 billion liras ($15 billion) of assets under management as of Wednesday, according to Turkey’s electronic fund platform Tefas. The firm, founded by Emre Tezmen, came under scrutiny earlier this year for the soaring performance of its main fund. That portfolio has returned more than 66,000% over the past three years by pouring billions of lira into a tight circle of related companies and amplifying the bets with borrowed cash.

“The situation we now face is a speculative attack of an extraordinary and unprecedented scale, aimed at causing destruction, which no domestic or foreign financial institution could withstand on its own and which carries the risk of spreading throughout the entire market,” Tezmen said in a post on X late Wednesday.
Shares of Tera Portfoy’s parent, Tera Yatirim Menkul Degerler AS, slumped 9.97% on Thursday, near the 10% limit under stock exchange rules.

Pusula Portfoy had about 143 billion liras assets under management as of Monday, down from 431 billion liras at the end of August, Tefas data shows. Atlas Portfoy had about 80 billion liras assets under management as of Wednesday, Tefas data shows.

items.title: What Francis Fukuyama Is Seeing at 'The End of History'
body: Listen to Odd Lots on Apple PodcastsListen to Odd Lots on SpotifyWatch Odd Lots on YouTubeSubscribe to the newsletter

Francis Fukuyama’s essay “The End of History?” was published in the summer of 1989, a few months before the fall of the Berlin Wall. The essay’s argument — that liberal democracy would not only defeat communism, but that its partisans might, in victory, miss the “courage, imagination, and idealism” that defined the ideological battle — lives on as one of the most cited pieces of political theory in the last three decades. In his new memoir, In the Realm of the Last Man, he revisits “The End of History?” and for today’s episode he talks to us about how his essay’s argument has evolved in a world now defined by the intense technological change brought on by AI and by the many electoral defeats liberal democracy has suffered as of late. We also talk about how the Internet and social media are helping fuel the listlessness that “The End of History” brought about, how he uses AI, and what, if anything, will come after liberalism.

items.title: Wizz Air Aims to Double Passenger Goal By 2030 in Market Rebound
body: Wizz Air Holdings Plc plans to almost double its annual passenger goal in the next four years as the budget carrier seeks to expand in its core markets and rebound from high costs that have weighed on the business.

The Hungary-based airline aims to fly 127 million passengers by fiscal 2030, up from the almost 70 million passengers it carried in fiscal 2026. Wizz set out medium-term targets for the end of the decade including revenue of €10 billion, an operating profit margin of 10% and an investment grade balance sheet, it said in a statement ahead of its capital markets day in London.
Shares rose as much as 4% on Thursday in London after the update. The stock has slumped more than 22% so far this year.

“Our next chapter is about turning that structural advantage into consistently stronger returns by concentrating growth in core and growth markets, restoring fleet productivity, maturing our network and executing with discipline,” Chief Executive Officer Jozsef Varadi said in a statement.

Wizz has suffered from soaring oil prices and suppressed demand caused by the Middle East conflict. The airline was also hit with maintenance issues on its Pratt & Whitney-made engines, leading to Airbus SE aircraft groundings over the past few years.

While Wizz’s core network is in central and eastern Europe, Varadi had ambitions to push the carrier into the Middle East to reach destinations in India and Pakistan. But he decided to pull out of the Abu Dhabi base last year because of engine troubles, regulatory hurdles and geopolitical challenges that made it costly to operate in the region.
“We think the share price credits Wizz with more of a “hockey stick” recovery than we forecast,” Ruairi Cullinane, analyst at RBC, said in a note.

items.title: Russia's Attacks on Europe Are Getting More Brazen and More Dangerous
body: Over the course of the summer, Russian attacks have been pushing ever deeper into European territory.

On Aug. 11, military divers destroyed two drones floating off the coast of Romania near a €4 billion ($4.7 billion) energy project. Nine days later, Bucharest scrambled two F-16s to take out a maritime drone near the same Black Sea gas platform with hundreds of workers on board. Earlier that month, German police detected an armed UAV at Leipzig airport, while this week NATO jets downed another unmanned aircraft that entered Lithuanian airspace from neighboring Belarus, an ally of Moscow.
In all these cases, the authorities pointed the finger squarely at the Kremlin.

As  Vladimir Putin’s war on Ukraine grinds on with little movement on the battlefield and thousands of casualties each week, so-called hybrid attacks on Europe are increasing not just in number, but in their recklessness. Companies on the frontline find themselves caught in a gray zone between war and peace and European officials, who asked not to be named discussing sensitive issues, fear that it’s only a matter of time until there are civilian casualties.

“It’s clear that the European defense industry is working in a different security environment than a few years ago,” said Kuldar Väärsi, CEO of Estonian defense firm Milrem Robotics, which was targeted by a suspected arson attack in August. “As a company whose systems are used by several NATO member states and other ally and partner nations, including Ukraine, we need to take the resultant risks into account.”
Germany is the “daily target of hybrid warfare” by Russia, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said Sept. 1. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said those accusations were “completely unfounded.”

The past two months have seen a shift in Russia’s focus toward defense-industrial and logistics targets directly connected to support for Ukraine, according to one NATO country official, who added that this more aggressive campaign presents higher risks. With Moscow continuing to structure operations so that it can deny direct responsibility, the campaign is more significant strategically than for the physical damage caused so far, the official said.

That assessment could change as Russia ups the ante with incidents such as last weekend’s drone assault at a train station near the Ukraine-Polish border as European and US dignitaries were passing through. Such attacks had been largely taboo until now, offering further evidence of a growing brazenness and willingness to risk foreign victims.

Where once Russia stood accused of election interference and weaponizing migration, it’s now suspected of sabotage, arson, tampering with critical infrastructure, cyberattacks and airspace violations, including an incident last week that resulted in two civilian deaths at a border post between Ukraine and fellow EU aspirant Moldova. The EU’s foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, says Europe is experiencing “a wave of increasingly kinetic hybrid attacks.”

The difficulty in responding to hybrid attacks has at times led to a reluctance to blame Russia openly, both to avert escalation and avoid revealing intelligence methods, officials say. Many incidents, especially cyberattacks and hacks targeting critical infrastructure, are barely reported if at all, meaning the scale of the problem is far wider than is made public.

Many arms makers in Germany are targeted by regular cyberattacks, according to a person familiar with the matter. In 2024, arsonists set fire to the home of Armin Papperger, the chief executive officer of defense giant Rheinmetall AG, and western intelligence agencies warned that Russia was plotting to kill him. He now travels with a heavy security detail and Rheinmetall has increased its overall security measures.

German radar and sensor maker Hensoldt AG is increasing drone and perimeter surveillance at its plants and wants to build the infrastructure required to down drones itself, CEO Oliver Dorre said in an interview. It needs approval from the federal police to do this, and Dorre said guidelines are needed sooner rather than later, before the situation becomes worse.

Poland, as a key conduit for aid to Ukraine, has suffered a spate of suspicious incidents, with multiple cyberattacks on public utilities like water, energy infrastructure and hospitals, and damage to the rail line between Warsaw and the Ukrainian border attributed to Russian intelligence. Prime Minister Donald Tusk described a fire at a plant for one of Europe’s largest drone makers, WB Electronics, in August as an “act of sabotage,” though no public link was made to Russia.
Poland announced this month it’s expanding protection of its airspace and strengthening rapid-response defenses, citing the threat from “Russian provocations.”

Europe’s largest weapons makers are mostly undeterred by the increasing level of Russian activity aimed at their facilities and personnel, according to a person at one such company. Security has been tightened, and lingering “muscle memory” from the Cold War is feeding a vigilance that borders on paranoia, the person said.

Other key businesses are less well able to defend themselves. Achieving 100% protection of electricity networks is impossible, “especially when you may not even know what you are facing,” said Juha Räsänen, CEO of Savon Voima, an energy company in eastern Finland.

“Physical security, physical monitoring, cameras and different types of detection methods are being increased all the time,” he said. “But the most important thing is that people learn to tolerate power outages.”

That kind of resilience points to another reality: Russia’s campaign has so far failed to substantially reduce European support for Ukraine. The rise in high-profile incidents has instead reinforced arguments for more European defense spending, tighter counterintelligence coordination and new sanctions.
As one official put it, the Kremlin’s campaign may be disruptive but is proving counterproductive for Moscow.

Germany, for example, made it known after Leipzig that a delivery of additional Iris-T air-defense missiles to Ukraine is planned for September, and that Berlin will also soon provide Kyiv with several thousand strike drones.

As hybrid actions move deeper into Europe, the lid is occasionally peeled back to reveal what authorities are confronting. In early September, a British man was arrested and charged under the National Security Act with giving details about drone manufacturing sites in England to a Russian intelligence unit and preparing to commit sabotage. His lawyers said his allegiance lies with the UK.

That comes on the back of suspected arson attacks on former British Prime Minister Keir Starmer’s home, Russian submarine activity around critical infrastructure in the British Isles, and drones launched from shadow fleet vessels in UK and Irish waters, including during Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s visit to Ireland this year.

Governments from London to Warsaw are scrambling to ratchet up their individual and collective responses before more serious damage spirals into open conflict with Russia. NATO is strengthening deterrence in the nations affected, officials say, but a coordinated strategy continues to elude member states.

The understanding among security officials is that Putin is testing how far he can push NATO members to expose indecision among the allies while staying below the threshold that would trigger retaliation under the Article 5 collective-defense clause. Yet that probing raises the chances of miscalculation and accidents.

“Russia is consistent in identifying weaknesses in NATO’s infrastructure and is willing to attempt multiple tactics and targets in a flexible and increasingly risk-taking manner,” said Emily Ferris, associate fellow at the London-based Royal United Services Institute.
Ferris published a report in March on sabotage attacks attributed to Russia in NATO countries and found the alliance “unprepared.” Six months later, her verdict hasn’t changed.
“In the absence of clear red lines from NATO about the consequences of attacks like this, Russia is expanding to fill the space of the uncertainty,” she said.

The only time that Article 5 was invoked was by the US after the Sept. 11 attacks of 2001. Western intelligence agencies are now applying counter-terrorism methodology developed since then and the fight against al-Qaeda and Islamic State to Russian hybrid warfare, according to two officials.

Russia and terror groups both use proxies, often recruited online. Hence for western agencies, there are similarities in identifying threat actors. The difference is that those recruited to Moscow’s service are not ideological, but paid.
Western security officials say that Moscow is acting out of desperation after Ukraine’s drone attacks targeting energy infrastructure and logistics warehouses damaged the Russian economy.

The view from Moscow is that the more painfully Ukraine hits Russia, the stronger will be the voices who want to make Europe pay. A person close to the Kremlin put it more bluntly, saying that Russia will make life hell for Europe through asymmetrical hybrid operations over its support for Kyiv.
To those on the front line like the Baltic states, Russia has long since crossed any notional boundaries.

“This is not hybrid, this is about explosives that can cause damage. There can be casualties. People may die,” said Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys. “If we won’t stop this, it will escalate.”

items.title: Next Raises Profit Guidance as Overseas Sales Rise But Warns on UK Tax Hikes
body: Morning, I’m Louise Moon from Bloomberg UK’s breaking news team, bringing you up to speed on today’s top business stories.
Next has, typically, raised guidance.

The clothing retailer is a bellwether for the UK high street so at first glance, an upgrade to its profit outlook — for the fourth time this year — bodes well. But its boss Simon Wolfson is known to be conservative, which allows for guidance to be lifted. Next is benefiting from strong online demand for its clothing overseas. Shares rose 2%.

Still, the company cut its sales growth target for the UK for the back half of the year by £18 million. It noted rising inflation, higher mortgage interest costs and a weak employment market, and warned about the impact of possible tax hikes in the upcoming budget.

“It might be tempting to think that higher taxes on investment affect only a relatively small number of investors. They do not,” it said. “Lower investment means less growth, and that affects everyone.”
Next said it was among many companies that warned higher taxes and regulation on jobs will hit employment. “Unfortunately, that concern now appears well-founded.” Punchy stuff.
What’s your take? Ping me on X, LinkedIn or drop me an email at lmoon13@bloomberg.net. Oh, and do subscribe to Bloomberg.com for unlimited access to trusted business journalism on the UK, and beyond.

Budget airline Wizz Air has set some ambitious new targets, demonstrating hope it will bounce back from huge volatility sparked by the Iran war. It’s aiming for €10 billion in revenue by 2030 and 127 million passengers (vs 69.7 million in 2026). It also notched up some guidance for this year. Shares rose over 3%.
Power generation company Drax said it expects earnings at around the top-end of current expectations, boosted by lower costs and better performance at Drax Power Station. Shares rose 3%.

King Charles plans to ask some of AI’s biggest names for reassurance they can keep their inventions under control. He’s hosting a private event in Scotland and attendees include Google DeepMind’s co-founder as well as senior people from Nvidia, OpenAI and Anthropic.

Chelsea Football Club owner Clearlake Capital is buying out chairman Todd Boehly and director Mark Walter, who is under scrutiny from US authorities, setting an enterprise value of about £5 billion. It ends a turbulent period with Clearlake and Boehly falling out over the club’s direction.

Lest we forget, the Bank of England will decide on interest rates today. Bank rate is expected to hold at 3.75% as rate-setters wait for more evidence that fresh inflation risks a wage-price spiral. It’s complex, as my colleague Sam details below, but we’ll have you covered.
Here’s your daily snap analysis from Bloomberg UK’s Markets Today blog:
It’s Bank of England day! Just me saying that should be enough to get London Rush readers tuning into our blog later, but just in case you’re not convinced.

The BOE is expected to keep rates on hold as it continues to assess a morass of global uncertainties, most of which stand to have an impact on inflation. That’s primarily around energy but it takes in topics like climate change, El Nino, AI and domestic politics too. There’s lots to consider, including that the Federal Reserve raised rates.

Policymakers have pushed back in recent weeks on traders betting on more hikes through 2027. Even with a pullback yesterday, investors still see four increases. This week’s data on an increasingly fragile jobs market and yesterday’s quite benign inflation data (for now, anyway) is likely to keep the BOE in wait-and-see mode and scouring for signs that second-round effects are starting to appear.

Beyond this month, however, the picture will get ever more complex. Those uncertainties listed above are likely to rear their heads and, by definition, working out what impact they’ll have is very difficult. One should have a little sympathy for central bankers these days.
— Sam Unsted
Check Bloomberg UK’s Markets Today blog for updates all day.
A couple of smaller company updates are due tomorrow, as well as retail sales data for August and GfK’s consumer confidence index for September.

Hi, it’s Kate, food editor at Pursuits. It seems line-standing has become much more standard practice. There was the nine hour-long virtual queue for tickets to see the Bayeux Tapestry, and another, physical one around the British Museum when it debuted. Here are three lines worth waiting for while the weather holds up.
Yo-Chi, Notting Hill

The popular Australian frozen yogurt company opened its first London outpost in late August and the lines were immediately epic, with reports of two-plus hour waits. By most accounts, it is worth it: along with flavours like Signature Tart, Strawberry Cream and Seasonal Matcha, there’s a vast array of toppings from kiwi to chocolate pretzels — and a DJ booth.
Frida: The Making of an Icon, Bankside

The Tate Modern’s blockbuster summer show broke the museum’s existing records by pre-selling over 41,000 tickets, and demand has stayed strong. The exhibit features more than 30 of the artist’s paintings as well as rooms of memorabilia, and delves into one of the art world’s early modern rock stars.
It’s Bagels, Primrose Hill

This New York style bagel shop is proliferating around London — its fourth outpost opens in Hampstead next week — and, like in the Big Apple, the doughy rounds have people contentedly queueing. It’s not unusual to find a 50-strong line at the original location on Regents Park Road, and at its spot in Soho you’ll see the line before the sign.
— Kate Krader

New Bloomberg Intelligence research found users of GLP-1 pills curbed snacking less than those taking injections, which could reduce the negative impact on food makers’ sales. By 2030, what percentage of the US population is expected to be on a GLP-1 drug?
Clue: this year will be 7.5%, projects BI.

items.title: Switzerland Boosts Growth Outlook After Strong Second Quarter
body: Switzerland said economic growth this year will be almost twice as fast as previously expected, while predicting inflation will stay comfortably within the central bank’s target range.

The State Secretariat for Economic Affairs now sees gross domestic product, adjusted for large sports events, expanding 1.7% in 2026, up from its June projection of 0.9%. For next year, it kept its projection at 1.6%.

The upgrade to the near-term outlook follows a surprisingly strong second quarter. But the agency, known as SECO, said that performance was driven by the volatile pharmaceutical sector “is likely to overstate underlying economic momentum.”

The improved outlook chimes with that of the OECD, which earlier this week significantly raised its own estimates. The Swiss economy has proven remarkably resilient this year amid high oil prices and ongoing tensions in the country’s trade relationship with the US. On Thursday, SECO highlighted both as risks to the outlook.
The agency kept its inflation forecasts unchanged, at 0.6% for this year and next.
That’s in line with the Swiss National Bank’s June forecasts. The central bank — which has an inflation target of 0-2% — will issue new predictions when it meets again on Sept. 24.

Policymakers are widely expected to keep their interest rate at zero then, while they may tweak language on their willingness to intervene on the franc, given that the currency has depreciated considerably against the euro recently.
Officials expect to leave the key rate on hold until the end of 2027, people familiar with the thinking inside the central bank told Bloomberg in July.

items.title: India Outsourcing Shifts Upmarket as AI Reshapes Jobs, ING Says
body: India’s outsourcing industry is showing little sign of losing ground to artificial intelligence as the country moves up the value chain into services that are harder to automate, according to ING Bank NV.

Software services exports have climbed to roughly 5.2% of gross domestic product from 3.3% before the pandemic, ING economist Deepali Bhargava wrote in a note Wednesday. Business services — including finance, accounting, engineering, research and analytics — have more than doubled their share of GDP to 3.3% over the same period.

The performance challenges concerns that generative AI could undermine one of India’s most important industries by automating work traditionally outsourced to lower-cost markets. India commands more than half of the global outsourcing industry and earns around $205 billion annually from software services exports, which support about 5.8 million workers, according to ING. Software and business services exports together are equivalent to about 8.5% of GDP and provide an important source of foreign exchange.

“AI disruption fears look premature in India and the Philippines,” Bharghava, who heads ING’s Asia-Pacific research said. “The evidence points to adaptation, not decline. AI is reshaping what gets outsourced, not shrinking demand for it.”

Growth is shifting away from repetitive tasks such as data entry, document verification and customer support toward higher-value work including analytics, and software development. India is also seeing strong demand for services such as risk management, engineering design and research and development.
India’s digitally delivered services exports have grown 45% since 2022, compared with 32% globally, allowing the country to gain market share, according to ING.

items.title: Japan Appoints Bear Control Czar as Attacks Surge to Record
body: Sign up for the Next Japan newsletter, for an inside view of the forces reshaping Japan, and what’s next for its businesses, markets and consumers.
Japan will have a cabinet minister in charge of dealing with bear attacks, reflecting heightening concern as the number of deadly incidents surges.

Hiroyoshi Sasagawa, a ruling party lawmaker who was named environment minister in a cabinet reshuffle on Thursday, will take on the newly created portfolio of bear control czar. He’ll also serve as minister in charge of nuclear emergency preparedness.

Bear sightings skyrocketed in the year ended March to 50,776, more than the previous two years combined, according to government data. The number of people injured in attacks reached a record 238, while deaths jumped to 13 from just three the previous year.
Read more: Japan Turns to Anime to Help Kids Avoid Bears As Attacks Triple
The government attributes the increase to bears being drawn to farmland abandoned by aging farmers as well as a decline in the number of hunters, among other factors.
