items.title: The Best Portuguese Egg Tarts in Hong Kong and Macau, Ranked
body: In this week’s Hong Kong Edition, Tara Mulholland guides you through the very best egg tarts in Hong Kong, Venus Feng interviews the former star athlete CEO of AS Watson Group and David Ingles offers a glimpse of his musical tastes to highlight a key stock market trend. For the Review, Will Davies gives in to the temptations of cheese to test a fondue place.
To subscribe to this weekly newsletter for free, click here.

Mid-Autumn festival is upon us, and with it, a craving for small round pastries. Having already ranked Hong Kong’s best mooncakes last year, we’re turning a critical eye on another bakery staple — the humble egg tart.
Hong Kong and egg tarts go together like yuen and yeung, with recommendations for the beloved custard-and-pastry confections topping every city tourist guide.

And just as New Yorkers never agree on the best pizza place, Hong Kongers can have wildly different preferences for their favorite tart purveyor — from local bakeries to major chains, Hong Kong or Macau brands, and a growing array of flavors, toppings and sizes.

A recent influx of international bakeries has threatened to upset the delicate pastry ecosystem, with London’s Santa Nata and Lisbon’s Manteigaria setting up shop a few streets apart and drawing long queues in Central this summer.
It’s forced the Hong Kong Edition team to confront an eternal question: Who really makes the best egg tart in town (and in our equally pastry-loving neighbor Macau)?

As we can’t visit every bakery out there, we narrowed our scope to the top eight Portuguese-style egg tarts on the market, distinguishable from the Hong Kong style by their flaky crust and caramelized top. During the blind taste test, our discerning panel of judges drew on childhood memories, culinary training and good old-fashioned gluttony to declare one clear winner:
1. Bakehouse - 8/10

What is there left to say about the Bakehouse egg tart? For all its ubiquity — around 30,000 are produced every day — it still managed to top our blind taste test, and surprised some judges who didn’t recognize it or had never eaten one. Since the chain launched in Wan Chai in 2018, its blue-and-white bags have become a mainstay on Instagram and Xiaohongshu, with branches stretching from Sha Tin to Victoria Peak and, soon, Hong Kong International Airport. It’s all built on the back of the little sourdough egg tart, its teacup-like shell encasing a distinctive crème brûlée filling, winning points for its deep, slightly roasted flavor and firmness.
Various locations in Hong Kong, HK$14 ($1.80) per tart.
2. Manteigaria - 7.5/10

This much-hyped new addition to Central’s bakery scene was also one of the highest-praised by our judges — they loved the tarts’ thin, flaky crust, the cinnamon notes in the sweet filling and the harmonious balance between the two. (One also noted the crust had stayed crunchy even after sitting in the fridge.) For those who want even more cinnamon in their custard, a cute spice sachet comes with every tart.
Shop B G/F, Man Hing Commercial Building, 79-83 Queen’s Road Central, Hong Kong, HK$15 per tart.
3. Lord Stow’s - 7.35/10

The birthplace of the Macanese egg tart — less lemony and cinnamony than its Portuguese cousin — still produces the Platonic ideal of the pastry for some of our judges, who singled out the balanced buttery egginess of the filling. But the bakery’s adherence to tradition was met with shrugs from some of the panel who were looking for variations on the form.
Various locations in Macau, 10-14 patacas per tart.
4. Hashtag B - 6.6/10

Technically a Napoleon egg tart, Hashtag B’s viral offering stands out for its wavy, crunchy crust and hefty proportions. (We tried the mini tart — the maxi version is even larger.) Some judges found the crust overwhelmed the delicate filling, though its consistency was singled out for praise.
Various locations in Hong Kong, HK$14 per tart.
5. Margaret’s Café e Nata - 6.2/10

Margaret Wong co-founded Lord Stow’s bakery in 1989, and now runs Macau’s other major producer of traditional egg tarts. Judges praised the flake factor of the pastry, though the slightly more subdued filling provoked a mixed response.
17B R. do Cmte. Mata e Oliveira, Macau, 11 patacas per tart.

“Is this really Portuguese?” one judge queried, not unkindly. These tarts look pretty different to their Macanese neighbors at Lord Stow’s and Margaret’s Café, and their lack of egginess is distinct from the more traditional egg tart formula. But the flakiness of the wavy-edged pastry found some fans.
Various locations in Macau, 12 patacas per tart.

The biggest egg tart supplier on the list has taken the oddest route to get there. Not content with dominating the chicken side of fast food, KFC aimed for the other side of the world’s oldest question in 1999 when it bought Margaret Wong’s egg tart recipe (yes, her again) after a blind taste test. Its long history as an affordable China-wide treat has lodged it in the memory of some judges, with one commenting that it reminded him of his childhood egg tarts. However, it lost points for an overly eggy flavor and “factory-made” feel.
Various locations in Hong Kong, HK$8 per tart.
8. Santa Nata - 5.1/10

The other new challenger for the egg tart crown won both very high and very low scores, with its extremely gooey, vanilla-y custard dividing opinion. The chewy crust had some fans, though one judge noted a flowery aftertaste. The exterior of Santa Nata’s Central branch has a large bell bearing the legend “ring the bell if we do well!” Sadly, Hong Kong Edition will not be ringing it.
25-27 Lyndhurst Terrace, Hong Kong, HK$14 per tart.
—Tara Mulholland

Hong Kong unveiled its first five-year plan yesterday and while it largely hewed to expectations, there were a few surprises. As we surmised in our preview, there was extensive discussion of the Northern Metropolis, with some actual hard targets sprinkled in. Predictably, there was also an expression of the city’s ambitions for wide-ranging areas, from building a global gold trading hub to attracting more international students.

The biggest new measure, though, was probably a plan to cut the property stamp duty for new parents — the latest attempt to address the city’s spiraling demographic crisis. A plan to radically expand public housing also sounded more forceful than what we heard before.

On the finance front, those expecting more clarity on some much talked-about plans for bolstering the bond market did get something to chew on. The main goal is to deepen Hong Kong’s role as an offshore yuan hub and the city will also promote dim sum bond sales.

Malina Ngai has had to handle various twists and turns in her life. She was a track-and-field athlete before a knee injury made her pivot to rowing, despite not knowing how to swim. No matter, she still won a bronze medal in the lightweight double sculls at the 1994 Asian Games. Ngai later entered the corporate world, where she’s risen all the way to CEO at one of Hong Kong’s most storied brands, AS Watson, now in its 185th year.

We caught up on the sidelines of the PBC Forum, convened by the Hong Kong Jockey Club Charities Trust, to chat about Ngai’s daily routine, her successes and journey into the heart of retailing in the city. —Venus Feng
What drove you to the retail business more than 20 years ago?

Crisis management. It was the first year I joined CK Hutchison, and there was a crisis related to AS Watson in one of the Asian markets. I was sent by the headquarters to be on site to support the local managing director to handle the crisis. It was like just one month in and I was very new to the company.

Because of my athlete background, we are normally quick to analyze facts and the environment and come up with decisions. I was able to stay cool and manage the people I didn’t really know at the time. We managed to get out of the crisis in three days. After this mission, they started asking if I would like to join.
What’s your daily work schedule like as the CEO of a brand with outlets across the world?

If I am in Hong Kong, I usually wake up at 6 a.m. and then I check my emails because they will be coming from Europe overnight. After refreshing myself, the first thing I do actually is two minutes of planking, because that helps me to clear my mind and think through the day — what are the key events and what I really want to achieve. Then I get on the treadmill for about 30 minutes, and after that I will have breakfast and go to work. Breakfast is very important for me to start the engine. My typical day could have 10 to 12 meetings and I try to leave the office at 7 p.m. latest. I might check work emails when I arrive home, but I also try to sleep right after 10 p.m.

But if I’m traveling, it could be like four days in four different countries when I am heading to Europe. Waking up at 5 a.m., then get to the airport and get to the work location, finish a whole day of meetings with the local teams and customers. Then the next day, all over again before I head home.
What’s a typical breakfast to help you keep up all this energy?
Boiled eggs, sweet potatoes and a glass of milk or protein drink.
It’s a quite interesting fun fact from the panel just now that you cannot swim but won a bronze medal for rowing at Asian Games decades ago. Do you still go rowing these days?

I’m so embarrassed that I still cannot swim. The good thing is, when you can’t swim, what would you do? You focus on staying on the boat and getting back to the pontoon as soon as possible. So you row very fast!

I am scared of water in general. But I’ve also tried to go indoor rowing on a rowing machine. The muscle memory comes back to me, like how the coach asked me to row all out in the old days. I just do it once in a while now.
What do you think is the biggest trait you learned from sports that can re-apply in your management life?

It’s the resilience. When I was an athlete, I didn’t even know this word. As an athlete, we lose more often than we win. Or when you have been winning medals, setting records, and suddenly you have an injury — it’s like your whole world stops. I recall at the time for my first serious injury on the knee, I didn’t know what to do and it took me nearly a year to get back up — I was really upset and kept asking why, but then I decided to move on and focus on what was next. I really wanted to represent Hong Kong so I chose to switch to rowing.

When you have a challenge in the business environment, what do you do? You can’t keep asking why we have so many competitions and why we have this and that. It’s about focusing on what you can control. I can’t control the macroeconomics. I can’t control competitions, but I can control how we improve the business day after day for the customer.
The retail and business landscape in Hong Kong has changed a lot in recent years. How would you see a historic brand like AS Watson adapting to the new trends?

We are 185 years old, but there’s one thing that hasn’t changed — we are very focused on our customers. Imagine walking into a store called Hong Kong Dispensary 185 years ago. It was a small pharmacy selling Western medicines and the store manager Alexander Skirving Watson kept focusing on one thing: Where do you feel sick and how can I treat you? It’s not about thinking about where to grow and where to open more stores. It’s the same for us today, although we have grown into an international retailer. It’s still all about thinking about the customers.

It’s not that retail is dying because no one goes to the shops. It’s about focusing on what the customers need — how do they shop now and how can we support them? Over my journey of more than two decades here, we grew from an Asia player to a global player with acquisitions in Europe. Then we became more specialized in categories, from pharmacy to health and beauty. Then the digital evolution came, and we built the online shop so customers can look for products anytime, anywhere. Now with AI, we are also transforming, and seeing how we can make the whole company more intelligent.
Each week, David Ingles, chief markets editor for Asia at Bloomberg TV and host of The China Show, looks beyond the headlines at some of the less obvious moves in financial markets.

It’s been 25 years since the release of one of the greatest songs ever written (editors note: opinions expressed in this segment are David’s). So I’m taking this random opportunity to crowbar the title into this week’s chart.

The top panel shows turnover in Hong Kong’s equity market. The bottom panel tracks the amount of Hong Kong-listed stocks that mainland investors are buying. Suffice to say, flows in Hong Kong are now largely determined by the amount of money flowing across the border.

Hong Kong unveiled its first-ever five-year plan this week, aligning the city’s long-term economic strategy even closer with China’s. Looking at how the two equity markets are tied at the hip, it does make a lot of sense.
The song’s chorus goes on to say, “Way up high or down low, I’ll go wherever you will go.” It’s like The Calling wrote the anthem for this market moment way ahead of schedule.
We scope out the dining scene to let you know where to eat — everything from hole-in-the-wall joints to establishments with three Michelin stars. Read all our reviews here.

I’m pretty sure the last time I’d had a cheese fondue was up a snowy Swiss alp in winter, a world away from Hong Kong’s 30-degree (86 Fahrenheit) heat and humidity levels that could melt a marmot. But I’m a sucker for cheese, regardless of the conditions, so Stübli in Kennedy Town piqued my interest.

Tucked away on Cadogan Street, Stübli is on the western end of Kennedy Town where Bistro du Vin and Piccolo used to be. Several restaurants have come and gone on this short stretch of road over the years, but it’s not a complete culinary deathtrap — a few yards up, a branch of pasta chain Pici does a decent job of anchoring a crowd, and Stübli’s been around a few months now.

Cheese fondue’s been around a lot longer — a couple of centuries at least. It was a way for farmers and herders in the Alps to turn hardened cheese and stale bread into a hearty meal when fresher ingredients were in short supply. Given its popularity among peasants, I decided to take my two kids along.

Stübli means cozy room, and the restaurant is decked out accordingly, with wooden tables and chairs, Swiss flag bunting hanging from the ceiling and cowbells and other alpine paraphernalia on the walls.

For the fondue, we opted for a small caquelon of the classic “Neuchâtel Style” (HK$169) — gruyère and emmental cheese, white wine, garlic and kirsch, which I’m only just realizing now is an alcohol. There can’t have been much in there as it didn’t taste of much beyond cheese, and my children didn’t start a brawl.

The fondue comes with baguette chunks for skewering and dipping. Once they’d been wolfed down, we ordered a side of pickles (HK$39), which was a couple of gherkin slices, some carrot and a pickled onion or two.

The large versions of the other two fondues, Summer Black Truffle and Lobster Thermidor, cost HK$358 and HK$428, respectively — enough to alarm 19th-century Swiss peasants everywhere. Add-ons include cuts of air-dried beef and salami (HK$59).

Service was slightly haphazard. Our starter — wagyu beef tartare mixed with smoked egg yolks and topped off with crispy strips of potato chips (HK$129) — was served after the fondue. The waiter gently warned us it packed a bit of a punch, a point reflected in my younger daughter’s live review: “It’s really good but I can’t eat any more because it’s spicy, so can you take the rest of the ‘meat thing’ please?”

Child one was a bit more insightful, describing the dish as having a good mixture of texture and flavor, with the soft beef and crunchy chips complementing each other nicely. I agreed. I also said it was a bit spicy.

The menu has three so-called Stübli classics as well — veal strips, homemade sausage, and breadcrumbed veal loin though the last item was unavailable. We were steered in the direction of the wurst, served with thick red wine (oh dear) gravy and mashed potatoes (HK$189). It was decent but expensive at that price.

The medium-rare Australian grain-fed striploin steak (HK$266) came with creamy peppercorn sauce and a side of Swiss salad that was well doused in a honey-infused dressing. We skipped ordering more sides, which — at HK$59 per serving — were rösti, fries and mashed potato.

There was just about enough cheese left over in our caquelon to smear on the slices of steak too. We tucked in, only pausing for a moment after learning that the cheesy crust in the bottom of the pot is known as the grandmother.

Feeling fairly stuffed at this point, we still pushed on into desserts, ordering the Coupe Peach Melba (HK$89) — vanilla gelato and white peach sorbet with poached peaches, raspberry sauce, toasted almonds and whipped cream — and a chocolate tart (HK$99) with a deliciously crispy base.
The vibe: Cozy and relaxed. Music plays at an appropriate volume and included classics from the likes of Duran Duran and Phil Collins — hardly an album of authentic yodeling, but frankly preferable.
Who’s next to you: The place was about three-quarters full when we arrived at 7 p.m. on Tuesday, mostly twentysomething friends and couples, and a family or two.
Can you conduct a meeting here? While the tables are packed closely together, yes, you could.
What we’d order again: It’s no great friend of the lactose intolerant, but it would have to be the classic cheese fondue. Also the chocolate tart. I’d give the rösti fries a go too.

Need to know: Stübli is located on 39-41 Cadogan Street in Kennedy Town, connected to sister restaurant Nocino, which leans more toward Italian-Swiss cuisine like pasta. It’s open Monday through Sunday from 11:30 a.m. to 10 p.m., and you can reserve a table in advance. —Will Davies

items.title: Hong Kong Property Stocks Fall as Rate Hike Threatens Recovery
body: Shares of Hong Kong developers dropped after the city followed the Federal Reserve with an interest rate increase, fueling concerns that higher borrowing costs may derail a nascent housing market recovery.

The benchmark Hang Seng Index’s property sub-gauge fell as much as 2.4%, heading for its lowest closing level since early January. Sun Hung Kai Properties Ltd. and Hang Lung Properties Ltd. led declines by losing at least 3.4% each.

The latest rate hike by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, which moves in lockstep with the Fed to protect the local dollar’s peg to the greenback, threatens to weaken demand in a property market that’s just emerged from a prolonged slump. Investor sentiment has already started souring after China stepped up efforts to curb outflows of mainland capital, once a strong growth driver for the city’s housing sector.
READ: Hong Kong Follows Fed With First Rate Hike in Over Three Years

“Hong Kong’s reinvigorated housing market may face softening investment demand if the US fed funds rate rises another 25 basis points in 4Q after its latest hike by 25 basis points,” said Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Patrick Wong.

Earlier this year, there were expectations for home prices in the Asian financial hub to head for their strongest growth in nearly a decade, driven by robust mainland Chinese demand, tight inventory and rising rental yields.

Hong Kong’s first five-year development plan unveiled on Wednesday also offered no major support for housing demand, according to Morgan Stanley. “We think additional supply in the Northern Metropolis and higher public-housing output should not materially alter current residential supply-demand dynamics in the near term,” the brokerage’s analyst Praveen Choudhary wrote in note, referring to the technology hub in the northern part of the city.

items.title: Goldman Says Go for Gasoline as Global Fuel Crunch Morphs
body: Gasoline stands to extend gains as tightness in global fuel markets spreads, according to Goldman Sachs Group Inc., which shifted a trading call to the popular motor fuel and away from diesel.

“The key reason for this new recommendation is that refiners’ switching output from gasoline to diesel is rapidly tightening gasoline markets,” analysts including Yulia Zhestkova Grigsby and Daan Struyven said in a note.

Global fuel markets have been squeezed this year by the combined impact of the US-Iran conflict and the war between Russia and Ukraine, with Kyiv pummeling Moscow’s refineries. In the US, diesel futures have settled at a record, and average retail pump prices for the fuel have rallied to an all-time high, as gains in product prices far outstrip advances in crude oil.

While diesel may yet climb further, gasoline now offered “more upside price opportunities,” the analysts said in the Sept. 16 report, citing reasons including more resilient demand and relative shifts in stockpiles.

As a result, the bank closed an earlier call for gains between different diesel contracts, betting on shifts in so-called timespreads, and recommended a long position in European gasoline for mid-2027, the analysts wrote. “High diesel prices cause high gasoline prices,” they said in the report’s title.

items.title: Warsh's Fed Soars Like a Hawk Into a Hiking Cycle
body: To get John Authers’ newsletter delivered directly to your inbox, sign up here.

Heading into Wednesday’s Federal Open Market Committee meeting, it was a truth almost universally acknowledged that the central bank would raise rates. New Chair Kevin Warsh’s speech last month at Jackson Hole appeared to leave him no choice. Many were unconvinced a hike was necessary, and expected Warsh to draw the sting by hinting this would be “one and done,” not the start of a hiking cycle.
He didn’t do that. By the close, markets were convinced that more hikes would come, and that Warsh was happy about it. A potentially contentious meeting  ended with unusual clarity.
Why so convinced? Key clues were:

Perhaps the single clearest indication of intent was the dot plot, which Warsh dislikes. The other members submitted projections that showed their average predicted fed funds rate for the end of the year had risen 25 basis points since the last dot plot in June. Their estimate for the end of 2027 rose half a percentage point:
The accompanying statement revised the previous version from July subtly but clearly in a hawkish direction. Here it is, with changes annotated in red by Oxford Economics:

References to supply shocks are out, while there is now a broader nod to geopolitics rather than the specifics of the war with Iran. Then came the Warsh press conference, in which reporters weren’t allowed to ask follow-ups to their questions. It was truncated to 29 minutes from the usual 45, but the way stocks and bonds traded during his brief back-and-forth showed that he’d had enough time to make his point:

The biggest reaction was in foreign exchange, portending confidence in the Fed but also a tightening of financial conditions in the emerging world. The JPMorgan EM FX index of emerging currencies dropped to its lowest since March, while Bloomberg’s broad dollar index enjoyed its best day since Warsh’s first FOMC meeting sparked a rally three months ago:

To some extent, the key was what Warsh didn’t say, rather than what he did. There was no suggestion that this was a one-off. Instead, he said the FOMC has “removed a dose of accommodation” — not all of it, implying the rate was still accommodative and that there would be more doses in the prescription. He added that the hike “starts to show we’re serious about this.” If that was only a start to the seriousness, the direct implication is to brace for more.

As a result, the market priced in a lot of tightening. Implicit fed funds rates, as gauged by the Bloomberg World Interest Rate Probabilities, were projected to peak below 4% when Warsh took office in May — at a point when the market had already had time to adjust to the energy shock from the Iran war. Expectations crept up a bit by the time he spoke at Jackson Hole; and since then the market has braced for three more hikes before the Fed is done:

This turnabout is made all the more remarkable by the fact that inflation has declined since Warsh took over. There’s no obvious change in the environment in that time to force the central bank to shift direction. It also, of course, runs directly counter to the express wishes of President Donald Trump, who nominated him. He responded to the news with a social media post calling for rates to come down to 1%.

Trump didn’t, however, attack Warsh by name, and in comments to reporters appeared to suggest that his chairman was the prisoner of a hostile committee: “You might as well vote with the board because it’s not going to matter. The board is very hostile, very political.”

That’s not the way everyone else saw it, with the unanimity widely interpreted as showing that Warsh was beginning to exert control. Steven Englander of Standard Chartered PLC, who earlier cautioned that a hike wasn’t necessary, explained how the chairman convinced investors that it was his idea to tighten further:

Given the Fed’s stark change of direction, and the heated political environment, the market reaction was remarkable chiefly for its moderation. Stocks fell, but by the close the S&P 500 had shed only 0.45% while the Nasdaq 100, home of the big tech groups that lead this bull market, was flat — a non-reaction that implies investors don’t think the AI boom has much to fear from a hiking cycle. The 10-year yield rose to 5.02%, but it had gone slightly higher on Tuesday. This wasn’t the much-feared disorderly bond selloff, implying some degree of confidence in Warsh.

In the longer term, this moment could yet seem more significant. It’s a big step away from the “new normal” conditions that followed the Global Financial Crisis, and implies the destination is not the pre-crisis “old normal” driven by globalization and favorable demographics. Salman Ahmed of Fidelity International argued:

The calm reception so far shows investors’ acceptance that the world is more expensive and could require higher rates. That calm can continue if bonds move in orderly fashion, and whether the strengthening dollar drives crises in the many countries that have big overhangs of government debt.

Bitcoin investors were seriously disappointed by the US Senate’s inability to advance the Clarity Act — legislation aimed at providing clear legal parameters for the crypto industry (or, to its critics, make life far too easy for crypto scammers). Their disappointment is understandable. Cryptocurrency had been enjoying a rare good spell, driven predominantly by renewed concerns about debasement after Scott Bessent’s Treasury buyback announcement, which prompted a 30% rebound in a matter of days.  But it never regained all its losses for the year, and the Senate vote not to move the Clarity Act forward knocked the wind out of Bitcoin’s sails again:

For crypto enthusiasts, this setback stings. Until Bessent’s announcement, Bitcoin had been in the doldrums, and losing support from institutional investors. The return of the debasement trade had raised the prospect of a sustained rally.

Before the legislation failed, Bitcoin exchange-traded fund flows had surged, attracting $3.5 billion in August and another $600 million so far in September. Bloomberg Intelligence’s analysis shows that Bitcoin funds have attracted a cumulative $55 billion since the launch over two years ago, down from a high of $63 billion.

However, the latest tumble by more than 4% underscores how much investors needed the Clarity Act. To quote Bitwise Asset Management’s Matthew Hougan, “If Clarity had passed, crypto would have been the consensus smart money trade in Q4.”

This administration continues to be the most crypto-friendly by an awesome distance. Still, some of the Senate sticking points should have investors questioning its staying power. Democrats raised concerns over ethics provisions concerning governing officials’ crypto holdings, an apparent dig at the Trump family’s huge stake in crypto.

It’s unclear how much that affected the vote. It’s plausible that this is not the end of the road, especially if Republicans make concessions as they did last year with the GENIUS Act — which established a regulatory framework for issuing stablecoins and also failed its first cloture vote. But as Frnt Financial’s Stephane Ouellette notes, the two scenarios are slightly different:

How realistic are the odds that the Clarity Act sees the light of day? Prediction markets give a very slim probability that it ever passes. Regardless, Trump’s crypto empire and his commitment to the asset class suggest that there will likely be more policy tailwinds from Washington.

Meanwhile, the war in the Middle East could determine crypto’s trajectory. Bitcoin hasn’t worked as a safe haven. It’s hard to see how it could weather a possible escalation, particularly one that coincides with tighter monetary policy.
Of course, enthusiasts have seen worse. Between 2017 and 2020, Bitcoin went more than 1,100 days without making an all-time high. The current drought stands at less than 350.
—Richard Abbey

items.title: New GLP-1 Pills Curb Snacking Less Than Shots in Survey
body: Users of GLP-1 pills for weight loss curbed their snacking less than those taking the treatment through shots, according to new research from Bloomberg Intelligence.

Among those taking the drugs orally, 74% said they were eating fewer salty snacks, compared to 80% for those taking a GLP-1 via injection, according to the BI report. Similarly, 76% of pill users said they were eating fewer baked goods, lower than the 82% for those taking a shot. That pattern was repeated in other categories, including confections and shelf-stable foods like soup.

“Though oral GLP-1s still pose a challenge for food makers like Mondelez, Hershey, Kraft Heinz and General Mills, growth in pill use could reduce the negative impact of weight-loss drugs on product sales,” Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Jennifer Bartashus and Keana Bloomfield said in the report, which is based on the findings of a survey of 1,001 people in the US in July.
Mondelez and Hershey are still among the most exposed to potential sales declines, Bartashus and Bloomfield wrote, since GLP-1 users cut back most dramatically on candy, baked goods and salty snacks.

The GLP-1 pills also showed slightly less effectiveness in curbing how often people snacked, according to the survey. Among people who used to eat three snacks per day before going on a weight-loss drug, 49% of those injecting the treatment curbed their snacking to once a day. Among pill takers, 39% did the same.
Those on shots also increased their consumption of fruits and vegetables by more than those taking the pill form, according to the survey.
In studies, GLP-1 pills have been linked to slightly less weight loss than shots. However, drugmakers caution against using cross-trial comparisons.

While the pill version of the treatments may be less effective than injections, their introduction is expected to spark rising GLP-1 use over the coming years, in part because it’s easier for most people to take. By 2030, more than 19% of the population is expected to be on a GLP-1 drug, up from about 7.5% this year, according to the BI report.

The increasing prevalence of GLP-1 medications has emerged as a threat to food companies’ sales growth since users eat less. However, companies say they’re adapting to changes in preference and have bolstered their selection of products with higher contents of protein, fiber and other nutrients. PepsiCo Inc., for example, now offers high-protein Doritos and Smartfood FiberPop popcorn.

Food company executives have pointed to past data that shows GLP-1 users reverting to their previous eating habits when they go off them. However, BI’s survey found that 46% of those who stopped taking the medications said they’re consistently maintaining their grocery shopping habits, and 41% said they’ve consistently maintained lower consumption of soft drinks.

items.title: Inside China's $7 Trillion Green Finance Market
body: When it comes to green tech, China is a list of superlatives. It produces more solar panels, wind turbines, electric vehicles and batteries than anywhere else in the world. But is finance the real climate hero?

This week on Zero, Akshat Rathi is joined by Ma Jun, chairman of the Hong Kong Green Finance Association and former chief economist of China’s central bank. They discuss how the country became a green-finance superpower and how other nations can speed up their own transitions.
Listen now, and subscribe on Apple, Spotify, or YouTube to get new episodes of Zero every Thursday.
Our transcripts are generated by a combination of software and human editors, and may contain slight differences between the text and audio. Please confirm in audio before quoting in print.
Akshat Rathi

Long gone are the heady days of 2021, where week after week, enormous financial institutions made commitments to transition to a net-zero world. Take the example of GFANZ, the Glasgow Financial Alliance for Net Zero, one of the signature pacts to clean up the sector. It was once on the lips of every climate finance expert.

Now, it barely gets a mention. And yet, without the right kind of finance, there is no way to tackle climate change. The money dictates what gets built, where and how quickly. If spent right, it can turbocharge the transition. If not, we will be saddled with polluting assets.

Joining me this week is Dr. Ma Jun, chairman of the Hong Kong Green Finance Association and former chief economist of China’s central bank. This is Zero, I'm Akshat Rathi, recording live at  Hong Kong Green Week. Today: where next for climate finance?
Akshat Rathi

Dr. Ma Jun, thank you for joining us here at the BloombergNEF event. So today we are going to talk about the opportunities and challenges that Asia faces on the energy transition. And maybe we start by looking back first, because we are sitting in a region that is seeing some of the fastest rollouts of green technologies anywhere in the world. Be it solar panels in the Philippines, wind turbines in Vietnam, or electric cars in Thailand. Or, all of those technologies in China. This needed technology development, it needed policy, it needed finance, and of course it needed people. But from your vantage point, having worked on finance and green finance for such a long time in this region, what do you think finance did to help Asia get to this point in the transition?
Ma Jun

Well, thank you very much, Akshat, and also thanks to BloombergNEF for inviting me once again. Your question of the three key pillars of  transition — one is policy, one is technology, one is finance — I've been working on all of these, but finance has been my real focus in the last 12 years. Since 2014, when I joined the PBOC, the People's Bank of China, I began to work on green finance policies. Before that, I actually spent 13 years in Hong Kong. I was the chief economist for Deutsche Bank in the Greater China region. And in that transition between Deutsche Bank and PBOC, I turned myself from a macroeconomist into a climate finance specialist.

In my PBOC time, starting from 2014, I began to work on the need for green finance. Initially, in China, we were talking about air pollution. Some of you, if you were in Beijing back 12 years ago, you were wearing masks, right? It was not because of Covid. Everybody was fearing the health impact of PM2.5 exceeding 100 and so on. Our proposal at that time for the Chinese central government was that you need to raise something like 4 trillion renminbi a year to fix pollution, which included air pollution, land pollution, water contamination, and so on. But the government had no money, the government had only 10% of the required budget. That's why green finance had to kick in.

So very quickly, within a few months, my team was able to convince the central government to do it. In 2015, this proposal of setting up a green financial system was written into a central government document called the Eco-Civilization Plan. Then it became a mandate for the central bank to lead the coordination of the seven ministries and drive the framework for green finance. I was doing this job from 2015 to 2016, essentially coordinating the central bank, the ministry of finance, environmental ministry, NDRC (National Development and Reform Commission), securities commissions and also banking insurance committee, drafting the guideline for green finance. Within the guideline, which at that time contained about 35 actions, we are now seeing the largest green lending market and largest green bond market in the world, with the outstanding Chinese green loans and green bonds amounting to about $7 trillion. It's about 50 trillion renminbi. It's a mind-boggling number.

These financing instruments in the form of loans and bonds went into renewables and into electric vehicles. That's why China now has 70% of renewable production capacity — not necessarily deployment in China — and also 70% of the EV production, 70% of batteries in the world.
Akshat Rathi

Have the lessons from what China has been able to do, maybe let's take the central bank policy, has that been used or applied or translated in any other part of the world, looking at how China has been able to create this lead in green technologies?
Ma Jun

Yes. China is unique in the sense that the central bank is part of the government. It's not a so-called independent central bank. When a central bank is independent, it anchors its policy only on one or two objectives, which is, for example, CPI (Consumer Price Index) being 2% and financial stability. These narrowly focused central banking policies actually restrict the ability of the central bank to deliver climate-related actions.

The Chinese central bank responds to the government’s responses, which is carbon neutrality and all of these. That's the government objective, then the central bank has to do its part. For example, the Chinese central bank put out this decarbonization facility, which now offers a funding cost of 1.25% for renewables. No other central bank can do that, because all the central banks say, ‘it's not my mandate,’ and ‘why should I give cheap money through a commercial bank and to renewable projects?’

Also, the central bank in China, we actually rank the commercial banks on their green performance because we mandate each bank to report the green loans. China, I think, is now the only country that has a central bank mandate for commercial banks to report green loans based on taxonomy. That's why each of the 4,000 banks report the green loan ratio, and we can see which ones are doing better. The high ones have like a 35% green loan ratio, the low ones 5%. Obviously, 35% is being praised and being recognized as a good performer, and they get other incentives as well. This is a very unique incentive, which only China does.
Akshat Rathi
Would you say then, one thing that maybe central banks abroad can look at is actually growing their mandate from these limited mandates they have, which are based on employment and on inflation?
Ma Jun

Some central banks try to be more open-minded and are breaking these traditional rules of central banking. For example, the central bank of Hungary, a few years ago, was telling me that they have adopted a practice of giving capital relief on green loans, meaning the risk or weights on green assets is being lowered by the central bank of Hungary. In fact, yesterday, I was moderating a session, and to my surprise, the central bank of Macau, which is the monetary authority of Macau, said that they gave a 15% discount to the capital charge on green assets as well, which is wonderful. So, they are not following the traditional central banking practices and conventions, but they are now making innovations. But these cases are still quite rare.
Akshat Rathi

Now, let's talk a little bit about the green bond market, but also just green finance in general. You talked about how in China alone, there's $7 trillion worth of outstanding green finance, if you include bonds, loans and equities. Now, some of the green bond issuances have been done in London, for example, and they've been very successful for China, and they're looking to do more of these. What is it from the China green bond experience that other countries can learn?
Ma Jun

Yeah, some things other countries wouldn't be able to replicate because China is so big. And I was talking to some of the smaller economies about how China issues 1,000 green bonds every year. They were shocked because some of the smaller countries do a few issuance every year. So, that's a size thing. And given the size, you've got an advantage because the cost goes down for all the infrastructure. For example, back in 2015, when I was initiating the green bond market, we were worried about not having enough third-party verifiers, and they were struggling to incubate these guys. And then within a year 18 verifiers popped up. And initially, the cost of verification was very high, something like 100,000 renminbi per piece. And now it goes down to 10,000 renminbi because of competition and also the scale of the economy. And a lot of companies in China are working on AI tools to label green loans.

In smaller markets, the labeling is very expensive because you hire consultants before accounting firms and so on, they charge very high service fees. And now the Chinese scale of economy involves using AI technology to reduce the cost of these services by 99%. That's a part that we benefit from, a scale economy.

But one of the things I think a lot of countries' economies can learn from is incentives. Some of the Chinese local governments offer interest subsidies for green loans and green bonds. And some actually give awards to the first issuance of every green piece, whether it's a green bond for this sector or a sustainability bond for that sector or a social bond for this sector. So every new innovation is being encouraged, which is very cheap in terms of a dollar amount that you need. But it has a very good encouragement in terms of setting examples and creating momentum for the market. So these are things I think that can be delivered in other places.
Akshat Rathi

And we talked about how a lot of the transition success has been in the electricity sector, partly because the technologies have been scalable, but also modular, and so prices have come down faster. There are other sectors in the economy that really need to catch up on the transition.

The Iran war, for example, has really made countries think about energy security and they are moving away from fossil fuels, but they can only do so in the sectors that are economic. And they are doing that on electricity, as we've seen from the import figures from Chinese technologies going into other countries.

In other parts of the economy, industry for example, there's still a long way to go to try and bring in green technologies. I know you've done some work on the steel sector, but there's steel, there's cement, there's plastics. So many of the industrial sectors still need ways to be able to transition. What can finance do to help the industrial sector transition?
Ma Jun

Yeah, for the carbon intensive sectors that you mentioned — steel, cement, petrochemical, coal-fired power generation, aviation, shipping and so on — this is what we call transition finance. Back a few years ago, we were focusing on pure green activities like renewables, electric vehicles, batteries and so on. And these were very big already, as I said, you know, 50 trillion renminbi or $7 trillion in China, largely for pure green.

But now in the last couple of years, we began to move towards building an ecosystem for transition finance, which is serving the hard to abate sectors. And in China, some experiments by the central government, central banks and also local governments, are putting out what they call transition taxonomies. Now, 11 sectors have transition taxonomies — by each sector.

Like steel, now the central bank has put out the pathways, whether you use scrap steel to make steel that has reduced carbon or uses hydrogen or uses clean energy. All of these pathways are able to help you to reduce carbon intensity of the steel sector. So once these pathways are done, then we're requiring the companies to develop their transition plans, which means that you need to have a credible transition plan and set targets for three years, five years, seven years of decarbonisation. And then you have to make the government structure work right for implementing the targets. At the same time, developing the instruments, for example sustainability-linked loans, to assist these companies to transition with lower costs. At the same time, a lot of pilot cities are asking them, don't lay off people because you have to take care of the social impact, right?

And then this transition process will be accompanied by, for example, retraining and reskilling programs. So all of these elements are incorporated into the ecosystem for transition finance. It's still small in terms of the total dollar amount, but the growth has been rapid. I've seen a lot of places where I've seen 100% growth of transition finance in China.
Akshat Rathi

And so the thing that is required over here is there is a little more complexity involved, right? In a green bond, you are very clear about what you're going to do and you raise finance toward that purpose. And so investors who are investing in a green bond know what they are getting as a result. Whereas with transition finance, you have to create a plan: for some time, there'll be higher emissions and then the emissions will lower. And each sector will have, as you said, different taxonomies, different plans. Are there ways in which that complexity can be managed or simplified? Or is this just how finance works, that complexity is part of the business?
Ma Jun

No, since evolving… a few years ago, we were talking about every transitioning company developing a transition plan in a formal way, setting targets, and getting third-party verification and having a governance structure, and so on and so forth. Now, after three years, we find that this is applicable only to large companies. A lot of small-medium companies are unable to develop the full version of the transition plan. They are unable to find a third party to verify the numbers because it's too expensive.

That's why recently my colleague was developing a new model for SMEs (small and medium-sized enterprises) to get into the transition finance space, which they call ‘look-back transition instruments’. Meaning that you don't have to pre-develop a transition plan, just try yourself and see if you can reduce carbon. Once you actually reduce carbon, come back to the bank, say, ‘can we claim this as transition finance?’ If it's not meeting the standards, then we forget about it and treat it as a regular loan. Now, this is being practiced in a couple of regions in China and elsewhere. And it’s now being documented in one of my colleague’s research reports. I think it's worth looking into.
Akshat Rathi
After the break, more of my conversation with Dr. Ma Jun. If you're enjoying this episode, please take a moment to rate and review Zero on whichever platform you're listening on.
Akshat Rathi

One other hot topic is AI data centers and how the demand for electricity is coming from these data centers. If AI becomes the promised land that it is, data centres will come here, and they will create a challenge for this region. It may not be an electricity supply challenge, it'll be the challenge of how to ensure that the electricity supply is clean. Is there something you can do, before this boom starts, before we see data centers getting powered by coal. Is there a way to ensure that they remain clean? So it's a different type of transition challenge from the industrial sector. You don't need to convert something that is dirty into clean, you want to start to build something clean from the get go.
Ma Jun

Yeah, I think data centers are facing two types of challenges. One is it competes for energy against other users. For example, this electricity supply is supposed to be for normal civilian usage — households, manufacturing, buildings — and so on. Now you compete, which will push up the power price. It has a social implication, which is negative for the community. That's one thing.

And the second challenge is that I see a lot of data centers are being built with dirty energy, dirty new energy, which means that they couldn't find a clean energy supply and they had to build coal-fired power plants and also maybe burn natural gas. And simply because they say, ‘Hey, I'm the project owner and have no other choices, this is the most convenient one that I can deploy.’

This problem needs to be addressed at a higher level, not at a single company level, because many of the renewable resources are not in the place where you want to build a data center. And it may be somewhere else. For example, recently we were looking at one project which does what we call geographical arbitrage. Basically, the data center is in Singapore, it doesn't have enough power, it doesn't have enough green power. So they found a place in a nearby island of Indonesia, and they built a large solar panel production facility to generate hydrogen. And they shipped hydrogen to Singapore to power the data center. And still the economics work, because the power tariff is high enough in Singapore and it's still cheaper and they become greener. But it requires coordination and requires import-export arrangements. So it's not a simple one company issue, it requires government-to-government geographical coordination.
Akshat Rathi

Now, coming to one of your hats, which is the Hong Kong Green Finance Association. Hong Kong remains among the top financial centers in the world. Can you talk through the role that Hong Kong has played in green financing, especially in the last 10 years? And where does it go from here?
Ma Jun

Yeah, Hong Kong started its journey towards building a green finance center, I think in 2017-18, when the government began to issue its sovereign green bonds. And I think Hong Kong remains the largest sovereign issuer in the green-bond market in the world. And this sets a very good example for the private sector in terms of how to identify what is green, how to do the labeling, how to do transparency and disclosure and so on.

And now Hong Kong offers a very sophisticated set of green financial products, including syndicated loans and green bonds, sustainability bonds, and now insurance and equity services for all kinds of green activities. Not just in Hong Kong, the majority of the fundraisers are actually coming from mainland China and ASEAN (Association of Southeast Asian Nations) countries to use the Hong Kong green financial services. And going forward, I think the demand is going to be even stronger, as I said yesterday at the Hong Kong GFA annual meeting.

China is now implementing its five-year plan, which requires a 17% reduction of carbon intensity in the next five years. It will drive massive demand for transition. Hong Kong can be the offering place for a lot of transition products. And ASEAN, I use this example of why ASEAN is going to be growing even faster than China in terms of green demand, because in Indonesia, on average you have three babies per family. In China, you have only 0.7. So in the future, you will see a massive growth of demand for virtually everything — for housing, for transportation, for energy, for water. All of these are required to be green, and the green investment growth, I think, in ASEAN countries will be even faster. And that's why financing and China’s technologies combined, I think, really can make a big difference there.
Akshat Rathi

And maybe let's talk about one finance instrument that is being used for all sorts of activities, but increasingly for green activities. So panda bonds, for example, which are these Chinese yuan denominated bonds that are issued by entities outside the mainland, but have investors from the mainland. Now, they've been issued in places like the Philippines, Indonesia and Pakistan, but also in Europe — in Hungary and in Portugal.

And some have been specifically… The goal for them when they are announcing the bond issuance is to go toward green activities, sometimes buying green technologies from China for those purposes. How do you see the panda bond market evolving and whether that can help the transition in other parts of the world?
Ma Jun

Yeah, I think it's developing very fast. In fact, a little more than a year ago, I was beginning to write about the panda bond market beginning to play a bigger role in transition — green transition for the global south. Now I've seen very rapid growth of this take up. In fact, in the last eight months, the issuance of panda bonds in the mainland market was about 200 billion renminbi. And similarly, we have a renminbi denominated market, which is the offshore renminbi market in Hong Kong. It's called the dim sum bond market and it saw something like 1 trillion renminbi of issuances.

And this means that the renminbi funding is cheap enough to attract a lot of issuers relative to US dollar funding. More recently, I think there was the Pakistani issuance of a panda bond in China, which was issued at a coupon rate of 2.5%. You cannot imagine that in any other markets. Of course, it had a guarantee from AIIB (Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank) and ADB (Asian Development Bank). But even with that, I think it substantially reduced the total cost of financing for those green activities in Pakistan. And many others are lining up to do that.

Also recently, there was issuance from Suzano, which is a company in Brazil that tapped into the Chinese green panda bond market, and there are many more in the Hong Kong dim sum bond market. So it's a matter of a promotion because the platform is there, the cheap funding cost is there, liquidity is there. But not everybody knows it.

In fact, when I was in Central Asia just a couple of weeks ago, I was talking to three banks in the Kyrgyz Republic. None of them knew that China has the panda bond market and Hong Kong has the dim sum bond market, which offers a much cheaper funding cost. And  they all showed interest immediately in this potential fundraising opportunity for them. So I think we need to do more. In fact, BNEF can be a good distributor of this message to potential issuers.
Akshat Rathi

We've also seen some countries actually change their sovereign bond issuances from being dollar denominated to yuan denominated because of the rising trade relationships they have. So Kenya has done it, Ethiopia is looking to do it. There is clearly a demand for more yuan denominated debt. But when we come to that, let's then talk about the tensions that are rising as a result.

The global bond market has been a dollar dominated one. And now the yuan is offering these options for many countries to try and get lower financing costs, which is — especially at this time of higher cost of living, but also really squeezed government finances is — something that they are tapping into. How do you manage to ensure that the tensions that are rising don't derail the transition?

So take Europe, for example. Europe has created a carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM) that is creating tensions between Europe and China, but also Europe and India. What are ways in which finance can try and help manage around the geopolitical tensions that are going to perhaps keep rising?
Ma Jun

Yeah, some of the tensions you mentioned are geopolitical in nature. Others are basically trade frictions. For example, a lot of EU actions are trade-related because they're fearing China taking over their jobs and China is becoming too competitive in certain markets and so on. But some of the tensions, especially on the US side, is more geopolitics — restricting access to all these high-tech products and other technologies.

But I think in the global south in general, we don't have that much concern. You know, China and ASEAN countries, China with Latin American countries, China with African countries, the trade is still largely free, and largely because we are quite complementary to each other in terms of economic structure. Most of the stuff that China produces, they don't produce, and they need our stuff.

Of course, China would like to invest more in these developing countries and relocate part of the supply chain, whether it's EVs or other manufacturing processes, so that we can not only lower the cost, because they are producing locally, and also creating jobs and building skills and building a long lasting mutually beneficial relationship between China and the global south. I think overall this is doing well.

But there's a way for China to enter the US and the European market by relocating production to some emerging market developing countries. For example, I was in Morocco recently and there are industrial parks there. They welcome Chinese companies to invest in industrial parks. And as long as you have enough local content developed in Morocco, then you can sell to Europe legally. It's not just illegally bypassing regulations. It's a legal pathway towards the European market. But that requires a lot of cooperation, engineering and the legal advice and the structuring of these transactions.
Akshat Rathi

Is there anything in the finance sector that can help this transition happen? So, for example, you mentioned Morocco, but also Brazil is another place where Chinese companies are relocating some of their manufacturing, BYD opened a plant recently. Is there anything that finance can do to help make these moves for Chinese companies easier in emerging markets?
Ma Jun

Finance plays a bigger role for mid-sized companies to drive their actions. For the very large companies, they don't worry about finance because they are very strong in terms of internal financing capabilities. And the banks are looking for them, begging them to borrow money.

But in the mid-market, a lot of companies are not capable of investing in big projects just using their internal resources, so they rely on external financing. That's why these financing sources, whether it's a multinational development bank or sovereign wealth company or large commercial banks, they can drive the company's relocation or production and help them to structure a transaction which is suitable for them to enter into multiple markets. And this is exactly what the Green Accelerator, which I launched yesterday, intends to do, because we're bringing these large finance institutions to influence these companies in terms of future decisions.
Akshat Rathi
Can you give an example of what the Green Accelerator might do?
Ma Jun

The Green Accelerator is set up as a non-profit entity in Hong Kong, which is supported by donors and also the Hong Kong government to prepare green projects in developing countries. Of course, there might be pilot projects in Hong Kong before we go out and scale up the operation. And the founding members, actually the seven founding members of the Green Accelerator, include the AIIB, the Chinese sovereign wealth company called the Silk Road Fund, and GenZero under Temasek, and also HSBC. A couple of others, including my Institute of Finance and Sustainability in Beijing, and also the Cambridge Institute for Sustainability Leadership, plus the Hong Kong EPD (Environmental Protection Department).

So we are coming together with the goal of really accelerating and helping these companies to prepare bankable projects, which can be investable by large organizations such as the ones that I just mentioned. And in the process, a couple of things need to be done by the accelerator.

Number one, we identify the right green technologies for other markets. Just to give you an example, a Chinese company that can produce desalinated water at a much lower cost than otherwise. They are now using this modular-based approach to build a desalination plant within one month instead of doing this within 12 months. And as a result, they are able to cut the cost of water by about 50%. So we're looking into how to help this company locate their production in Indonesia. Indonesia needs desalination services. This is just one of the many examples of how finance can help them to think about this deployment of their good technology in new places that need them more than in China.
Akshat Rathi

I live in London. When we look at conversations around the transition or around climate politics, it feels like a step back because many of the governments, especially in the US, but also some European governments, have slowed down the transition or have reversed some of their climate policies.

The pressure that investors had on corporations, on big multinationals and with the headquarters in Europe and America to come up with a transition plan to meet their net zero commitments, that pressure has gone down a little bit. Conversations here are very different. Over here, the pressure to come up with transition plans, etc., is newer, but it is growing. If you talk about the carbon intensity goal from China, that is really going to drive many of the Chinese companies to look at cutting emissions alongside, of course, all the profitable things that they have to do. Do you see this bifurcation slowing down progress on the climate front?
Ma Jun

I think one big problem in some of the Western countries is that the government is short of money. Before the Iran war and a lot of geopolitics development, they were still able to allocate some money to subsidize the green transition. And now, they are given the mandate to increase budget spending and they're doing a lot of other things. So there's little room, fiscal room, to subsidize.

And now it becomes a game of competing for very, very limited fiscal favor, whether you want to do this for health care, for the elderly, for immigration, or for the transition. And if you're squeezed, then everybody complains about who’s going to pay for that. I think the way out of this is to not rely on government subsidies. Instead, rely on technology. A couple of examples which show how technology can save the journey towards net zero.

In China, in the last seven years, the cost of batteries went down by 70%, the cost of solar panels came down close to 70%, and the cost of EV came down by 50%. If countries can engineer this kind of a reduction in cost, you don't need government subsidies. These green goods and services become competitive by themselves. They compete away the fossil fuel-powered alternatives. This, I think, should be the real focus of government and industrial policy, rather than competing for limited fiscal resources for subsidies.
Akshat Rathi

We saw in some of the numbers that even in the US, where we are seeing probably the clearest step back on climate policy, renewable investments go down a little bit over the next few years, but then they rise up again. Speaking to your point about technology, because the cost makes the difference. But then you look at that versus what is needed. We are living through an El Niño year right now, giving us a flavor of what global warming will look like in five or 10 years time.

This year will be the hottest year, and then next year is likely to break that record again, because El Niño is going to continue. In the face of what we are seeing in rising impacts, are there ways in which finance can come to help on adaptation, for example?

There was a typhoon recently here in the southwest of China, there were massive heatwaves in Europe over the summer, five or six of them continuously, and we don't have air conditioning like you guys have here in Hong Kong. Are there ways in which finance can help adaptation?
Ma Jun

Yeah, let me talk about two climate resilience issues. One is the heatwaves you're talking about. The other one is water shortages. We can address it with very cheap energy here, cheap solar energy. Chinese solar power, if you deploy properly, in fact, in one of the pilots my institute has done, within my institute, we generated power at about 30 cents-renminbi per kilowatt, which is about $0.04. It's five times the price in the UK and Europe. If it's cheap, everybody has air conditioning. If it's too expensive, you can't afford it. Make it cheaper, the technology is available, it’s just a matter of deployment. I think heatwaves are not a problem here, as long as you can arrange cheap power that's being deployed in every corner of the country.

Water, as I said, we've got a lot of water technologies, especially in the portfolio that we're proposing to promote in the green accelerator. We have at least 10 technologies. For example, the water saving technology for agriculture, which is called smart irrigation, reduces use of water 30-40%, while at the same time increasing crop yields by 20%. Also, what they call rain enhancement technology. Basically, in a place that's close to a desert, you can shoot sound waves into the sky, and it rains within 30 minutes. And climate resilient seeds, which mean that you can plant new seeds that could be rice or wheat that reduce the use of water by 30-40% as well. There are many, many technologies available. Just deploy them, it will address a large part of the drought problem.
Akshat Rathi

If I'm taking one big message from our discussion is that you started as a macroeconomist and you focused on green finance, but so much of what you talk about now is how to enable finance to really unlock technology deployment. Because the technologies that have been developed it’s really the deployment of these technologies that is uneven and that needs to be sped up in different parts of the world. Do your colleagues in finance see it the same way? Or are you evangelizing in a place where others aren't seeing it?
Ma Jun

This is exactly what I told a lot of bankers last night at the HSBC event. I see most of the bankers, they're sitting there waiting for the technology companies to come to them, waiting for the bankable projects to come to them. But what we need now is we go out and create bankable projects. This requires the bankers to know technology and understand the new technologies that can reduce the cost of services and production so that we can assemble these projects.

The real problem, especially the global south’s system of finance, is that they don't lack money, but they lack bankable projects. In fact, I quoted a number yesterday saying that 90% of the green projects proposed to the local banks in emerging markets are being rejected, which means that we need a lot of service, a lot of help making these projects more bankable, especially using the proper technology.
Akshat Rathi
Thank you, Ma Jun.
Ma Jun
Thank you very much.
Akshat Rathi

And thank you for listening to Zero. This episode was recorded live at Hong Kong Green Week. Now for the sound of the week. That's not the sound of a chainsaw chopping through a tree. That's the sound of a lyrebird, an incredible natural mimic that lives in Australia.

If you liked this episode, please take a moment to rate and review the show on Apple Podcasts YouTube and Spotify. This episode was produced by Oscar Boyd. Special thanks to the team at BloombergNEF and also to Sommer Saadi, Ishika Mookerjee and Alyssa McDonald. I’m Akshat Rathi, back soon.

items.title: Small City in Greece Hopes Huge Data Center Will Revive Local Economy
body: The central square in Kozani has what you’d probably expect from a small Greek city. There’s an Orthodox church, the mayor’s office and a crop of tavernas and cafes. There’s little to suggest it lies at the heart of a transition that the country has a lot riding on.

Where lignite coal was once heaped to feed a power station near Kozani, electricity provider Public Power Corporation SA plans to build one of Europe’s largest data centers. It’s part of a €5.8 billion ($6.7 billion) investment to turn the former lignite mining area into a technology and clean energy hub.

It’s also the sort of project that’s spawned protest movements from Sacramento to Scotland amid claims that they drain power, water and land. In Kozani, though, it’s being seen as a potential lifeline, a test of Europe’s ability to scale up in a place that might actually welcome  a data center, and of faith in the Greek government ahead of elections expected next spring.

Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis has gone all-in on Kozani’s regional regeneration. As well as the hopes of one of Greece’s poorest regions, it reflects the revival of PPC, which raised money from the stock market this year.
The company, whose biggest shareholder is the Greek state, accounts for about 40% of the Western Macedonia’s economic output and the aim is to ensure that most of that is replaced by new activity.
“The most important thing is to give the region prospects,” said Theodoros Pilalidis, a pensioner in Kozani who worked for 33 years in PPC’s lignite mines. “That’s not the case so far.”

Indeed, locals complain that since the government declared an end of lignite power plants in 2019, the jobs haven’t yet arrived that are needed to mitigate the impact. Mitsotakis said on a visit to the region last month that more, better jobs would come as he promised “to mobilize all available European resources so that we can support Western Macedonia in this truly difficult transition.”

In the meantime, the lignite-fired Agios Dimitrios plant 18 kilometers from Kozani has ceased operations after a gradual decommissioning. PPC said that 58 workers remain there compared with 420 at the start of the year.
Lignite mining, meanwhile, has all-but finished, with any remaining coal going to feed PPC’s other big plant in the area, Ptolemaida V. That facility will stop using lignite by the end of the year.
Kozani Mayor Yiannis Kokkaliaris lauded the data center and energy projects planned for his region. But he questioned whether they’ll be enough to offset job losses.

“No one is saying that the units should not be closed, but they should tell us exactly what will happen the next day in our region,” the 49-year-old mayor said in an interview in his office in July before Mitsotakis’s visit. “If there were a similar business that would be better environmentally with 3,000 employees and the same or similar salaries, there would be no problem.”

Kozani is very much a company town. Everyone knows someone who works for PPC or is related to them. At the peak in 2010, PPC employed about 5,500 people in the Western Macedonia region. The region is also famous for its saffron, though that industry employs a fraction of the people.

“We’re ready for the next step,” said Paraskevi Georgiou, 50, who works at the Ptolemaida power plant. Her father was also a PPC employee and she has worked for the company since 2010. “So far, PPC has not shown us that it has abandoned us or that it’s not by our side, or that it will leave us to an uncertain future.”
Walk a little further from Kozani’s busy central square and the boarded-up storefronts betray signs of better times.

Some 650 shops out of a total of 1,500 have now closed, said Athanasios Dragatsikas, head of Kozani’s trade association and owner of a department store in the city’s center. Young people have been abandoning the area in droves.
“The worst thing you can do to people is to make them feel despair,” Dragatsikas said on the top floor of his department store. “They have seen nothing all these years, not even a little light.”
The government and PPC say that’s going to change as Greece scales up to cater to demand for AI.

The company, whose future was in doubt when Greece decided to phase out lignite, will develop the 300-megawatt data center in Kozani by the end of 2028 in addition to green energy projects in the area. The center will be designed with the potential to expand to a gigawatt by 2031.

PPC is currently in talks with so-called hyperscalers to find a company that would lease the data center. One of the key selling points is that the power supply will be provided through PPC’s regional energy network under a long-term power purchase agreement without putting pressure on Greece’s electricity grid. The data center is expected to need about 0.6% of the water the lignite operations required, PPC said.

Demand for data centers in Europe continues to accelerate, driven by AI. But growth is increasingly constrained by energy availability and grid readiness, according to the European Data Centre Association. The number of data centers worldwide has grown from 500,000 in 2021 to about 8 million today, with electricity consumption nearly doubling from 2022 to 2026.

“The multipliers in the economy from the creation of a data center are very large,” said Alexandros Soumelidis, a former manager of one of the plants near Kozani who now oversees PPC’s development projects in the region.

Locals are also no strangers to impact on the environment. For decades, they were used to living in a place where for a lot of the time, smoke from burning coal replaced clouds. What concerns them is whether there will be jobs that can halt an exodus to Athens or Thessaloniki, Greece’s biggest cities, or abroad.

“We welcome any investment that comes here — it’s jobs,” said Giannis Fasidis, president of the Spartakos PPC workers labor union said. Only one thing is non-negotiable, he said, that any project must be done by PPC employees.

Currently, PPC has around 1,250 workers in the region. At the peak of construction work, some 7,500 workers will be required, Soumelidis said. The projects will create at least 2,200 permanent jobs, of which 1,500 people will be needed for the data center operation when it reaches 1 GW, he said.
The transition is also designed to shift the focus of the local economy toward startups and IT businesses.

PPC is working with the University of Western Macedonia in Kozani to create educational programs that will help students become specialists in what the new projects will need. Just as the company created a satellite economy around lignite mining and power generation, the next one will be around the new data center, said Theodoros Theodoulidis, the university’s rector.

“What is missing from the region is a large investment to change the psychology,” said Theodoulidis, whose father was a lignite miner. Apart from PPC’s projects, there’s nothing else, “so we must embrace this large investment.”
