items.title: The French Election Is Ignoring the Bond Market
body: The chief executive officer of insurance company AXA SA, Thomas Buberl, didn’t mince words Tuesday about the severity of France’s debt problem as global bond yields rise and the country’s risk premium over Germany hits its highest level in more than a decade. He called for reforms to get public finances under control and said a proposal by the far left to cancel debt held at the central bank was “dangerous” and “play(ing) with fire.”
He’s right, of course. But even as the clock ticks down to a presidential election in the spring, one wonders who’s listening.

A weekend poll showing French voter concerns suggests the country’s debt mountain, rising interest bill and persistent deficits have yet to fully cut through as an urgent priority. Concern about public finances is rising, but remains below the cost of living, the future of the social safety net, immigration levels and the environment. While markets flash red over France’s elevated borrowing costs and the government searches for billions in savings, the public is focused on the price of gasoline rising past 2022 levels and fishermen are protesting over pay.

The same poll showed a profound desire for change — but not of the pragmatic reformist kind that might benefit Emmanuel Macron’s would-be successors in the political center. The two presidential frontrunners right now are of the revolutionary variety and see no bond-market ships. Far-right leader Marine Le Pen is still promising to cut the retirement age to 62 from 64 and to save money by reducing immigration and spending on Europe. Far-left firebrand Jean-Luc Melenchon, polling just ahead of center-right contender Edouard Philippe in the No. 2 spot, has gleefully discovered that all the rational pushback in the world can’t extinguish a deceptively simple idea like canceling debt.

And then there’s the center itself, so inaudible that the cover of French magazine L’Express dismissed its candidates as “The Extras.” Former Macronist premier Philippe is the closest in theory to a reformist, but his entourage is nervous about running on a bean-counter platform; the result is a hesitant campaign with plenty of technical details, part of a self-described “tortoise strategy.” Center-left candidate Gabriel Attal, another former Macronist prime minister, is a fan of headline-grabbing trial balloons such as legalizing surrogacy. Together, their poll numbers would be enough to make the runoff, provided one pulls out to endorse the other; but Le Pen is the current favorite to win, whomever she faces.

This is surreal stuff. An optimist might say there’s still time for things to change. Seriousness tends to arrive late in French elections, after the primaries and polls weed out the minnows and consolidate a crowded field. The current government under Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu is also speaking honestly about what rising bond yields mean for the developed world’s biggest public spender, telling ministers in not so many words that there is no money left. The cost of servicing French debt is set to rocket to €65 billion ($75 billion) this year, broadly equivalent to its defense budget.

A realist might question whether the bond market entering the chat, as it were, will make enough of a difference. France is a land of near-ubiquitous fixed-rate mortgages, meaning tighter financial conditions take time to trickle down to homeowners. Meanwhile, anxious consumers are already cutting back and relying on savings, in keeping with twin pressures of inflation and near-recessionary economic growth. This is an electorate that might have trouble hearing the necessary message: The French work less and retire earlier than their European counterparts, pension outlays of approximately half the budget deficit are too high and taxing the private sector won’t fix the problem.

The other issue is that the centrist candidates know this so well that they have given up trying to hit on a radical message of their own. Talking up reform potential or criticizing populist ideas is an invitation to be dubbed part of the “failed system” that has driven France to its current ruinous state (a taunt that is admittedly hard to rebut). The result is a preference for a decent and reasonable set of half measures that promise a silent and painless age of fiscal rehabilitation rather than a short, sharp shock. That message has remained inaudible over the angry din.

If the AXA CEO’s words should be a call to arms for anyone, it’s the political center. Its cluster of candidates seems to be operating on an iOS from a decade ago, when geopolitics was predictable and inflation benign. Recent polls tracking favorability ratings in Europe put leaders like the UK’s Andy Burnham, Denmark’s Mette Frederiksen and Italy’s Giorgia Meloni on top — while clearly from different political camps, their ability to capture issues like the cost of living, immigration and realpolitik should be studied by France’s centrist contenders. The candidates must also try to give the French a clear destination or vision, however painful or long the economic path to get there.
As Buberl says, the extremes of French politics are indeed playing with fire — but the extinguisher has yet to be found.

items.title: AI Boom: How to Stop Data Centers From Taking Too Much Electricity
body: The rapid expansion of data centers has become one of the most tangible expressions of the artificial intelligence revolution. But debate about their environmental, economic and social impact threatens their future development. And rightly so. Although the digital economy is often seen as weightless, every cloud service and AI application depends on massive physical infrastructure that takes up land, consumes energy, uses water and requires ever-increasing investment.

International experience suggests that as the data center industry scales up, tensions emerge. In Ireland, data centers accounted for 21% of the country’s electricity consumption in 2023 and could reach 32% this year. In the US, their share of demand is expected to triple from 4% in 2023 to a projected 12% by 2028. No surprise, then, that this is a source of growing political and public concern. A Gallup poll found that 71% of Americans oppose data center construction in their local community.

Beyond concerns over energy and water consumption, evidence increasingly points to other unwelcome local effects. Researchers at Cambridge University have identified what they call a “data heat island effect,” whereby large facilities can raise temperatures in surrounding areas. And a recent study by researchers from Yale and the University of Chicago found that the development of a new data center is associated with an increase in nearby housing prices.
Given these realities, the question isn’t whether data centers are needed — they are — but how they are developed. What type of data centers do we need? And who will govern their expansion?

Economic experience teaches a simple lesson: that proactive regulation is more effective than reactive intervention. And it’s certainly much better than no intervention at all. Having clear rules from the start makes it possible to separate responsible projects from unsustainable ones, align private incentives with public interests and ensure that investment and growth go hand in hand with protecting critical resources and communities.

International experience is, again, instructive. Ireland tightened its rules only after data centers became a major source of pressure on the electricity grid. In the US, the state of New York has adopted a temporary moratorium, and a growing number of projects have faced delays or cancellation as local resistance intensified. The lesson could not be plainer: Failing to plan and regulate up front ends up being costlier and less effective.

Spain is still a long way from facing that kind of pressure. And yet, our healthy economy and renewable capacity has sparked huge investor interest in building data centers, meaning their energy needs are certain to outstrip expectations. Current estimates of electricity demand for computing power run as high as 4 gigawatts by 2030, but requests and permits granted for this type of facility exceed that target several times over.

While many of these projects are unlikely to materialize, the rapid upward trend is obvious. We are approaching a tipping point, and we must act to stay ahead. In August, my government launched a public consultation on a new regulatory framework designed to do exactly that. The proposal starts from a straightforward principle: Access to the electricity grid is a scarce strategic asset and should not be held up by projects that lack credibility, viability or a meaningful contribution to the economy and society.
Our proposal introduces energy- and water-efficiency standards. Data centers will have to disclose key performance indicators, letting us assess and compare their resource use and discourage waste.

Any increase in electricity demand must also be accompanied by additional renewable capacity. The framework includes requirements to make sure that a significant portion of data center consumption is supported by newly built clean-energy projects. The logic is economic and environmental.
Large new power consumers should not compete with existing demand or drive greater reliance on fossil fuels; they should help catalyze investment in the energy transition.

The regulation recognizes, too, that data centers are a strategic asset. In a world where Europe still relies heavily on non-European digital capabilities, the framework combines safeguards on how data is controlled — and how the infrastructure is managed — with incentives designed to expand Europe’s technology sector and strengthen the continent’s sovereignty.

Our objective must be to trade in bytes, not in watts. Spain wants to fully capture the opportunities created by data centers and AI. Yet the challenge is making sure the infrastructure expands in line with the capacity of the power system, that valuable energy resources are directed toward useful projects and that this all makes Europe less dependent technologically.

The goal is not to slow down growth or constrain innovation. Quite the opposite: It is to ensure that they remain economically sustainable, and environmentally and socially fair. Countries that understand this will be the ones best positioned to lead the next phase of the digital economy.

items.title: Ethiopia Bourse Approves 11 New Listings, With One Next Week
body: The Ethiopian Securities Exchange has given in-principle approval for 11 listings, almost tripling the number of publicly traded firms if all of them come to market.

The first of the firms, which operates in the financial-services industry, will begin trading next week, Chief Executive Officer Yodit Kassa said in an interview in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi, declining to identify the company.
“If all goes well, early January we should see at least six of them coming to the market,” she said on the sidelines of the Sustainable Capital Markets Conference.
ESX, as the bourse is known, currently has six listings comprising Ethio Telecom S.C. and five lenders: Abay Bank S.C., Awash Bank S.C., Bank of Abyssinia S.C., Gadaa Bank S.C. and Wegagen Bank S.C.

The exchange debuted in January 2025 to help attract capital into an economy that has been largely closed to foreign investment for decades. It has a total of 22 market intermediaries including seven investment banks.

State-owned Ethio Telecom, the first company to launch an initial public offering, is attracting a lot of interest from Ethiopians in the diaspora, who had been locked out because IPO was restricted to investors within the Horn of Africa nation, Yodit said.

ESX began a money market three months before it started trading in stocks. About $23 billion has been transacted on the interbank market in the past 18 months. It also has 48 treasury bills listed on the bourse although secondary-market trading is yet to take place.

“We are able to see opportunities around the debt market, which is not what exchanges focus on,” Yodit said. “We still have more to do because we haven’t seen activity on the secondary market for T-bills.”

items.title: Czechs Set to Hold Rates as Energy Risks Boost Tightening Bets
body: Czech policymakers are poised to hold interest rates for a second meeting, even as concerns over surging oil prices and a widening budget deficit fuel bets on more tightening to come.
The Czech National Bank will hold the benchmark rate at 3.75% on Thursday, according to the forecasts of all economists in a Bloomberg survey.

Officials delivered their first hike in four years in June to help tame price growth. But while headline inflation in August remained below target, the central bank said last week that the “elevated” outlook for 2027 warranted “increased caution in monetary policy.”
Money market rates indicate that investors have boosted bets on more hikes after the Middle East hostilities pushed the Brent crude price back above $100 a barrel this month.

A widening budget deficit is adding to concerns about the impact of soaring energy prices as Prime Minister Andrej Babis’s government seeks to ramp up spending on infrastructure, health care and defense. The billionaire premier himself reiterated his criticism of the central bank’s “incomprehensible” policy this week, saying high mortgage rates are making housing less affordable.
Read more: Czechs Plan Second-Highest Budget Gap Ever to Boost Investment

Still, central bank officials are also closely watching core inflation, which excludes the most volatile items like food and energy. That measure has been hovering near 3% due to strong domestic demand, suggesting price pressures haven’t been “completely trampled into the ground,” board member Jan Kubicek was quoted by the Novinky.cz website last week.

Forward rate agreements indicate market expectations of at least one more quarter-point hike this year and about four such increases in total within the next 12 months, though Kubicek said that seemed “excessive.”
Economists at Komercni Banka AS said that while the benchmark would probably remain at its current level for an extended period of time, more hikes couldn’t be ruled out.

“Energy-related risks and a public finance deficit of 3.5% of gross domestic product next year, compared with the central bank’s August forecast of 2.9%, are skewing the risk of the CNB tightening its monetary policy further,” Komercni Banka analyst Jaromir Gec said in a note.

items.title: Australia's Housing Slump to Slow Economy, Assist RBA, HSBC Says
body: Australia’s housing downturn is set to weigh on economic growth and help the Reserve Bank in its campaign to drag inflation back to its 2-3% target band, according to HSBC Holdings Plc.

HSBC’s Paul Bloxham pointed to a series of channels through which a deteriorating property market will cool the economy, headlined by the negative wealth effect, in a research note released Thursday. Under this, a 5% fall in housing typically weakens consumer spending by 0.8% over two years.
Based on HSBC’s forecast 13% peak-to-trough drop in home prices, this would see 1% less gross domestic product “over time,” he said.
Other factors include:

Governor Michele Bullock has been upfront that the RBA’s three interest-rate increases from February to May are aimed at slowing economic growth to ease price pressures. Economists and traders reckon the bank will hike again as soon as late this month to take the cash rate to 4.6%, exerting more downward pressure on property prices.
Read more: One of World’s Longest Housing Booms Is Cracking in Sydney
The RBA and Bullock have also pointed out that the economy is running up against capacity constraints, further fueling price gains.

“The overall weakening of growth will help the RBA to get inflation to head back to target,” said Bloxham, HSBC’s chief economist for Australia. “In a supply-constrained economy, an economic downturn is needed to get inflation to fall.”
The RBA has been battling to bring underlying inflation down to the 2.5% midpoint of its target for almost five years and only anticipates it will do so in early 2028.

items.title: China's MMG Commits to EU Nickel Supply After Deal Scrutiny
body: The European Commission warned that MMG Ltd.’s proposed purchase of Anglo American Plc’s nickel business may restrict competition and raise costs for stainless steel producers in Europe.

Anglo American agreed last year to sell its nickel operations in Brazil to China’s MMG for as much as $500 million, prompting EU regulators to investigate due to fears that the buyout could jeopardize supplies of ferronickel, a raw material for stainless steel.

In a preliminary opinion on Wednesday, the Commission said it’s particularly concerned that MMG would divert low-carbon ferronickel supply away from European markets, which may result in higher prices for stainless steel.

“Such a diversion of supply, combined with limited alternative supply sources, could adversely affect the price of low-carbon ferronickel” with negative implications for European stainless steel producers and costs, the Commission said.
MMG can now respond to the EU and request an oral hearing. The Commission has until Nov. 30 to make a final decision.

“Blocking this acquisition would create a lose-lose outcome for all stakeholders,” said Troy Hey, MMG’s executive general manager for corporate relations. “Rather than strengthening competition, it threatens to limit investment and jobs in Brazil and remove supply from the market.” He said the company will make a full response to the EU’s objections.

MMG’s acquisition of Anglo’s business would enhance China’s grip on global supplies of nickel, which includes major investments in Indonesia. The Hong Kong-listed firm operates projects from Australia to Africa and South America and is controlled by state-owned mining-to-trading giant China Minmetals Corp.

items.title: Tropical Storm Set to Drench Tokyo Over Long Holiday Weekend
body: A tropical storm in the Western Pacific Ocean is set to strengthen in the coming days and track toward Japan, threatening strong winds and heavy rain over the country’s ‘silver week’ holidays.

Tropical Storm Dujuan is currently 832 kilometers (517 miles) northeast of Guam, and is forecast to rapidly gain power as it passes over very warm waters, according to the US’s Joint Typhoon Warning Center. The system will likely bring heavy rainfall to a part of eastern Japan, including Tokyo, that’s already been drenched by two weeks of record precipitation, raising landslide and flood risks.

Dujuan will be the 10th tropical cyclone to affect Japan since June, a busier-than-usual storm season for the country that’s been fueled by the El Niño weather pattern, according to the Japan Meteorological Agency. It’s forecast to come closest to Japan on Monday, right in the middle of a five-day holiday that runs through Sept. 23. It’s still unclear if the cyclone will make landfall.

“In areas already affected by heavy rain, further rainfall could increase the risk of landslides and river flooding,” said Takahisa Nishikawa, senior decision support meteorologist at Atmospheric G2. “Even an offshore track would not eliminate these risks,” he said, adding that Chiba Prefecture, near Tokyo, could be particularly hard-hit.

The unusually active storm season is already having an economic impact on the country. There was a 10% year-on-year drop in foreign visitors to Japan in August as cyclones disrupted flights. Chiba, an industrial hub, is still recovering from record rains last month.

JTWC and JMA forecasts both show Dujuan charting a path that keeps it offshore as it nears Tokyo early next week. A direct hit is possible though, with the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts estimating a 40% chance of landfall over the Kanto region, which includes Tokyo and Chiba.

Rains are forecast to increase over Kanto from the weekend, and intensify as Dujuan gets closer, according to commercial forecaster Weathernews Inc. The region has already seen the most precipitation on record for the first half of September, the JMA said.

items.title: Indonesia to Review Staff Rotations Linked to Finance Chief Swap
body: Indonesia’s Finance Ministry is reviewing a surprise reshuffle of hundreds of staff that former minister Purbaya Yudhi Sadewa said helped trigger his dismissal.

The ministry will review the recent rotations after considering input from various department heads, newly appointed Finance Minister Suahasil Nazara told reporters late Wednesday after meeting with President Prabowo Subianto in Jakarta.
“We will make sure that there is good coordination and synergy within the Finance Ministry,” he said.

Purbaya last week rotated at least 400 staff across various departments, including large numbers of employees in the ministry’s tax and customs offices, angering their leaders and causing confusion, according to people familiar with the situation. He later said the rotations “partly” contributed to his ouster as minister on Monday.
Read: Indonesian Power Politics, Not Markets, Forced Out Purbaya

At the tax office, some names had been “magically” added to the rotation list despite not having gone through the proper selection process, Tax Director-General Bimo Wijayanto said on the sidelines of a conference in Jakarta on Wednesday, local media reported.

Wijayanto said he and the director general of customs had asked that the planned rotations be delayed or canceled after finding indications that some names had bypassed the selection process, warning that proceeding could send a bad signal to staff who had gone through assessments.
Any tax office rotations that had not followed proper procedures would be canceled, he said.

items.title: Copper Steadies as Traders Shrug Off Fed's Hawkish Rate Signals
body: Copper steadied as traders shrugged off hawkish messaging from the Federal Reserve chair following a widely expected interest rate hike.

Futures were little changed on the London Metal Exchange as the dollar strengthened. Policymakers at the US central bank penciled in an additional increase for later this year, a potential headwind for non-yielding assets like metals.

Copper is still consolidating after a long run to a record last week, driven by bets the US would hit the refined metal with tariffs. That sucked vast quantities into American stockpiles, triggering concerns about a supply squeeze elsewhere.

So far the US has held off on new trade measures, putting that rally in doubt. Expectations of high demand from data centers and renewable energy, as well as supply disruptions at key mines, are still providing support.

“Reports of no US copper tariffs unwound some of the physical market speculation,” RBC Capital Markets analyst Sam Crittenden said in a note. “Despite near-term price weakness, fundamentals remain constructive.”
Copper was 0.2% lower at $14,202.50 a ton on the LME at 10:30 a.m. in Singapore. Other metals were mixed, with aluminum down 0.5% while nickel added 0.4%.
Iron ore futures rose 0.2% to $96 a ton in Singapore.

items.title: Tata Sons Board Takes Up RBI's IPO Mandate and a Leadership Dilemma
body: Good morning... I’m Alex Gabriel Simon in Mumbai, where Tata Sons’ board meeting is set to take center stage.The stakes are high as the board of Tata Group’s holding company meets Thursday to discuss how to handle a share listing mandated by India’s central bank, and whether outgoing Chairman Natarajan Chandrasekaran should be asked to stay on. We bring you more details on that below.The other big focus for investors is the National Stock Exchange of India Ltd.’s long-awaited initial public offering. The bourse starts taking orders Thursday, testing investor appetite for a valuation that remains rich compared with some of the world’s biggest listed exchanges.The benchmark NSE Nifty 50 advanced 0.4% on Wednesday. The fact that it was the biggest daily gain in about three weeks says something about just how lackluster the market has been, with foreign investors once again turning net sellers of Indian stocks in September. They were buyers in the previous two months.Meanwhile, global markets have largely taken in stride the Federal Reserve’s widely expected interest-rate hike, its first since 2023. A further decline in oil prices has helped buoy investor sentiment.In today’s newsletter, we write about:

Tata Sons’ board meets today with two pressing issues on the table: how to respond to the Reserve Bank of India’s IPO directive, and whether outgoing Chairman Natarajan Chandrasekaran should be asked to stay on. We answer three important questions.
Why has the meeting taken on greater significance?

The RBI’s refusal to ease listing rules for Tata Sons has turned what was a routine board meeting into a discussion over whether the company should comply with or challenge the central bank’s decision. It has sought to preserve its closely held structure, which allows Tata Trusts to retain control and limits public disclosure.
Could Tata Sons challenge the RBI?

The board is expected to discuss whether to comply or seek legal relief. The central bank has filed a caveat in the Bombay High Court, ensuring its position is heard if Tata Sons approaches the court. One consolation, if any, for the Tata group is that the RBI has not given a timeline for the IPO.
Why is Chandrasekaran’s future back in focus?

A last-minute addition to the meeting agenda is a discussion of the Nomination and Remuneration Committee’s recommendations, according to people with knowledge of the matter. The so-called NRC is expected to recommend asking Chandrasekaran to reconsider his decision to step down, the people added, asking not to be identified discussing internal matters.
Brokerages may have to rethink pricing model

India’s retail stockbrokers are facing another potential squeeze on profitability with the introduction of merchant discount rates on UPI payments. Currently, brokers allow clients to transfer money into trading accounts without charge. Rules require brokers to periodically return unused client funds to their bank accounts. However, with charges on UPI, this could come at a cost “without any incremental benefit or revenue,” Zerodha co-founder Nithin Kamath said in a social media post. Industry players say the added expense could force some brokers to rethink their pricing and payment strategies. Firms may encourage clients to use funding channels such as net banking or reassess brokerage charges and free services as margins come under pressure.
Two-wheeler stocks rally on recovery in exports

Two-wheeler stocks have outperformed a Nifty gauge of auto stocks by a wide margin since the start of July, helped in part by a recovery in exports across Latin America, Africa and Asia. According to Kotak, demand in Latin America has been supported by motorcycles being used for work, while Africa has benefited from a strong motorcycle-taxi market and better access to foreign currency. In Asia, dealers rebuilding inventories has also helped. Kotak expects the pace to cool from fiscal 2028 as pent-up demand fades and comparisons get tougher. It also sees TVS growing faster than Bajaj, largely because more of the next leg of growth is expected to come from Africa, where the former has a stronger presence.
Strong SIP flows to underpin asset managers’ growth: Antique

The mutual fund industry’s assets kept growing in August, helped by fresh inflows and market gains. According to Antique, investors continued to favor small-cap, mid-cap and flexible equity funds, while large-cap funds saw outflows for a second straight month. Passive products also gained ground, with gold and silver ETFs seeing particularly strong demand. SIP contributions hit a new high, underlining the steady rise in retail participation. Antique remains positive on asset managers, citing the shift of household savings into financial products and deeper SIP adoption. Top pick: Nippon Life India Asset Management. The brokerage has trimmed earnings estimates for ICICI Prudential AMC and HDFC AMC, citing softer equity inflows.

India’s biggest stocks may be set for a comeback after lagging the broader market. A record 65% of the members of the Nifty 500 have beaten the index over the past six months, as weakness in the biggest stocks has dragged on the benchmark. If history is any guide, that trend may start to reverse as higher-rate worries at home make investors more cautious and inclined to favor large stocks. Also, oil’s rise above $100 a barrel is adding to those concerns by stoking inflation, while higher global bond yields are making stocks less attractive. Smaller stocks could be hit harder in such a setting because their valuations rely more heavily on expectations of strong earnings growth.

items.title: Australia Targets Family Visas, Overstayers to Cut Migration
body: Australia’s center-left government is moving to reduce immigration, planning a clampdown on people who have overstayed their visas as well as restricting most student-visa holders from bringing family members into the country.

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke outlined the changes in a long-delayed speech to the National Press Club on Thursday titled “The work of managing the migration program: Who arrives, who stays, who leaves.”

The government will target people who skip from one visa class to another, students and temporary workers, as well as their family members, according to a statement from Burke. It will also introduce a “no further stay” condition to all visitor visas, in an attempt to ensure that these are genuinely temporary and don’t become a pathway to staying long-term.
It will also do more to detain and deport those whose visas have expired, with Burke saying he expected that effort would encourage other overstayers to leave.
“Almost everyone who comes to Australia is a good guest in our country,” Burke said. “These reforms are to ensure that our migration system can be better targeted to the current needs of Australia.”

Australia is aiming to cap net migration this fiscal year at about 245,000 people — a target set in the budget in May — falling to 225,000 people in the following year. The government has repeatedly overshot its target for migrant numbers, opening it up to criticism from the political right.

More than 292,000 people moved permanently to Australia in the year through the end of March, according to data released Thursday morning before the speech. That was a decline of almost 6% compared to the preceding 12 months.

The new plan will use changed rules to target skilled migration at key sectors, including healthcare, construction, education, law enforcement, defense, resources, agriculture, aquaculture and fishing, according to the statement.

Authorities plan to limit the number of people who are in the country on working-holiday visas, which are popular with backpackers, instituting a ballot for those who wish to continue on these visas for a second or third year, Burke said in his speech. The government had already slowed or paused the issuance of new “working holiday” visas.

While there is popular demand and political agreement that immigration should be lowered, there’s also concern from industry that it will lead to fewer workers, and there was a swift backlash to the announcement.

The agricultural industry called it a “low blow” that risked food security, and regional economies. “Working holiday makers fill about one in seven farm jobs making them central to getting food and fiber produced, harvested, packed and into supermarkets,” National Farmers Federation President Hamish McIntyre said in a statement.

Independent lawmaker Helen Haines from rural Victoria state told parliament Wednesday that her district is experiencing a worker shortage, and asked the government to speed up approvals for some categories, including nurses, to come to Australia.
Read more: Far-Right Firebrand Rises in Australia After 30 Years on Fringes

Earlier this week, the far right One Nation party proposed cutting the number of temporary migrants by 750,000 over three years to drive down the country’s population, before returning to a policy of allowing 130,000 people to move permanently to Australia each year.

items.title: Russia Taps North Korean Workers to Make Drones Under Fake Visas
body: Russia is increasingly mobilizing North Korean workers to build military drones for use against Ukraine in defiance of international sanctions, giving Pyongyang a key source of revenue to fund its unlawful weapons programs, the US and its allies said in a report.

Up to 25,000 North Koreans are believed to be working in Russia’s drone industry, including at facilities in Alabuga, Tatarstan, where unmanned aerial vehicles are assembled, the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team said in a report released Wednesday.

The report said North Korean workers abroad are estimated to have earned up to $800 million for the Kim Jong Un regime last year, providing funds for its unlawful nuclear and ballistic missile programs in violation of UN Security Council resolutions.

The development underscores how the deepening military ties between Russia and North Korea are expanding beyond weapons and troops into labor and industrial production. Russia gets a new pool of workers for industries supporting its war in Ukraine, while Kim’s regime gains access to foreign currency that helps finance its nuclear and ballistic missile programs, further eroding a sanctions framework Moscow itself once helped enforce.

North Korean workers in Russia are disguised as students under a visa scheme to evade sanctions, the report said. A North Korean worker there earns an average of $7,500 in wages a year, most of which is confiscated by the Kim regime. In some cases, the forfeited amount exceeds their actual earnings, the report said.
Read more: Kim Jong Un Flouts Sanctions to Amass $22 Billion Windfall

Monthly wages earned by North Koreans working in Russia may be up to five times higher than what they can earn in China, making Russia an increasingly lucrative destination for Pyongyang. At the end of 2025, an estimated 20,000 to 70,000 North Korean laborers were working in China, while another 15,000 to 30,000 were in Russia, the report said.

“DPRK authorities exercise extreme control over laborers’ movement and interactions with outsiders in order to prevent defections, while laborers who do defect risk reprisals against family members remaining in North Korea,” it said. DPRK is the abbreviation for North Korea’s official name, the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea.
Read more: North Korea’s Nuclear Arsenal Is Outgrowing US Missile Defenses

The US and its allies, including South Korea and Japan, are part of an 11-nation team that monitors the enforcement of sanctions on North Korea. The group was launched after a Russian veto in 2024 ended the mandate of a United Nations panel that had reported on North Korea’s sanctions evasion and development of its nuclear arsenal for 15 years.
items.title_zh: 俄罗斯利用朝鲜劳工持假签证制造无人机
items.summary_zh: 美国及其盟友称俄罗斯动员多达2.5万名朝鲜工人为其建造无人机，去年为朝鲜创收约8亿美元，用于资助其核与弹道导弹项目。

items.title: Treasuries Gain as Growing Confidence in Warsh Calms Market
body: Global bond yields retreated Thursday as the Federal Reserve’s rate hike and vow to tame inflation calmed a pressured market, leaving traders to look ahead to Friday’s key Bank of Japan decision.

Yields on 10-year Treasuries fell three basis points to 4.99%, ending eight days of gains. Those on similar-tenor notes declined three basis points and less than one basis point in Australia and Japan, respectively.

The average yield on global government bonds climbed to a 19-year high this week as escalating Middle East tensions drove up oil prices, fanning inflation expectations. The Fed raised interest rates by a quarter percentage point in a widely expected move on Wednesday, while the median policymaker projection indicated one more hike later this year.

“The Fed had no choice but to give the market a hike or risk a much bigger bond market selloff,” said Byron Anderson, head of fixed income at Laffer Tengler Investments. “The market narrative is on a collision course with the Fed from here on out, which means more volatility.”

The central bank’s favored inflation gauge stood at 3.7% in July, close to the highest since 2023 and above the Fed’s long-run target of 2%. Warsh said inflation readings during summer don’t tell him that underlying trends have meaningfully improved.

“For the bond market, this is likely to cast a long shadow rather than create a short-lived storm,” said Hebe Chen, a market analyst at Vantage Global Prime. “The front end now has to price the possibility of further Fed tightening, while the long end is already wrestling with inflation, heavy issuance and fiscal concerns — meaning even when the initial volatility settles, the gravitational pull of higher yields may remain.”

While digesting the Fed decision, investors were also shifting their attention to the Bank of Japan as it started its two-day policy meeting on Thursday. All BOJ watchers surveyed by Bloomberg expect the central bank to raise its policy rate to 1.25% from 1%.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has expressed strong support for Japan’s decisive market and monetary steps to address the substantial undervaluation of the yen, according to a readout.

“The chances have risen significantly that the BOJ will hike on Friday and signal further increases” after the Fed’s projections pointed to one more rate hike this year, Eiji Kinouchi, chief technical analyst at Daiwa Securities Co., wrote in a research note. If that happens, “there’s a risk of a repeat” of the surging yen and the slump in Japanese stocks seen in 2024, he wrote.
items.title_zh: 全球债券回升，沃什抗击通胀安抚市场

items.title: Nvidia Partner GMI Cloud Seeks Loan to Buy Chips for Thai Site
body: GMI Cloud, a Nvidia Corp. partner, is seeking a $300 million loan to buy chips for its facility in Thailand, according to people familiar with the matter, adding to a growing list of similar deals in Asia.

The US-based data center operator has approached banks and private credit funds for the financing, said the people who asked not to be identified as the discussions are private. The proposed deal would pay yields in the low-teens, they said.

Proceeds from the self-arranged funding would be used for chip purchases for GMI Cloud’s facility, housed in STT GDC Pte.’s site in Thailand, they said. Tencent Holdings Ltd. would be the user of the chips, they said.
Spokespeople for GMI Cloud and Tencent had no immediate comment when contacted, while a spokesperson for STTGDC declined to comment.

Chip financing is emerging as the next frontier for AI lenders, as banks and private credit expand beyond data centers to the hardware that powers them. GMI Cloud recently signed a NT$13.9 billion ($436 million) loan, backed by contracts for computing power from advanced chips, for a project in Taiwan.
That deal secured bank commitments of more than double the amount sought.
items.title_zh: 英伟达合作伙伴GMI Cloud寻求贷款为泰国工厂购买芯片
items.summary_zh: 英伟达合作伙伴GMI Cloud寻求3亿美元贷款，为泰国数据中心购买芯片，腾讯将是芯片用户。

items.title: Singapore's Gold Hub Plan Gets Lift With DBS Vault Expansion
body: Singapore’s push to become a major gold hub is gaining momentum, with DBS Group Holdings Ltd. adding bullion storage capacity and other banks considering similar moves.

DBS, Southeast Asia’s largest lender, increased its vaulting space this year to support growing demand from both private wealth and institutional clients, the bank said in an emailed response to Bloomberg’s request for comment on Wednesday. Oversea-Chinese Banking Corp. Ltd. has also approached precious metal storage providers about securing more space, according to people with knowledge of the matter.

Deutsche Bank AG is similarly considering an expansion, said another person. The scale of vault growth for the banks is under discussion and plans are subject to change, the people said, asking not to be named as the conversations are private.
Read More: Singapore to Launch Gold Clearing With JPMorgan, Other Banks

Banks typically contract logistics providers to manage storage and movement of gold, though some, including Singapore-based United Overseas Bank Ltd., operate their own vaults. The third parties lease space at private facilities such as Le Freeport, a high-security premises in Singapore dubbed “Asia’s Fort Knox”, which is owned by a crypto billionaire.

Le Freeport has been facing rising demand for gold storage in recent years and its basement vaulting space is nearly full, the operator said in an interview in May. Several people familiar with the matter said some banks may not be able to store bullion in its basement, their preferred location due to its enhanced security and higher load-bearing capacity, which enables more bars to be stacked than on upper floors.
A Deutsche Bank spokesperson declined to comment. An OCBC spokesperson said the bank has seen “steady interest” after it entered the physical gold business, especially from private banking clients.

The expansion of vault capacity is crucial to Singapore’s plan to launch a gold clearing system as part of its push to become a global hub for the precious metal. All clearing banks will need sufficient capacity to store and settle large volumes of bullion.
The city-state’s ambition runs alongside regional rival Hong Kong, which began a trial run of a new clearing system in July while courting foreign banks to store gold.
Read More: Hong Kong Seeks Dominant Asia Gold Hub With New Clearing System

Singapore can currently store at least 2,200 tons at privately-owned facilities; 1,700 at Le Freeport and 500 at The Reserve, according to the operators. Hong Kong has pledged to expand its total storage capacity to 2,000 tons within three years.
items.title_zh: 星展银行金库扩张助力新加坡黄金中心雄心
items.summary_zh: 新加坡推动黄金枢纽建设，星展银行增加金库容量，华侨银行和德意志银行等也在考虑扩充存储空间。

items.title: Casinos Posing as Beauty Salons, Bakeries Spur Philippine Digital Payment Review
body: Electronic payment providers need to be more diligent in vetting companies that use their platforms in order to protect people from fraud, the Philippine central bank said.

The requirement came after Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas found thousands of illegal businesses on the payment platforms, including many online casinos masquerading as more ordinary companies like beauty salons and bakeries.

“We want to protect consumers from online fraud, illegal activities and also from money launderers,” Deputy Governor Mamerto Tangonan said in an interview. “You cannot expand digitalization if people’s money is being stolen” or they’re being scammed.
His comments came after Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas released a draft document that puts the onus on payment service providers to improve screening of the merchants they partner with.

Alarm bells starting ringing for the central bank after surveillance discovered many merchants, which on paper were unremarkable, were accepting thousands of payments of as little as 50 pesos ($0.80) past midnight and into the early hours of the morning, according to Tangonan.

Authorities discovered the payments were bets on online casinos, he said. Mom and pop stores were also among the enterprises used by over 8,000 merchants whose accounts have now been shuttered for allegedly illegal activities.

Philippine Amusement and Gaming Corp. Chairman Alejandro Tengco said the state regulator is aware that many innocuous sounding businesses are in reality unregistered online casinos and is working with the central bank. “Unfortunately, we don’t have control over that,” Tengco said.

The discovery also highlights the problems that arise when e-payments companies use intermediaries, called merchant aggregators, to help them aggressively expand their business. Financial inclusion is a big push in the archipelago of over 7,000 islands, and merchant aggregators are incentivized to link many small — mostly legitimate — businesses in far-flung areas to formal payment channels.

The Philippines central bank will now require payment platforms to collect more information on merchants being linked up, including owner details and licenses. It also wants them to set up databases of legitimate merchants.

Repeated violations could lead to revocation of payment licenses, the central bank official said. “If there are illegal activities and you’re not able to stop it, then you are accountable,” Tangonan said.

Use of online payments in the Philippines has exploded in recent years amid the popularity of mobile wallets like GCash, whose parent Mynt Inc. is set to hold a record initial public offering next month. Maya, a large e-wallet and digital bank operator backed by KKR & Co. and PLDT Inc., is also considering going public.

Maya said the company supports measures that “strengthen the integrity, safety and trustworthiness of the digital payments ecosystem,” adding that Maya has merchant on-boarding, due diligence and monitoring processes in place.

The EMoney Association of the Philippines said the group fully supports the central bank’s goals of safeguarding and improving the country’s payment system. “It is important that there is accountability from the industry to ensure that we have a safe digital ecosystem for the market,” a representative said in a text message. The association is currently reviewing and evaluating the BSP’s proposed circular.

GCash said it backs the BSP’s efforts to protect consumers from illegal and fraudulent merchants. “We remain committed to working closely with regulators and industry partners toward a safer, more trusted, and inclusive digital economy for all Filipinos,” it said.

Digital payments accounted for around two-thirds of total retail transactions in the Philippines in 2025, up from 57% in 2024 and a share of just 10% in 2018, when the central bank started reporting data.
While more stringent due diligence may temporarily slow the expansion of digital payment activities, Tangonan said it should set the sector up for more sustainable growth.
“You shouldn’t sacrifice safety for growth,” he said. “There’s no trade-off there.”

items.summary_zh: 菲律宾央行要求电子支付商加强审查商户，因发现超8000家非法企业借支付平台伪装成美容院等，实为在线赌场。

items.title: Trump Returns to Trail in North Carolina With Senate in Play
body: President Donald Trump visited North Carolina in his first campaign stop since the GOP’s Dallas midterm convention, seeking to boost Republican Senate candidate Michael Whatley, who is trailing Democrat Roy Cooper in the polls.

The race in North Carolina could be critical to determining which party controls the Senate, and the president’s rally at an airfield in Gastonia, outside Charlotte, offered a sign of the deep concern within GOP ranks over their prospects for holding onto the chamber.
“A vote for Roy Cooper is a vote to give control of the US Senate,” Trump said Wednesday, casting the race as having stakes far beyond the state.
“Ultimately, forget about him, he’s not a leader or anything,” Trump continued. “But he’s going to vote, and we can’t lose that vote. It’s too close. He’ll turn around everything.”

Trump’s trip is the kickoff of what he has billed as a nationwide sprint to Election Day with a number of hotly contested races, including many in the Senate. The White House has promised a slew of travel by the president to help his party retain control of Congress in November’s midterm election and Trump himself pledged in Dallas last week that he would be on the trail. Trump’s aides have previously pledged a stepped-up presidential travel schedule that did not materialize.

Polls show Americans have soured on Trump’s handling of the economy and the war in Iran, which has pushed up fuel prices across the country. Republicans currently have slim majorities in the House of Representatives and the Senate. A takeover by Democrats in one or both chambers would lead to curbs on Trump’s agenda and investigations that have been absent during the first two years of his second term.
In the Tar Heel State, Trump recited many well-worn Republican criticisms of Cooper that have so far failed to close the polling lead the Democrat has enjoyed throughout the race to date.

Trump has repeatedly sought to cast Democrats as too extreme for most voters. He assailed Cooper, a former North Carolina governor, on crime, targeting pandemic-era releases of some prisoners, and his response while in office to the devastation brought by Hurricane Helene.
Cooper’s campaign refuted claims Trump and Whatley have made about his record, including about the former governor’s record on crime and hurricane recovery.

“Independent fact-checkers have called these attacks false – Michael Whatley is getting desperate and it’s shameful that he’s using heinous crimes to try to deceive North Carolinians,” Cooper spokesman Jordan Monaghan said in a statement. He also faulted Whatley for his role in federal storm recovery efforts.

Election analysts rate North Carolina as Democrats’ best chance to pick up a Senate seat in November, even though it’s a state Trump carried in all three of his presidential runs. Cooper leads Whatley by 7.8 points, according to polling average by RealClearPolitics as of Wednesday afternoon, as they battle to replace retiring GOP Senator Thom Tillis.
Polls show Trump’s approval at record lows and Whatley’s decision to tie himself closely to the president brings its own risks in a swing-state.

Trump has urged Republicans around the country to pretend that he is on the ballot in an effort to boost turnout among his loyal political base, an appeal he made again Wednesday. And he touted his pledge to offer a $5,000 dividend to Americans if his party holds both chambers of Congress, though with a price tag topping $1 trillion the idea has been met with bipartisan skepticism.
items.title_zh: 特朗普重返北卡罗来纳州竞选，参议院席位成焦点
items.summary_zh: 特朗普赴北卡罗来纳州为共和党参议员候选人拉票，该州选情可能决定参议院控制权，目前民主党对手民调领先。

items.title: NSE's $2.4 Billion India IPO Opens With Valuation in Focus
body: National Stock Exchange of India Ltd.’s long-awaited initial public offering starts taking orders Thursday, testing investor appetite for a valuation that remains rich compared with some of the world’s biggest listed exchanges.

The shares are being offered at 1,700 rupees to 1,785 rupees a share and will close for subscription on Sept. 21. NSE reduced the number of shares on offer to 126.44 million from 148.9 million planned earlier, according to its updated prospectus. The offering is entirely a sale by existing shareholders, meaning the exchange won’t receive any of the proceeds.
The IPO was subscribed 15% as of 11 a.m. local time, with bids come mainly from retail investors and wealthy individuals, according to data on the BSE Ltd.’s website.

At the top end of the range, the deal is set to raise 226 billion rupees ($2.4 billion), the second-most ever for an IPO in the country behind Hyundai Motor India Ltd.’s 2024 listing, which netted 279 billion rupees. That price would value NSE at about 42.9 times its earnings for the year ended March. While that’s a discount to domestic rival BSE Ltd., it’s well above the roughly 24 to 25 times ratio for some of the world’s largest listed exchanges.

The premium reflects NSE’s dominant position in one of the world’s fastest-growing capital markets and its high profitability. The exchange reported net income of 103 billion rupees on revenue of 166 billion rupees in the year ended March 2026, according to its prospectus, translating into a profit margin of about 62%, above most large global peers.

“NSE is well positioned to benefit from structural tailwinds and remains the best franchise among peers” because of India’s deepening capital markets and rising global investor participation, SBICAPS Securities said in a note to clients.

Still, analysts and investors are divided over whether NSE’s market dominance and growth prospects justify the premium. NSE’s gray-market premium has fallen to about 160 rupees a share from as high as 285 rupees on Sept. 7, according to ipowatch.in.

“While the long-term growth opportunity in India’s capital markets remains favorable, the sustainability of earnings growth will depend on trading activity, regulatory stability and continued market participation,” Religare Broking said in a note to clients as it initiated the stock with a neutral recommendation.

One of the biggest risks is tighter regulatory scrutiny of speculative derivatives trading, a business central to NSE’s profitability. Options trading accounted for about 60% of operating revenue in the year ended March, leaving the exchange exposed to measures aimed at curbing activity in the segment.

NSE first filed for an IPO in 2016, but its listing was delayed by corporate-governance concerns and a co-location controversy, in which some brokers were alleged to have received preferential access to the exchange’s trading systems. The exchange recently settled the cases by paying 14.91 billion rupees.

On Wednesday, investment bankers advising on the deal allocated 37.79 million shares to anchor investors at 1,785 rupees apiece, the top end of the marketed range, raising 67.46 billion rupees, according to an exchange filing.

Goldman Sachs, HSBC, Fidelity and Eastspring were among major investors in the anchor book. Sovereign wealth funds including GIC and Abu Dhabi Investment Authority also participated, the filing showed.

The anchor book also drew strong demand from local mutual funds and insurers. Life Insurance Corp., SBI Funds Management Ltd. and ICICI Prudential Asset Management Co. were among the largest anchor investors.
items.title_zh: 印度国家证券交易所24亿美元IPO启动，估值成焦点
items.summary_zh: 印度国家证券交易所今日启动IPO，发行价1700至1785卢比，拟募资2260亿卢比，估值达42.9倍市盈率，认购率暂为15%。

items.title: Taiwan Holds Rate for 10th Straight Quarter as Inflation Slows
body: Taiwan is expected to hold its benchmark rate for the 10th straight quarter, the longest stretch since 2019, as consumer inflation slows even with the economy soaring on AI.

Some 21 of 28 economists surveyed by Bloomberg expect the Central Bank of Republic of China, as the monetary authority is officially known, to hold the interest rate at 2% when it convenes its quarterly meeting on Thursday.
The seven who predict the central bank soon join the US Federal Reserve and others in the region in tightening foresee a hike of 12.5 basis points.

While Taiwan’s economy has been skyrocketing — it clocked the fastest first-half growth since 1976 on demand for its high-end tech exports like semiconductors — the consumer price index for August was well short of expectations. Power costs in Taiwan have been held in check somewhat because the government has been giving state-owned energy firms subsidies to offset rising costs due to the fighting in the Middle East.

“Softer inflation has given policymakers more room to wait, with headline CPI easing toward the CBC’s 2% alert line as food prices moderated,” Hyosung Kwon, Korea and Taiwan economist for Bloomberg Economics, wrote. Local elections set for November “also argue for patience, as the CBC is likely to avoid any move that could appear politically motivated.”

Kwon added that Taiwan was expected “to begin a gradual tightening cycle in December” because “core inflation remains sticky, while the AI boom is increasingly spilling over from exports into investment, wages and domestic demand.”
Core CPI rose 2.30% in August, while the producer price index surged more than 16.7%, near the highest level in data going back to 2021.

The US Federal Reserve may have given Taiwan another reason to boost its policy rate. A quarter percentage point hike by the Fed on Wednesday — the first since 2023 — could spur the CBC to do the same eventually because any widening of the rate gap with the US spurs capital outflows.
Lenders in Taiwan will welcome a hold by the central bank. Liquidity in the banking system has been tight this summer and a lower rate would allow them cheap access to funding.
items.title_zh: 台湾通胀放缓后料维持鹰派立场
items.summary_zh: 台湾央行预计连续10季维持利率2%，因通胀放缓，尽管AI推动经济飙升。

items.title: Trump Denied Rate Cut as Federal Reserve Targets War-Stoked Inflation
body: A year ago, when Kevin Warsh was angling to lead the Federal Reserve, he called out the central bank for keeping interest rates too high and touted a technological revolution that would spur growth without driving inflation.

The sunny outlook drew comparisons with the 1990s boom overseen by then Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan and helped convince President Donald Trump, who has lashed out at policymakers for not cutting rates, to pick Warsh to run the world’s most important central bank.
Now, less than four months after being sworn in as Fed chairman in May, Warsh has defied skeptics with a unanimous decision to deliver the Fed’s first interest-rate hike in over three years.
That’s as war, tariffs and booming investment into artificial intelligence have stoked inflation and shredded expectations of an easy path to lower borrowing costs.

Trump responded on social media hours after officials raised their policy rate to 3.75%-4%, demanding that rates be quickly cut to 1% or lower. In comments to reporters later, Trump blamed a “very hostile board” and stopped short of criticizing Warsh — a marked difference from the repeated attacks on his predecessor Jerome Powell.

Bond investors had a different reaction than the US president, welcoming the move as a sign the Fed remains independent and committed to fighting inflation. Traders quickly priced in additional rate increases from Warsh and his colleagues and pushed down their expectations for inflation in coming years.

Yields on two-year Treasuries, the maturity most sensitive to Fed expectations, climbed to 4.74%, the highest since 2024. Longer-term Treasuries, which are more vulnerable to inflation, trailed the move — an indication investors’ anticipate the Fed will keep on top of price pressures. Long-term inflation expectations receded and US stocks fell.
“The market is taking this as a much more credible Fed chair,” Jeffrey Rosenberg, a senior portfolio manager at BlackRock, said on Bloomberg Television.

Warsh framed the decision to hike with a delicate dual message of an economy that continues to speed up while inflation remains too high. There was also a clear signal that inflation hits lower-income workers hardest.

Analysts said that was aimed at two audiences: investors seeking assurance that the Fed is serious about curbing inflation and a White House nervous about rising interest rates ahead of crucial elections. In a February interview with NBC, Trump said Warsh “would not have gotten the job” if he had indicated support for higher rates.

While Warsh didn’t signal his preference for what comes next on Wednesday, he made it clear there’s more work to do. “The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long,” Warsh told reporters.

Stress tests are still ahead. The Fed’s next policy meeting in October falls just days before critical mid-term elections and analysts warn if inflation continues to simmer, policymakers may be forced to hike on the eve of the vote.

“I have a little more skepticism that we are seeing a Fed that is on a pathway to significantly higher rates to ensure a return to price stability,” said Lindsey Piegza, chief economist at Stifel Nicolaus & Co.

With inflation exceeding the Fed’s 2% target for over five years, traders had priced in more than a 90% probability of a hike at the September meeting. Whenever expectations for a rate increase have been that high, the Fed has invariably delivered one, according to Bloomberg-compiled data going back to 2008.
The decision capped months of twists and turns by Fed policymakers who had hoped they could hold rates steady and allow inflation more time to return toward their 2% goal.
A decision to leave rates unchanged in July, followed by a press conference by the Fed chairman that investors found unconvincing, sent bond yields soaring.
Warsh — who had a reputation as an inflation hawk when he served as a Fed governor from 2006 to 2011 — then reaffirmed his commitment to returning inflation to target in a speech last month.
In the end, the tipping point came after price pressures in August accelerated more than expected.

Just weeks ahead of the decision to raise rates, key Fed officials had continued to argue that policymakers had time to wait, a dynamic that Olu Sonola, head of US economics at Fitch Ratings, likened to monetary policy whiplash.
“Patience has clearly not worked,” Sonola said.
In a new set of rate projections released Wednesday, Fed officials’ median outlook for interest rates at the end of 2026 rose to 4.1% from 3.8%, signaling growing support for a series of rate hikes.

Nearly all officials — 16 of the 18 who submitted forecasts — penciled in another rate hike this year. Investors see an almost-even chance that it comes before the midterm elections, risking Trump’s ire as Republicans fight to retain control of Congress.
Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, said persistent inflation ultimately left Warsh with little option.
“I don’t envy him,” she said. “But it’s almost easier to do it now than to do it when you’ve really got a problem in December.”
items.title_zh: 特朗普降息请求遭拒 美联储聚焦战争引发的通胀
items.summary_zh: 沃什任美联储主席不到四个月即推动三年多来首次加息至3.75%-4%，特朗普要求降至1%以下，债市欢迎此举。

items.title: Malaysia's Battered Bonds Face Risk of Japan Fund Exodus
body: Malaysia’s struggling bond market may see an outflow of Japanese capital as its yield premium shrinks.

The premium that 10-year Malaysian bonds command over equivalent Japanese notes has shrunk to around 115 basis points, well below the five-year average of 278 basis points as borrowing costs jumped in Japan, data compiled by Bloomberg show. That’s also down about 70% from a 2022 peak.

The Southeast Asian country’s bonds have been under pressure in recent months, due to increased supply and a stronger-than-expected economy that raised the odds of monetary tightening. The weakness may extend if the Bank of Japan delivers a widely anticipated interest rate hike on Friday, a decision set to intensify worries about the departure of Japanese investors holding a record amount of Malaysia debt.

“Malaysia government bonds face pressure from elevated US Treasury yields, while higher Japanese government bond yields raise the opportunity cost of overseas duration, increasing the risk of yen carry-trade unwinds and Japanese repatriation flows,” said Michelle Chia, regional head of treasury and markets research at CIMB Bank.

A selloff in US government debt has deepened in recent weeks, sending the 10-year Treasury yield to the highest in almost two decades this week. Meanwhile, a sharp rebound in the value of yen has upended the once-popular carry trade that involves borrowing cheaply in the Japanese currency to seek higher returns elsewhere.

Japanese investors owned 1.1 trillion yen ($7.1 billion) worth of Malaysian debt securities as of the end of 2025, according to the Bank of Japan’s latest data. This was the largest amount since the data became available in 2014 and constituted 13% of Japan’s total bond investment in Asia. The exposure to Malaysia was higher than that to regional peers such as Thailand, Indonesia and the Philippines.

Japan’s 10-year yield rose to a three-decade high earlier this month, fueled by concerns over inflation and fiscal spending, as well as the prospect of a fresh BOJ rate hike. As Japanese bonds become more attractive, chances are rising for a long-discussed risk for global investors to materialize: the nation’s vast pool of overseas capital returning home.

Even if that prospect doesn’t materialize in the near term, there are enough local factors weighing on Malaysian bonds, especially the growing bets on a hawkish-turning Bank Negara Malaysia. The country’s central bank extended its interest rate pause earlier this month but signaled that borrowing costs could start rising.

The local swaps market is now pricing in an 80% probability of a half-percentage-point rate hike over the next 12 months, versus less than a full quarter-percentage-point at the end of August, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.
The yield on benchmark 10-year Malaysian government paper has risen 54 basis points since the end of June, on track for its biggest quarterly jump in nearly a decade.

Other headwinds for the Southeast Asian nation’s debt market are robust economic growth, inflation risks and fiscal pressures from increased fuel subsidies, said Chandresh Jain, EM Asia rates and FX strategist at BNP Paribas SA. “We anticipate further selloffs in Malaysia bonds.”
items.title_zh: 马来西亚受创债券面临日本基金撤离风险加剧
items.summary_zh: 马来西亚债券较日债收益率溢价缩至约115基点，远低于五年均值278基点，日本央行加息或引发日资撤离，日资持有1.1万亿日元马债。

items.title: BOJ Faces Higher Bar to Support Yen After Fed's Hawkish Hike
body: The yen’s sharp drop after the Federal Reserve’s hawkish hike is raising the stakes for the Bank of Japan’s policy meeting Friday, with strategists warning the currency could weaken further unless officials convince markets that more tightening is coming.

The Fed lifted borrowing costs Wednesday for the first time since 2023 and projected further increases, prompting traders to price three additional hikes by the middle of next year. That threatens to keep the US-Japan rate gap wide even as the BOJ is expected to raise its own policy rate this week.

The yen weakened as much as 1% overnight to 156.42 per dollar in the wake of the Fed move. The reversal comes after a sharp rally earlier this month, fueled by expectations of faster BOJ tightening, an unwind of yen-funded carry trades and speculation that Japanese pension funds could shift more money to domestic assets.

“Japan is certainly facing an enormous amount of pressure to both hike and deliver a hawkish message to minimize the damage,” said Glenn Yin, director of research at ACCM in Melbourne. If the BOJ disappoints, “the 160 level in short order is not a risk you can write off.”

The bar is high. A 25-basis-point increase is almost fully priced by overnight index swaps, leaving traders focused on BOJ Governor Kazuo Ueda’s post-decision press conference for clues on the pace and scope of further tightening. Hawkish board member Hajime Takata has even kept the door open for an outsized interest-rate increase or back-to-back hikes.

The yen’s renewed decline gives the BOJ greater reason to emphasize upside risks to inflation, according to Rinto Maruyama, senior rates and FX strategist at SMBC Nikko Securities. Higher oil prices could provide policymakers with further justification for tighter policy, he said.

Friday’s expected increase would take Japan’s policy rate into estimates of the neutral range, making it unlikely officials will signal either a 50-basis-point move or a sequence of back-to-back hikes, according to Maruyama. He sees 158 as the next upside target for dollar-yen if the meeting is interpreted as dovish.

That leaves the currency vulnerable if investors conclude the BOJ’s tightening cycle will struggle to keep pace with the Fed’s. Over time, Maruyama sees scope for dollar-yen to grind back toward 160 if US rates rise faster than those in Japan.

That said, there are reasons to expect any renewed yen selling to be less aggressive than before. Carry traders were burned by the currency’s recent rally, while hedge funds have already pared bearish positions. Leveraged traders halved their wagers against the yen in the week through Sept. 8, according to Commodity Futures Trading Commission data.

The threat of renewed intervention could also temper the yen’s depreciation. Japan and the US have already shown a willingness to step into the market jointly, while Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has continued to signal support for a stronger yen.

A rate hike Friday may not be enough to support the currency. The central bank “may not adopt a stance as hawkish as the Fed’s, which could serve as an immediate catalyst for yen weakness,” said Akira Moroga, chief market strategist at Aozora Bank Ltd. He sees 158.50 per dollar, around the 200-day moving average, as the next key threshold.

items.title: Thai Protest Leader Who Seized Bangkok Airport Is Back in Action
body: A Thai protest leader whose mass demonstrations nearly 20 years ago closed the capital’s airports and helped oust governments is now focused on Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul, and aims to build a political force capable of outlasting him.

Sondhi Limthongkul, 78, is launching a campaign called “Take Back Thailand,” seeking to harness anger over living costs, corruption, alleged political interference and foreign criminal networks to put sustained pressure on Anutin’s government.
His immediate goal, he says, isn’t to bring it down, but to ensure the administration “can’t live in peace” unless it responds to public demands.

“I want to mobilize Thais across the country, bring together people who are dissatisfied with the government and pressure it to act,” Sondhi told Bloomberg News in his first interview with international media since launching the movement. “I want to give people the tools to demonstrate and question the government.”

Sondhi’s efforts may not pose an immediate threat to Anutin or herald a return of the mass rallies that paralyzed Bangkok in the 2000s and led to the downfall of then-Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra. But they mark the re-emergence of street politics after several years of relative calm and point to discontent building beneath the surface.

Speaking at his Bangkok office, which has become the headquarters of his latest political campaign, Sondhi sat in front of a large painting of himself as he described what he calls his “last mission”: create a permanent counterweight to whoever governs Thailand.

The usual remedies, Sondhi says, don’t work. Forcing out a prime minister just leads to a similar replacement from within the same factions of power. Even amending the constitution, which has happened often, just results in the elites protecting their power structures.

That has been the preferred route of the country’s top opposition group, the People’s Party, which advocates for sweeping political, economic and constitutional reforms. Despite its popularity, the progressive group has never been able to truly gain power. (Sondhi described the party as, in principle, “quite OK.”)

His idea echoes a broader strain of anti-establishment politics elsewhere in Asia, where activists have sought to turn public frustration into movements that endure beyond individual elections or leaders. In India, for instance, the so-called “Cockroach” movement has similarly sought to build a nationwide grassroots network designed to survive political cycles rather than focus on winning a single election.
“I want to create bargaining power for the people,” he said. “No matter who comes after Anutin, they will have to face us. It’s people’s power.”
Taking on disparate issues is part of his strategy: each controversy gives him another opportunity to mobilize supporters and potentially expand the movement beyond his traditional political base.
That might not be as effective as his earlier focus on just Thaksin, according to Yuttaporn Issarachai, lecturer at Sukhothai Thammathirat Open University.

“The risk of an all-issue movement is that it lacks focus. Sondhi’s previous movement had one clear target, Thaksin, and one goal that supporters could rally around,” he said. “Many of the issues he is raising now don’t directly affect people’s livelihoods, making it harder to mobilize them. But if the economy deteriorates and people feel worse off a year from now, that could provide the catalyst for a much broader movement.”

Anutin won a sweeping election victory in February on a promise of stability after years of political discord, helping restore investor confidence and propel Thai stocks into the ranks of the world’s best performers this year.
Asked on Saturday about Sondhi’s movement, Anutin said it could hurt Thai people more than the government.

“Does Sondhi want to make people unhappy?” Anutin said. “This administration is determined to work for the Thai people every second of every day. I believe Thai people are still willing to give me a chance and still believe in my government.”

Sondhi was already one of Thailand’s most colorful tycoons before becoming one of its most consequential protest leaders. He built a sprawling publishing business during the country’s 1990s boom and fashioned himself as an Asian Rupert Murdoch, only to see his heavily indebted media empire battered by the 1997 financial crisis.

Sondhi helped lead the yellow-shirt People’s Alliance for Democracy, a royalist movement backed largely by Bangkok’s middle class, business elites and conservative establishment that mobilized against Thaksin. The former telecom tycoon, who built a formidable electoral base among rural and working-class Thais, was ousted in a 2006 military coup.

In 2008, yellow-shirt protesters occupied Bangkok’s two airports, including Suvarnabhumi, the country’s main international gateway, shutting it for about a week and stranding about three thousand travelers as they sought to force another Thaksin-aligned government from power.

The conflict spawned the rival red shirts, largely supporters of Thaksin and his political allies. Years of competing street protests, court interventions and two military coups helped topple successive governments and entrenched a cycle of political instability that weighed on policymaking and investment.

Thailand is still struggling with the economic consequences of that era. Successive civilian and military governments have failed to reverse a structural slowdown that has left one Southeast Asia’s largest economies lagging many of its regional peers.

Unlike two decades ago, Sondhi is operating without the powerful conservative allies, which had opposed Thaksin’s grassroots political machine. Today, much of that establishment is aligned with or sympathetic to Anutin and his Bhumjaithai Party.
“This government is worse,” he said. “Thaksin only interfered, but Anutin dominates political institutions.”

Despite being branded ultra-conservative much of his career, Sondhi now resists that label and says he doesn’t have to back Anutin just because of his image as a conservative champion. That is, the old yellow-red divide has lost its meaning, as political parties, powerful businesses and other vested interests have become part of an interconnected establishment.

His Facebook following exceeds 5 million, while his Sondhi Talk YouTube channel has about 2.5 million subscribers. His programs range from Thai politics to international affairs and more personal subjects, including his health.

He says Sondhi Talk generates about 100 million views a month across major platforms, with numbers skyrocketing to 171 million views in August as he prepared for mobilization. Yet he acknowledges that converting that digital audience into protesters is harder than mobilizing the television viewers who followed him two decades ago.

That will soon be put to the test. Sondhi plans to travel to several provinces in the coming weeks to rally supporters and build pressure ahead of a Sept. 28 Constitutional Court ruling that could invalidate the results of the February election that returned Anutin to power.

Last week, he offered an early demonstration of his multi-issue approach, leading hundreds of activists to Israel’s embassy in one of Bangkok’s busiest commercial districts to demand action over Israeli visitors he accused of disregarding Thai laws and customs.
Read More: Thailand Presses Israeli Ambassador Over Badly Behaved Tourists
Sondhi has stopped short of calling for Anutin’s removal. But he describes the government as creating the conditions for its own downfall.

“The bad things just keep piling up. Every single thing done by the government is like adding fuel to the inside of the house,” Sondhi said. “People’s dissatisfaction takes time. But one strike of a match, and it would all go up in flames.”
